stem: A vendor sent a fax to a potential buyer offering to sell LED lights at a discount of £2 each per 100 light units ordered, stating that the offer would be kept open until the following Monday. On the Monday morning, the potential buyer replied by fax enquiring whether the vendor would accept 60 for delivery over two months, or if not, the longest time limit it could give. The vendor did not reply and sold the LEDs elsewhere.
ask: Later on Monday, the potential buyer sent a second fax accepting the Which of the following statements best describes the parties' legal position?

options.en: The offer was not open when the potential buyer accepted it, because its second fax amounted to a counter-offer
The offer was still open when the potential buyer accepted it, because its first fax amounted to a mere request for further information
The offer was still open when the potential buyer accepted it, because its second fax amounted to a counter-offer
The offer was still open when the potential buyer accepted it, because its first fax operated as an acceptance of the vendor's offer
The offer was still open when the potential buyer accepted it, because its first fax amounted to a counter-offer

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is the best answer. The substance of the fax was put as a request for information. Here there is no counter-proposal. There is nothing specific by way of offer or rejection, but a mere enquiry, which should have been answered and not treated as a rejection of the offer. Since it was clearly only an enquiry, the vendor's original offer still survived, and the potential buyer was entitled to accept it when it sent the second fax. Lead case: Stevenson v McLean (1880).

stem: Three people are the trustees of a charitable trust. They disagree over the investment strategy of the trust, with the first two trustees favouring a cautious approach to investment while the third trustee wishes to invest in high-risk, high-return investments. The third trustee instructs the trust's investment manager to invest all of the trust's cash in an enterprise which no reasonable or prudent investor would invest in. The investment fails and the trust's assets are lost.
ask: Which of the following circumstances best describes the position?

options.en: All of the trustees are jointly liable to the beneficiaries for the breach of trust
All of the trustees are jointly liable to the beneficiaries for the breach of trust • but the first two trustees would have a right of contribution from the third trustee
Only the first two trustees are liable to the beneficiaries for the breach of trust but would have a right of contribution from the third trustee
Only the third trustee would be liable to the beneficiaries but would have a right of contribution from the first two trustees
Only the third trustee would be liable to the beneficiaries

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Where a trustee undertakes a unilateral action that constitutes a breach of trust, the liability of the other trustees is not engaged (see Twinsectra v Yardley [2002]). The third trustee's actions, in failing to exercise the statutory duty of care when directing the investment of the trust fund, would constitute a breach of trust. However since the third trustee's actions were clearly done without the consent of the other trustees, their liability to the beneficiaries would not be engaged.

stem: A local authority had a duty under both primary and delegated (or secondary) legislation to provide accommodation only where there was a priority need. The English High Court found that the primary and secondary legislation were both incompatible with the local authority's obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention).
ask: Which option best describes the action the court can take if the legislation cannot be interpreted compatibly?

options.en: The court can strike out both primary and delegated legislation where it is incompatible with rights protected under the Convention

The court can strike out both primary and delegated legislation where it is incompatible with rights protected under the Convention and instruct Parliament to remedy the situation within a reasonable time
The court can make a declaration of incompatibility in relation to the primary • legislation and strike out the secondary legislation provided the primary legislation does not prevent this
The court can make a declaration of incompatibility in relation to the delegated legislation and strike out the primary legislation provided that the delegated legislation does not prevent this

The court can declare both the primary and delegated legislation to be incompatible with the local authority's obligations under the Convention, but it must still apply both until Parliament decides otherwise

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is the best answer. The power to disapply is effectively an extension of the power to declare delegated legislation ultra vires in judicial review proceedings. The introduction of the Human Rights Act (HRA) 1998, however, has provided the courts with greater stimulus to challenge the actions of public bodies. One of the consequences of the HRA is that higher courts can make a declaration of incompatibility in relation to any piece of primary legislation. In respect of delegated legislation, the courts do not need to make a declaration of incompatibility and are not therefore obliged to apply it. stem: A woman is the freeholder of 123 The Street. She has leased a first floor flat in the property to a man on a 99 year lease. The man has in turn granted a sublease of the property to his friend for ten years. The man has fallen behind with his rent and service charge payments to the woman. The woman issues proceedings to forfeit the man's lease.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Both the man and his friend's lease have determined and both can apply for relief from forfeiture
Both the man and his friend's lease have determined and only the man can apply for relief from forfeiture
Both the man and his friend's lease have determined and only the man's friend can apply for relief from forfeiture
Only the man's lease has determined and only he can apply for relief from forfeiture
Only the man's lease has determined and both he and the friend can apply for relief from forfeiture

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Where a lease is forfeited, any sub lease created out of it will also be terminated. However both the man and his friend (as well as their mortgagees) would have the right to apply directly to the court for relief from forfeiture. This would usually be granted provided that they remedied all breaches of the terms of the lease.

stem: A man is a director of ACo Limited. He wishes to borrow £3,500 from the company and has doubts whether he needs to seek approval of the shareholders.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the Companies Act 2006 requirements?

options.en: All loans to directors must have approval of the shareholders.
Only loans above £25,000 must have approval of the shareholders
The company cannot loan money to a director
Loans under £10,000 do not require approval of the shareholders
The need of shareholders' approval will depend on the purpose of the loan

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Following the Companies Act 2006, loans to directors can be made in some situations. Generally speaking, shareholders' approval is required but there are circumstances set out in s204-207 which state that such approval is not required. These include situations where the funds are to meet expenditure in the company business (providing it is not over £50,000) or where the loan is less than £10,000.

stem: A woman is about to inherit her father's estate. Her father owned three properties and the woman believes they will be valued using the amount her father paid for the properties many years ago meaning the estate will be less than the threshold and will avoid Inheritance Tax. A friend tells her she's wrong and that they will be valued using current figures.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal?

options.en: Assets are valued at the price that was paid when they were acquired
Assets are valued at the market value at the time they were acquired
Assets are valued at the open market value immediately before death
Assets are valued at the open market value at the time the beneficiary will inherit
An individual can assign a value to each asset at the time of making a will

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Assets are valued at the open market value immediately before death. In this instance, the properties that belonged to the woman's father will be valued at the open market value immediately before his death and not at the price he originally paid for the properties.

stem: The English constitutional theory, as expounded by A.V. Dicey, does not recognise a separate system of administrative courts that would review the decisions of public bodies (as in France, Germany and many other European countries). Instead, it is considered that the government should be subject to the jurisdiction of ordinary Common Law courts. Historically the basis of the courts' intervention was the ultra vires doctrine, which covers both substantive and procedural matters.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the role played by the ultra vires doctrine in judicial review proceedings?

options.en: Under the ultra vires doctrine, a decision of a public authority must be consistent with constitutional conventions
Under the ultra vires doctrine, a decision of a public authority will be set aside for procedural impropriety even if there is no denial of natural justice
Under the ultra vires doctrine, a decision of a public authority can only be set aside if it exceeds the powers granted to it by Parliament
Under the ultra vires doctrine, courts must constitutionally engage Parliamentary intention when considering judicial review applications

Under the ultra vires doctrine, parties are expected to have exhausted all other remedies, before commencing a claim, including alternative remedies such as statutory appeals and appeals to relevant tribunals

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The constitutional theory of judicial review has long been dominated by the doctrine of ultra vires, under which a decision of a public authority can only be set aside if it exceeds the powers granted to it by Parliament. Broadly, in order to succeed, a judicial review applicant will need to show that either: (1) the person or body is under a legal duty to act or make a decision in a certain way and is unlawfully refusing or failing to do so; or (2) a decision or action that has been taken is 'beyond the powers' (in Latin, 'ultra vires") of the person or body responsible for it. stem: You are advising a client in respect of the sale and purchase of a property and an endowment mortgage. Your client asks you to advise him about buying a life policy. You are not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). You supervisor suggests that can you claim the exemption for professions.
ask: Which of the following best represents your professional responsibilities in this case?

options.en: You would normally need FCA authorisation to purchase a retail investment product such as a life policy
You would need FCA authorisation to give generic advice about a retail investment product such as a life policy
You can rely on the professional exemption to purchase a retail investment product such as a life policy
You can rely on the professional exemption to give generic advice about a retail investment product such as a life policy
You cannot rely on the professional exemption to give generic advice about a retail investment product such as a life policy and require FCA authorisation

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. You could not claim the exemption for professions - as the purchase of a retail investment product (such as a life policy) is prohibited under the Rule 5(1) of the Scope Rules. You could only give generic advice, or use an ATP to provide any specific advice; you could also endorse any advice of the ATP. B is not correct. You do not need authorisation or any exemption to provide generic advice. C is not correct. stem: Where a duty of care has been imposed in an earlier analogous case, a court will be more inclined to impose a duty on the facts of the case before it. Conversely, where the precedents are against the recognition of a duty of care, the courts will be reluctant to impose a duty unless they are convinced that, reasoning incrementally and by reference to the precedents, an extension of the scope of liability is justified.
ask: Which of the following statements most accurately records the requirements for establishing whether a duty of care exists under the 'incremental test'?

options.en: The requirements for establishing whether a duty of care exists are: • foreseeability of damage, proximity, physical injury and whether it is just and reasonable to impose a duty
The requirements for establishing whether a duty of care exists are: • foreseeability of damage, proximity, psychiatric injury and whether it is just and reasonable to impose a duty
The requirements for establishing whether a duty of care exists are: O l foreseeability of damage, proximity, public policy and whether it is just and reasonable to impose a duty
The requirements for establishing whether a duty of care exists are: • foreseeability of damage, proximity, damage to property and whether it is just and reasonable to impose a duty
The requirements for establishing whether a duty of care exists are: • foreseeability of damage, proximity, monetary loss and whether it is just and reasonable to impose a duty

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The requirements for establishing whether a duty of care exists are: foreseeability of damage, proximity, public policy and whether it is just and reasonable to impose a duty. Lead case: Caparo v Dickman [1990].

stem: Dishonesty is a fundamental and crucial part of the offence of fraud by false representation under the Fraud Act 2006. The definition of dishonesty is contained in a two-part test, which must be applied when determining whether or not an individual has behaved dishonestly.
ask: Which of the following best states the definition of 'dishonestly', if any, under the?

options.en: suffer losses

The definition of 'dishonestly' under the Fraud Act 2006 considers whether: the defendant's behaviour would be deemed dishonest by the ordinary standards of honest and reasonable people; and whether the defendant was aware that his behaviour was dishonest by those standards

The definition of 'dishonestly' under the Fraud Act 2006 considers whether: 'but for' the defendant's actions, the individual would not have suffered loss; and if so, it must be shown that the defendant's actions was the substantial cause of the victim's losses

The definition of 'dishonestly' under the Fraud Act 2006 considers whether: the • defendant's behaviour would be deemed dishonest by the standards of an individual sharing the same characteristics as the defendant; and whether the defendant was aware that his behaviour was dishonest by those standards

The definition of 'dishonestly' under the Fraud Act 2006 considers whether: the defendant's behaviour would be deemed dishonest by the ordinary standards of honest and reasonable people; and whether the defendant should have been aware that his behaviour was dishonest

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The R v Ghosh [1982] definition of 'dishonestly' applies under the Fraud Act 2006. This considers whether: the defendant's behaviour would be deemed dishonest by the ordinary standards of honest and reasonable people; and whether the defendant was aware that his behaviour was dishonest by those standards. Lead case: R v Ghosh [1982]. Statute; rule; constitution: S. 2 Fraud Act 2006.

stem: Client A sends £500 to the practice to cover a debt owed to the firm by another client, Client B. Client A's instructions are in a covering letter.
ask: Which of the following options is correct?

options.en: The money received may be paid directly to the office bank account
The account entry must be: • Credit Client B's ledger Debit cash sheet office account (£500) Client A's ledger account is not affected.
You must pay the money received from Client in the general client account and then transfer it to the office account, on behalf of Client B

The account entry must be: Debit cash sheet Credit Client A's ledger client account (£500) The payment out of the client account: Debit Client A's ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£500) The payment to the office account: Debit cash sheet Credit Client B's ledger office account (£500)
Written consent from Client A is sufficient. No records double entries are needed

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Answer A is correct. The money received from one client in payment of the bill of another may be paid directly to the office bank account, if the client instructs you to do that. Answers B and D both represent alternative, correct account entries and therefore neither are the only possible entry. Rather, the account entry may be as shown in B, or it may be as shown in D. Answer C is not correct, as you may either (1) pay the money received from one client in the general client account and then transfer it to the office account or E is incorrect. The consent of the payor and payee is required in order for one client to pay another client's debt to the firm.

stem: A prisoner's cell is grossly inadequate in living space, lighting and ventilation. The sanitary arrangements involve 'slopping out', which means the use of a bottle to urinate and a chamber pot to defecate in the cell. Further the stress on the prisoner consequent upon the conditions of his detention contributed to the resurgence and exacerbation of his pre-existing eczema. Which of the following statements best describes to what extent, if at all, the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention)
ask: Which of the following statements best describes to what extent, if at all, the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) is engaged in such a scenario?

options.en: The prisoner's treatment is a breach the Convention's exclusion of inhuman and degrading treatment
The prisoner's treatment is a breach the Convention's exclusion of torture

The prisoner's treatment would be a breach of the Convention's exclusion of inhuman and degrading treatment, but for the right of derogation permitted under the terms of the Convention itself in order to secure the fulfillment of any obligation prescribed by law

The prisoner's treatment would be a breach of the Convention's exclusion of torture, but for the right of derogation permitted under the terms of the Convention itself in order to secure the fulfillment of any obligation prescribed by law
The prisoner's treatment is a breach of under the Convention's exclusion of • torture or inhuman and degrading treatment, subject to designation order from the Secretary of State

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. There is a distinction between torture and inhuman treatment: stripping, stringing, attachment of electrodes to genitals, rape, beating, stripping and spraying - all amount to torture, while deprivation such as a lack of a toilet, a small cell or an aggravating medical condition have been held to amount to inhuman and degrading treatment only. Lead case: Napier v. The Scottish Ministers [2002] UKHRR 308. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 3 ECHR.

stem: A woman owns a successful hairdressing salon, employing top stylists who command large fees. The salon owner employs a senior stylist, whose contract of employment contains a restraint clause preventing her from carrying on business as a hairstylist within 10 miles of the salon owner's premises for two years after leaving the salon owner's employment. The stylist falls out with the salon owner, quits her job and tries to take her clients with her to a new salon 5 miles away from the salon owner. The stylist sets up HairCo Limited with a friend. The stylist and her friend are directors and members of HairCo Limited.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the?

options.en: The stylist has not breached the restraint clause in her contract with the salon owner as HairCo Limited has a separate legal personality
The stylist has not breached the restraint clause in her contract with the salon owner as she has set HairCo Limited up with a friend
The stylist has breached the restraint clause in her contract with the salon owner and HairCo Limited does not have a separate legal personality
The stylist has breached the restraint clause in her contract with the salon owner even though HairCo Limited has a separate legal personality
The stylist has bit breached the restraint clause in her contract with the salon owner as she is not carrying on the business herself

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. HairCo Limited has a separate legal personality to the stylist, however it would be clear to the court that HairCo Limited is being used by the stylist as a vehicle to avoid the legal obligation that she owes to the salon owner under her employment contract. Although the stylist is not strictly operating the business the court would be likely to disregard the distinction between the stylist and HairCo Limited and find that the stylist is acting in breach of the terms of her contract with the salon owner.

stem: A brother (aged 19) and sister (aged 20) are the beneficiaries of a trust which is administered by three trustees. The trust provides that the trust property shall be held on trust for the brother and sister until the brother reaches the age of 21, whereupon the capital shall be paid to them. No appointor has been named in the trust instrument. They wish to replace one of the trustees.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The brother and sister can not force the trustee's retirement
The brother and sister can only force the trustee's retirement under a court order
The brother and sister can only force the trustee's retirement if the trustee consents
The brother and sister can only force the trustee's retirement if the other two trustees consent
The brother and sister can force the trustee's retirement by giving all three trustees a written direction

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Section 19 of the Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996 provides that the beneficiaries can force the retirement of a trustee provided that (1) no appointor has been named in the trust instrument; (2) the beneficiaries are all of full age and capacity; (3) the beneficiaries are together are absolutely entitled to the trust property; (4) at least two trustees or a trust corporation will remain; and (5) the outgoing trustee will be replaced or the remaining trustees consent. As the brother and sister are proposing to replace one of the trustees, the consent of the other two trustees is not required. After you explain the meaning of the actus reus and mens rea of the offence, the woman asks for an explanation of the elements needed to be shown to satisfy the offence.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains the elements that need to be shown to satisfy the offence of theft?

options.en: Before a person can be convicted of theft, both the actus reus and the mens rea must be present
Before a person can be convicted of theft, the actus reus may be present but the mens rea must be present
Before a person can be convicted of theft, the actus reus must be present and the mens rea may be present
Before a person can be convicted of theft, the actus reus must be present
Before a person can be convicted of theft, the mens rea must be present

stem: When a passenger suffered a collapsed lung on a scheduled flight, another passenger came to her aid and carried out an emergency intervention. The intervention saved the passenger's life, but caused permanent scarring. She now wishes to bring an action in negligence against the other passenger. Which of the following statements best describes when necessity
ask: Which of the following statements best describes when necessity is available as a defence?

options.en: Necessity is available as a defence when harm is caused intentionally to prevent a greater evil
Necessity is available as a defence when harm is caused intentionally to prevent no evil
Necessity is available as a defence when harm is caused intentionally to prevent a lesser evil
Necessity is available as a defence when harm is caused intentionally to prevent a lesser evil and no evil
Necessity is available as a defence when harm is caused intentionally to prevent no evil and a greater evil

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Necessity is available as a defence when harm is caused intentionally to prevent a greater evil.

stem: The distinction between the status of terms is of most importance when the consequences of any breach are being considered. In this regard, the context in which a breach occurs will be important, as will its effect on the rest of the contract.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes a warranty?

options.en: A warranty is where the parties have communicated to one another that the form of words is to be a part of the contract between them
A warranty is where the record of a transaction is embodied in a document, by which extrinsic evidence is not admissible to vary or interpret the document
A warranty is where the court considers that the parties intended it to apply • and did not mention something simply because it would be taken for granted by the parties
A warranty is where the term does not go to the root of the contract and will probably only entitle the other party to claim damages
A warranty is something which is vital to the main purpose of the contract

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. A warranty is a less important term: it does not go to the root of the contract. A breach of warranty will only give the injured party the right to claim damages; he cannot repudiate the contract.

stem: A local authority was statutorily obliged to provide homeless persons with accommodation. The applicants were a married couple, who lived with her two children (the family) in one room and applied to the local authority for aid. The local authority refused aid because it considered that the family was not homeless.
ask: Which of the following statements best identifies the relevant court the married couple should turn to?

options.en: The relevant court the family should turn to is the Family Division of the High Court
The relevant court the family should turn to is the Court of Appeal
The relevant court the family should turn to is the Chancery Division of the High Court
The relevant court the family should turn to is the Administrative Court
The relevant court the family should turn to is the Commercial Court

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Generally, unless other appeal processes are laid down in law, anyone who wants to challenge the validity of any decision of a lesser court, tribunal, government authority or local authority brings a claim for judicial review in the Administrative Court of the Queen's Bench Division.

stem: You act for a long-time friend on a residential property transaction, on a formal retainer. Your friend presents a cheque for the full value of the property in cash. This causes you suspicion as you have always known your friend to be of limited financial means. Your friend tells you he received the money from 'a group of mates'. You make a disclosure to your Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO) which results in a suspicious activity report to National Crime Agency (NCA).
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed?

options.en: You may disclose to your friend, in a personal capacity, that a report has been made
You may disclose to your friend that a report has been made and strongly advise him, personally and professionally, not to proceed with the transaction
You must cease to act for your friend and cannot communicate with him
You must ask your friend to make contact with NCA
You may proceed with the transaction as long as you do not disclose to your friend that a suspicious activity report has been made

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. On the face of it, you would be committing a 'tipping off' offence under s333A(1), as you would be disclosing that a suspicious activity report has been made, which might prejudice any investigation carried out. However, it is a defence to a 'tipping off' offence that the disclosure was made by a professional legal adviser to their client for the purpose of dissuading them from engaging in criminal conduct (s333D(2)). As you are formally retained, you are acting in your capacity as a professional legal adviser, and may therefore rely on this defence. Answer A is a 'tipping off' offence for which no defence is available. C may constitute tipping off due; you will not be able to rely on the 'authorised disclosure' defence (s338) as you have not yet received any consent from NCA.

stem: An activist organises a public assembly but receives prior notice from police informing her that they have decided to ban the assembly. The activist believes that they cannot do this and seeks further clarification.
ask: Advise the activist whether the police have the right to ban the public assembly?

options.en: The police can ban the assembly if they see fit to do so
The police can ban the assembly in order to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community
The police cannot ban the assembly
The police can ban the assembly only in order to prevent serious public disorder
The police can ban the assembly only order to prevent in serious criminal damage

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The police do not have the right to ban public assemblies but can impose limited conditions in order to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community.

stem: A trustee of a charitable trust - worth in excess of £100,000,000 - transfers £50,000 from the trust fund to a bank account in the name of his wife, in breach of trust. His wife, unaware of the transaction, uses the bank account, which also contains her own money used for paying her living expenses. The trustee's wife has recently lost her job and has been offered a new one. When she discovers the £50,000 in her bank, she immediately makes enquiries of the trust as to why the money has been sent to her, but a member of the administration staff tells her that she has obviously been awarded some money by the charity. She decides to decline the job offer and use the £50,000 to fund her living expenses while she stays at home and looks after her daughter.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The trust could follow the money into the wife's account
The trust could trace the money into the wife's account
The trust could not trace the money into the wife's account as she is a dishonest assistant
The trust could not trace the money into the wife's account as it has been mixed with non-trust money
The trust could not trace the money into the wife's account as the trust property can not be traced

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is B. The money could not be followed into the wife's account because the trust money has been mixed with non-trust money. Following is only available where the specific property remains identifiable, whereas tracing must be used to recover other property of an equivalent value where the original trust property cannot be identified but its value has passed into the other property. As with all equitable remedies, they are awarded at the court's discretion. The court would be very unlikely to order the wife to return the trust funds in these circumstances given that she has changed her position (by turning down the job) and relied on payment of the money to her detriment. It be inequitable to recover the money from her, especially where she has made enquiries of the trust. Note: while it would be possible to trace the trust funds, the question stresses that there is a discretionary power of the court to order any type of relief, following the tracing process which is initiated before an equitable remedy can be sought. Remedy is awarded where the court considers it equitable to do SO. Although the preconditions for tracing may be made nut it ic unlikelv that the court would award the in the circumstances. This is because it would not be equitable to do so given that: (a) the trust fund is very large compared to the wife's modest resources; (b) £50,000 is likely to be a substantial amount of money to the wife and not very much to the trust; (c) the wife has received and retained the money due to two errors on the part of the trust; and, most importantly, (d) the wife has changed her position and acted to her detriment in -alanas to when a remedy may be given, it is still up to the court to refuse if it thinks it will cause injustice- there is no "right" to a discretionary remedy!

stem: On Monday a car owner sent a letter to his friend by first-class post offering to sell his car to her and asking for a reply 'in course of post'. The letter arrived Friday, not Wednesday as the car owner expected, due to the car owner's use of the wrong postal code. The same day the car owner's friend accepted the offer by return of first- class post. The car owner only received the letter Tuesday; by which time he had already sold the car to another buyer.
ask: Which option best describes the parties' legal position?

options.en: A valid acceptance requires that it must have been communicated to and received by the offeror
A posted acceptance is complete on posting
No acceptance is effective until it is received and understood by the person to whom it is addressed
A posted acceptance is valid from when the letter is received by the offeror
A posted acceptance is complete on posting but should be supplemented by a confirmatory phone call to show good faith

explanation.en: return of first- You did not select the correct answer. B is the best answer. A posted acceptance is complete on posting. In such a scenario the car owner's friend could sue him for breach of contract. English law has adopted a rule that an acceptance via the post is valid from the moment of posting, not merely from when the letter is received by the offeror. Lead case: Adams v Lindsell (1818) 1 B & Ald 681; 106 ER 250.

stem: A man became very ill as a result of withdrawing from heroin, so his girlfriend, at his request, went out to buy a small quantity of the drug for him. She watched as he injected himself with it, but the heroin was so pure, it caused him to overdose. The girlfriend panicked and ran to the man's brother for help, but when they returned to the flat several hours later, the man was dead.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the girlfriend's criminal liability, if any, in respect of manslaughter?

options.en: No unlawful act for the purpose of unlawful act manslaughter occurred, • because the girlfriend only supplied the heroin to the man, who then in turn administered the drug to himself and died
A charge of manslaughter would be appropriate, because by simply supplying the class-A drug itself, the girlfriend caused harm to the man, and caused his death
The girlfriend committed an unlawful act; the unlawful act was a crime and her act was a significant cause of the man's death
Although the man voluntarily self-administered the heroin, the girlfriend was culpable of unlawful act manslaughter as an accessory to the man's act because she had assisted and encouraged it
The girlfriend would be liable for manslaughter as a secondary party as the man's act of self-administration led to his death, which was a criminal offence in itself

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The girlfriend supplied the drug to the man, who then had a choice, knowing the facts, whether to inject himself or not. The heroin had been self-administered, not jointly administered. Lead case: R v Kennedy (Simon) (2007) 3 W.L.R.612.

stem: Three people run a property development business in partnership. There is a formal partnership agreement in place which stipulates that all transactions over £500,000 must be authorised by all partners. Two of the partners have been in written correspondence with a potential purchaser of 123 Brick Lane for some time and meet with him to finalise the arrangements. They enter into a contract to sell him the property for £1,000,000. They try to contact the third partner before signing the papers but can not reach her to obtain her agreement and proceed in any event. The third partner has in fact been negotiating a sale of 123 Brick Lane for £1,500,000 and when this becomes clear, the partners attempt to rescind the first contract on the basis that the first two partners had no authority to sell the land.
ask: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.en: The first two partners had actual authority to bind the third partner and the • first sale contract would be enforceable against the partnership provided that the buyer was not aware of the restriction

The first two partners had implied authority to bind the third partner and the first sale contract would be enforceable against the partnership provided that the buyer was not aware of the restriction

The first two partners had apparent authority to bind the third partner and the • first sale contract would be enforceable against the partnership provided that the buyer was not aware of the restriction

The first two partners had no authority to bind the third partner, however the first sale contract would nevertheless be enforceable against the partnership provided that the buyer was not aware of the restriction
The first two partners had no authority to bind the third partner and the first sale contract would not be enforceable against the partnership

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. All partners are prima facie agents of the firm and are able to bind all other partners. The only exception is where a partner in fact has no authority and the third party knows this or does not believe him to be a partner. In this case, the buyer would be aware that the first two partners were in partnership because they would have seen the firm's notepaper. Provided that they had no knowledge of the restriction on the first two partners' ability to transact at over £500,000 without the third partner's consent, the first two partners' actions would bind the firm and it would not be entitled to rescind the first sale contract.

stem: A woman has the benefit of an easement over a man's freehold land, which is expressed to last in perpetuity.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the?

options.en: The woman has a legal interest in the man's land
The woman has a legal estate in the man's land
The woman has an equitable interest in the man's land
The woman has an equitable estate in the man's land
The woman has no estate or interest in the man's land

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. An easement is an interest that the owner of the dominant tenement has in the servient tenement. It is not an estate in land. An easement granted in perpetuity would subsist as a legal easement, whereas an easement granted for an uncertain period of time would take effect in equity only.

stem: Trespass to the person comes in three variants: assault; battery; and false imprisonment. The guiding principle behind all three is based on the statement of Goff, LJ, who stated in Collins v Wilcock that "any person's body is inviolate", excepting normal, day-to-day physical contact.
ask: Which of the following statements best defines the elements of assault?

options.en: Assault is defined as the infliction of any form of unlawful force by which a person intentionally or recklessly causes another to apprehend direct and unlawful violence
Assault is defined as the unlawful touching of another by which a person • intentionally or recklessly causes another to apprehend gradual and unlawful violence
Assault is defined as occasioning bodily harm by which a person intentionally or recklessly causes another to apprehend measured and unlawful violence
Assault is defined as any act by which a person intentionally or recklessly causes another to apprehend continuing and unlawful violence
Assault is defined as any act by which a person intentionally or recklessly causes another to apprehend immediate and unlawful violence

explanation.en: person intentionally or recklessly causes another to apprehend immediate and unlawful violence. Lead case: R v Ireland [1998].

stem: A husband and wife own a business registered for VAT. Despite being fully aware of their tax obligations, they attempt to evade paying VAT in order to obtain more profit. If caught, they believe they will face a civil fine, as it is not a criminal matter.
ask: Advise the husband and wife regarding issues concerning tax evasion under current?

options.en: If caught they will face a civil punishment only
If caught they will face a criminal punishment only
If caught they could face both civil and criminal punishments
The onus is on Her Majesty's Revenue and Customs to ensure payments that are made correctly, not the individual
There are no civil or criminal punishments for evading tax; you are merely required to pay the tax you have avoided, with some interest, and fine

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. If caught they could face both civil and criminal punishments. Evading tax is considered to be a serious offence and the perpetrator can face civil punishment (e.g. a fine) as well as a criminal punishment (imprisonment of up to 7 years).

stem: A public Bill is facing stiff opposition in the House of Lords. Political commentators speculate that the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 ("Parliament Acts") are likely to be invoked. The Bill originated in the House of Commons.
ask: How, if at all, can the House of Lords block or delay a Bill?

options.en: The Parliament Acts mean that the House of Commons may enact a Bill by bypassing all House of Lords stages
The Parliament Acts are not binding, so if there is no agreement between either House, the Bill is lost under the 'double insistence' rule
Under the Parliament Acts, the House of Lords may veto a Bill at any stage
Under the Parliament Acts, the House of Lords may not delay a Bill for more than two Parliamentary sessions, or one calendar year
Under the Parliament Acts, the House of Lords may not delay a Bill for more than four Parliamentary sessions, or two calendar years

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is D. Under the Parliament Acts, the House of Lords may not delay a Bill for more than two Parliamentary sessions, or one calendar year. Under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 (which do not apply for Bills seeking to extend Parliament's length to more than five years), the House of Lords may not delay most other public Bills for more than two parliamentary sessions, or one calendar year. The Bill is then submitted for Royal Assent, even though the Lords did not pass it. These provisions, however, only apply to public Bills that originate in the House of Commons.

stem: The courts have recognised certain fundamental rights as constitutional in origin. The classification of a right as constitutional is meaningful. It is testimony that an added value is attached to the protection of the right.
ask: Which of the following statements best defines constitutional law?

options.en: Constitutional law defines any legislation that affects the individual: it is linked to the relationship between state, government and members of the public

Constitutional law deals with the relationship between the state and individual, and the relationships between different branches of the state, such as the executive, the legislative and the judiciary
Constitutional law refers to the body of law which regulates bureaucratic managerial procedures and defines the powers of administrative agencies of the government
Constitutional law is a procedure in English administrative law by which the courts supervise the exercise of public power on the application of an individual
Constitutional law regulates individuals' behaviour by setting rules, like speed limits, and established rights and benefits, such as drivers license and Social Security benefits

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Constitutional law deals with the relationship between the state and individual, and the relationships between different branches of the state, such as the executive, the legislative and the judiciary. A constitution is a set of rules about power within a state. Most typically, constitutions establish institutions to carry out three distinctly identifiable types of governmental power: legislative, judicial and executive. These are often called the three "branches" of government. Legislative power is the power mentioned above to make general rules binding throughout society - to make laws, in other words. Judicial power is the power to apply and enforce those rules in individual cases - to decide

stem: A woman entered a competition at her local golf club for which there was a medal and £50 prize. The competition was subject to an 'honour clause'. The woman won the competition but the club has refused to hand over the prize of £50 and she only received the medal.
ask: Which of the following statements best advises whether the woman can enforce collection of the £50 prize?

options.en: The woman cannot enforce collection of the £50 prize, because an 'honour clause' does not mean a contract is not legally binding; it simply recognises that prior to the offer being made there had been no obligation to make such a payment

The woman can enforce collection of the £50 prize, because there was a unilateral contract under which the golf club was, in effect, saying 'If you enter our competition, we will give you the £50 prize'
The woman can enforce collection of the £50 prize, because public policy dictates that the parties' intention to rely on each other's good faith and honour should be enforced
The woman can enforce collection of the £50 prize, because this was a business agreement and there is a presumption, therefore, that the parties intended to create legal relations and make a contract
The woman cannot enforce collection of the £50 prize, because the agreement was not binding due to the 'honour clause'

explanation.en: E is correct. Commercial agreements 'binding in honour only' are not legal contracts so that a participant may not recover his winnings. Lead case: Jones v Vernons Pools [1938].

stem: The modern law of criminal damage is mostly contained in the Criminal Damage Act 1971, which redefines or creates several offences protecting property rights. The Act provides a comprehensive structure covering merely preparatory acts to the most serious offences of arson and causing damage with intent to endanger life.
ask: Which of the following best describes how courts consider how the life of another was endangered for the purposes of the law relating to criminal damage?

options.en: A defendant may be guilty, either if he intended to endanger life by danger to life resulting from the actual destruction of, or damage to property, which was intended to be done, or was reckless that life would be endangered by the damage

A defendant must be guilty, either if he intended to endanger life by danger to life resulting from the actual destruction of, or damage to property, which was intended to be done, or was reckless that life would be endangered by the damage
A defendant may be guilty, either if he intended to endanger life by damage, which was intended to be done, or should have been aware that life would be endangered by the damage
A defendant may be guilty, either if he intended to endanger life by damage, • which was intended to be done, or was reckless that life would be endangered by the damage
A defendant may be guilty, either if he would have realised he was endangering life by damage, which was intended to be done, or was reckless that life would be endangered by the damage

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. A defendant may be guilty, either if he intended to endanger life by damage, which was intended to be done, or was reckless that life would be endangered by the damage. Rv. Webster (1995) explored the relationship between the damage caused and the damage intended. That case involved the throwing of heavy items into the paths of moving vehicles, and it was held that a defendant may be guilty if he intends to endanger life by the actual damage intended, or is reckless that life will be endangered by that damage. Therefore, although a defendant does not necessarily intend to endanger life when he intends to break a car window, ignoring the likely risk that this will cause the •=3- ] 2 All E.R. 168, C.A Statute; rule; constitution: S. 1(2) Criminal Damage Act 1971. •*3-

stem: Your client owns a portfolio of shares. She transfers equitable ownership to her brother and sister. The sister can receive the dividends from the shares for the next ten years and then the brother is entitled to have the shares and do what he wishes with them.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Your client is the beneficiary, the brother is the settlor and the sister is the trustee
Your client is the trustee, the brother is the beneficiary and the sister is the settlor
Your client and her brother are the settlors and beneficiaries, the sister is the beneficiary
Your client is the settlor and trustee, the brother and sister are the beneficiaries
The brother is the settlor, the sister is the trustee and your client is the beneficiary

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Your client is the settlor as she created the trust. As she has retained legal title to the shares and only transferred equitable title, she is also the trustee. The brother and sister are the beneficiaries as they have the benefit of the shares.

stem: Your client wants to form a company but does not want the company's accounts to be made available to the public. Advise your client whether it
ask: is possible to form a company and at the same time ensure the company's accounts remain private?

options.en: All limited company accounts remain private
All limited company accounts remain private until the company is five years old
The accounts of limited companies must be submitted to Companies House but are only made available to government agencies
Limited company accounts are made available to the public but unlimited company accounts remain private
Both limited company accounts and unlimited company accounts are made available to the public

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. If your client wants to form a company (as opposed to operate as a sole trader or form a partnership) and keep the company's accounts private, he would need to form an unlimited company. Although this ensures privacy with regard to the company's accounts, it means your client's liability will be unlimited.

stem: A woman grants a man an option to purchase 123 The Street, an unregistered freehold property, at any time within the next five years.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man should register the option using a caution
The man should register the option using a Restriction
The man should register the option as a Land Charge
The man should register the option as a Local Land Charge
The man should register the option as an overriding interest

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. An option to purchase land ranks as an estate contract and accordingly would be registrable as a Class C(iv) Land Charge.

stem: Your client was injured when coming to the aid of a car accident survivor. The driver's insurance company asserts volenti non-fit injuria. You must explain the effect of the doctrine of volenti non-fit injuria to your client in these circumstances.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes how the availability of the defence of volenti non-fit injuria has been restricted?

options.en: The availability of the defence of volenti non-fit injuria has been restricted in rescue cases
The availability of the defence of volenti non-fit injuria has been restricted by the provisions of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977
The availability of the defence of volenti non-fit injuria has been restricted in drink-drive passenger cases
The availability of the defence of volenti non-fit injuria has been restricted in • drink-drive passenger cases and by the provisions of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977
The availability of the defence of volenti non-fit injuria has been restricted in rescue cases and by the provisions of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977

explanation.en: E is correct. The availability of the defence of volenti non-fit injuria has been restricted in rescue cases and by the provisions of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977.

stem: You are a partner acting for a client on a commercial property transaction. You have made a disclosure to your Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO) who has in turn made a disclosure to National Crime Agency (NCA). NCA have just denied you consent to allow the transaction to complete. You are considering whether to report the matter to your professional indemnity insurers.
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed?

options.en: You should not report the matter to your professional indemnity insurers, as you will be committing a tipping off offence
You should not report the matter to your professional indemnity insurers, as you will be prejudicing any investigation
You should report the matter to your professional indemnity insurers, but • should not advise that a disclosure has been made or that NCA have not given you consent to proceed
You should report the matter to your professional indemnity insurers, but only once the client intimates a claim
You should make a full and clear notification to your professional indemnity insurers immediately

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. You will not be committing a tipping off or prejudicing an investigation offence under POCA, as disclosure to a reputable professional indemnity insurer, who are themselves subject to anti- money laundering obligations, will not prejudice an investigation. You should make a full and clear disclosure and provide NCA's response. To fail to do so may breach your professional indemnity insurance terms. You should really have made the notification immediately on making a disclosure to your MLRO and in any event must do so immediately on receipt of NCA's refusal to proceed: this means you can no longer carry out the retainer and may face civil action from the client as a result.

stem: On Monday a car owner wrote to his friend asking whether she would be interested in purchasing his car. The following day, his friend wrote in reply, 'If I receive an acceptance of my offer by this Friday, I am willing to pay £500 for your car and will collect it from outside your house next Monday'.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the parties' legal position?

options.en: Where an offeree fails to reply to an offer his silence and inaction operate as an acceptance
Where the offeror has stated or given the offeree reason to understand that •assent may be manifested by silence or inaction, the offeree in remaining silent or inactive intends to accept the offer
Acceptance of an offer can be inferred from silence and creates a binding unilateral contract
Acceptance of an offer cannot be inferred from silence, absent a bilateral contract
Acceptance of an offer cannot be inferred from silence, save in the most exceptional circumstances

explanation.en: E is correct. There must be some act on the part of the offeree to indicate his acceptance. Silence on the part of the offeree (i.e. his mere failure to reject the offeror's offer) cannot of itself amount to acceptance. Lead case: Felthouse v Bindley (1863). - anateral

stem: Journalists were dismissed from a national television station for broadcasting a news item involving a banned political wing of an avowed terrorist organisation. It was asserted by the Secretary of State that such a broadcast would have been likely to promote or incite to crime or would have tended to undermine the authority of the State.
ask: The National Association of Journalists (NAJ) and National Freedom Association (NFA) applied to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) on behalf of the Taking in to account ECtHR jurisprudence, would the applicant trade unions have standing to bring proceedings?

options.en: The NAJ's petition would have standing, although the NFA's petition would not
The NFA's petition would have standing, but the NAJ's petition would not
Neither the NFA's nor the NAJ's petition would have standing
Both the NFA's and the NAJ's petition would have standing

The fact alone that the trade unions consider themselves as guardians of the • collective interests of their members suffices to make them victims within the meaning of the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The Court has consistently rejected applications by trades unions; the fact alone that trade unions consider themselves as guardians of the collective interests of their members does not suffice to make them victims within the meaning of Article 34. The NFA meanwhile bears all the hallmarks of a pressure group. Lead case: Purcell v Ireland (1991) 70 D.R. 262. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 34.

stem: A man and woman agree to rob a stranger. While the man keeps watch, the woman approaches the stranger with a knife and robs him.
ask: Which of the following best states who the principal actor is in the scenario?

options.en: The principal actor in the scenario is the woman
The principal actor in the scenario is the man
The principal actor in the scenario is the stranger
The principal actors in the scenario are the man and woman
There is no principal actor in the scenario because the man and woman are equal participants

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Under criminal law, a principal is any actor who is primarily responsible for a criminal offense, i.e., the woman. Such an actor is distinguished from others who may also be subject to criminal liability as accomplices, accessories or conspirators.

stem: 123 The Street is an unregistered freehold property which a brother and sister own as joint tenants. The brother dies and the sister puts the property up for sale, with a woman offering to purchase it. The woman is concerned that the sister may not be solely beneficially entitled to the property. Prior to his death, the brother was made bankrupt, but the conveyance to the woman states that the sister is the sole beneficial owner and there is no memorandum of severance endorsed upon the conveyance to the brother and sister.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The sister is solely beneficially entitled to the property
The sister is solely beneficially entitled to the property but should swear a statutory declaration to that fact
The sister should appoint an additional trustee to give a valid receipt for the sale proceeds
The sister must appoint the Official Receiver as an additional trustee to give a valid receipt for the sale proceeds
The woman will take the property free from the trust as long as she is not aware of it

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The brother's bankruptcy would have the effect of severing the joint tenancy and converting it into a tenancy in common. His trustee in bankruptcy would be entitled to his equitable share in the property. In order to ensure that the trustee's equitable interest is overreached, the woman should ensure that an additional trustee is appointed to transfer the property. This may be the Official Receiver, but this is not necessary.

stem: A husband and wife are the members of Example Limited, a private company limited by shares which has adopted model articles of association. The wife has £10,000 unpaid shares and has run into financial difficulty and wishes to dispose of her shares to her husband. Her shares are not fully paid up.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Whilst the shares remain unpaid, the directors can refuse to register the transfer to the husband if they do not approve of the transaction
The directors can only refuse to register the shares for a maximum of thirty days
The directors can not refuse to register the transfer of the shares unless they are in respect of the same class of share
The directors must register the transfer of the shares
The directors can not refuse to register the transfer of the shares in any circumstances

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. While shares remain unpaid, directors can refuse to register a transfer where they do not approve of the transferee. They can impose a blanket suspension of up to 30 days on the registration of the transfer of shares that they would otherwise be obliged to register in the interests of the good administration of the company.

stem: A newspaper reported that an accountant has retired. This is false, however, and has caused financial loss to the accountant as he has lost potential and existing clients who now believe that he is no longer in practice.
ask: Which option best advises the accountant?

options.en: An actionable claim for malicious falsehood may lie providing the accountant can show the report has caused damage to his reputation
An actionable claim for malicious falsehood may lie if the accountant can show • that the report discredits him even though it was an apparently innocent statement
An actionable claim for malicious falsehood may lie providing the accountant can show the report questions his fitness to practise
An actionable claim for malicious falsehood may lie providing the accountant can show the statement was made with malicious intent
An actionable claim for malicious falsehood cannot lie unless there has been an attack on a person's goods

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Dis the best option. An actionable claim for malicious falsehood may lie providing the accountant can show the statement was made with malicious intent. A malicious falsehood is a false statement made maliciously that is calculated to injure the property or business of another. While defamation discredits an individual, malicious falsehood is an attack on his goods or services. Malicious falsehood can also occur where the false statement causes damage to an individual, even though it is not a slur on his character or his fitness to hold a particular role. An example of this is to say that an accountant has retired. This is not defamatory since it does not damage his reputation. If it is false,. Since the statement does not damage the reputation of the accountant he cannot bring a claim for defamation. He may, however, have an actionable claim for malicious falsehood providing he can show the statement was made with malicious intent. -- 3----

stem: A potential client gives her married name. You ask her to provide identification of her contact details and she produces a passport and two bank statements in her maiden name. You conclude that the client must have recently got married and is now using her married name.
ask: Which of the following best describes your obligations under the Money Laundering Regulations?

options.en: The client must produce identity documents with her married name. Failing that you cannot represent her
You must ask the client to produce a marriage certificate
You can rely on the client's documents with her maiden name
You can rely on the client's wedding photographs
The client must produce identity documents with her married name. You can represent her in the meantime

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is the best answer. While it is indeed highly likely that the client recently got married and is now therefore using her married name, it is also possible that the client is seeking to establish an account in a false name which would show no connection to her. This being the case, you must ask the client to produce her married certificate to authenticate her married name and copies of all identification material must be retained on the file. A is not the best answer. You do not need to wait until the client obtains a new passport or documents in her married name. You can rely on a marriage certificate. you must ask the client to produce her married certificate to authenticate her married name and copies of all identification material must be retained on the file. E you cannot represent the client until you have adequate identity documents. This being the case, you must ask the client to produce her married certificate to authenticate her married name and copies of all identification material must be retained on the file. If the client is unable to produce the marriage certificate you will have to wait until she is able to produce some other satisfactory identity document, such as an updated passport, in her married name.

stem: Your client, an individual, has chargeable gains of £80,000 due to the sale of several assets. He has sold some other assets at a loss of £10,000 and believes this loss can be deducted from the chargeable gains. Your client thinks that if he gives £70,000 to charity this can also be deducted from his chargeable gains, reducing the amount he owes to £0.
ask: Advise your client regarding the current legal position?

options.en: Neither the £10,000 loss nor the payment to charity will reduce the client's chargeable gains
The £10,000 loss can be deducted from the client's chargeable gains, but the payment to charity cannot
Both the £10,000 loss and the payment to charity can be deducted from the client's chargeable gains
A maximum of £50,000 can be deducted from the client's chargeable gains, regardless of whether it's a payment to charity or a loss
If a payment to charity is to be deducted it can only be up to a maximum of £20,000

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. Whilst the loss from the sale of an asset can be deducted from the chargeable gains, payments to charity cannot be deducted. Your client, however, may claim a tax deduction of the payment donated to the charity through Gift Aid. While this may affect your client's adjusted net income for income tax purposes, this does not affect the chargeable gains made as a result of the sale of the assets.

stem: A woman drunk home-made wine at a friend's house not realising that it had such a high alcohol content. On the way home she got in to an argument with her boyfriend. She threw a stone at him, but missed and smashed a shop window.
ask: Which of the following best states the woman's defence, if any, to any criminal liability arising from her actions?

options.en: The woman would have a defence under these circumstances, because she was sufficiently intoxicated to negate the mens rea for the offence of criminal damage
The woman would probably have a defence of non-insane automatism under these circumstances
The woman would not have a defence under these circumstances, because the intoxication was voluntary since she knew she was drinking alcohol
The woman would have no defence under these circumstances, because involuntary intoxication does not negate mens rea for a specific intent offence
The woman would have a defence under these circumstances, because voluntary intoxication negates mens rea for a basic intent offence

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. If a defendant is aware that she is drinking alcohol, the exact nature or strength is irrelevant. The intoxication is still voluntary. Please note, criminal damage under s1 (1) Criminal Damage Act is an offence of basic intent. Lead case: Allen [1988] Crim LR 698, CA. Statute; rule; constitution: s1(1) Criminal Damage Act.

stem: The Monarch is gravely ill. A Privy Counsellor of the Accession Council is concerned about the steps that might be necessary for the proclamation of the Monarch's successor. He seeks guidance regarding the official legal term describing the end of the Monarch's reign.
ask: Which option best advises the Privy Counsellor?

options.en: The legal term describing the end of the Monarch's reign is known as the departure of the Crown
The legal term describing the end of the Monarch's reign is known as the demise of the Crown
The legal term describing the end of the Monarch's reign is known as the death of the Crown
The legal term describing the end of the Monarch's reign is known as the decease of the Crown
The legal term describing the end of the Monarch's reign is known as the discontinuance of the Crown

explanation.en: "*- concerned A You did not select the correct answer. B is the best option. The person who is the reigning Monarch - being a human being - must eventually die. On their death, their reign as Monarch ends, as does their corporation sole of the Crown. This is known as the demise of the Crown. As stated by Plowden, it is the "...natural dissolution of the king is generally so called; " an expression which signifies merely a transfer of property. By demise of the crown we mean only that, in consequence of the disunion of the king's natural body from his body politic, the kingdom is transferred or demised to his successor, and so the royal dignity remains perpetual..." 1 Bl. Comm. 249; Plowd. 234.

stem: A woman has won a substantial amount of money on the National Lottery and wishes to establish a trust for the purposes of promoting the amateur sport of cat fancying. This involves owners bringing their cats to competitions run by the British Cat Fanciers' Association the where they are judged and a winner declared.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman has created a charitable purpose trust that is valid
The woman has created a charitable purpose trust that is not valid
The woman has created a non-charitable purpose trust that is valid
The woman has created a non-charitable purpose trust that is not valid
The woman has created a trust in favour of the British Cat Fanciers' Association

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The trust that the woman has attempted to create does not fall within the list of charitable purposes and would not have sufficient public benefit to be regarded as a charitable trust. As it is not for the benefit of specific beneficiaries, it is a purpose trust. However since it does not fall within one of the established exceptions to the rule against purpose trusts, it would be held to be invalid.

stem: The European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) stipulates that judges must be of high moral character and must possess the qualifications required for appointment to high judicial office, or be jurisconsults (e.g. practitioners and academic lawyers) of recognised competence. Candidates must possess the necessary qualifications and expertise for such a senior judicial appointment. For how long
ask: do judges hold tenure at the European Court of Human Rights?

options.en: Election to the Court is for a fixed 4-year term
Election to the Court is for a fixed 10-year term
Election to the Court is for a fixed 6-year term
Election to the Court is for a fixed 8-year term
Election to the Court is for a fixed 9-year term

explanation.en: E is correct. Article 23 of the Convention states that judges to the ECtHR are elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected. The terms of office of judges expire when they reach the age of 70. The judges hold office until replaced. They do however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration. No judge may be dismissed from office unless the other judges decide by a majority of two-thirds that that judge has ceased to fulfil the required conditions.

stem: A man and woman own a freehold property at 123 The Street which they hold on trust for themselves as tenants in common in equal shares. The woman dies and the man decides to sell the property. His purchaser wants to make sure that that the man can give a valid receipt for the sale proceeds so that all beneficial interests in the property are overreached.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the?

options.en: The woman's beneficial interest in the property has automatically passed to the man in accordance with the Doctrine of Survivorship. The man alone can give a valid receipt for the sale proceeds
The woman's beneficial interest in the property has passed to her heir. The man alone can give a valid receipt for the sale proceeds

stem: Your trainee has been asked to enter a Notice on the Register of Title in respect of an HMRC charge concerning Inheritance Tax liability. Your trainee asks about the difference between agreed and unilateral notices and which notice

options.en: An agreed notice can only be entered in the Register of Title with the consent of the Proprietor or to the satisfaction of the registrar as to its validity, and can only be removed when the protected interest has come to an end or is invalid. A unilateral notice does not require consent of the Proprietor or satisfaction of the registrar but the Proprietor can have it challenged once entered. An agreed notice can only be entered with the consent of the Proprietor; the registrar has no discretion. The notice can be removed with the consent of both parties. A unilateral notice does not require the consent of the Proprietor but requires the consent of the registrar and can be challenged once entered. The charge must be registered using an agreed notice

An agreed notice can only be entered if the registrar is satisfied as to its validity; consent of the Proprietor is not required. The notice can be removed if challenged by the Proprietor. A unilateral notice is entered by the registrar at his sole discretion and can be challenged once entered. The charge must be registered using a unilateral notice
It is the HMRC that is responsible for entering the notice on the Register of Title, not your firm. The charge must be registered using a unilateral notice

An agreed notice can only be entered in the Register of Title with the consent of the Proprietor or to the satisfaction of the registrar as to its validity, and can only be removed when the protected interest has come to an end or is invalid. A unilateral notice does not require consent of the Proprietor or satisfaction of the registrar but the Proprietor can have it challenged once entered. The charge must be registered using an agreed notice

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. An agreed notice can only be entered in the Register of Title with the consent of the Proprietor or to the satisfaction of the registrar as to its validity, and can only be removed when the protected interest has come to an end or is invalid. A unilateral notice does not require consent of the Proprietor or satisfaction of the registrar but the Proprietor can have it challenged once entered. The charge must be registered using an agreed notice. The purpose of an agreed notice is to give notice of the interest to which it refers; it does not necessarily identify the beneficiary of the interest and does not note the devolution of any title to an interest. There are two elements to a unilateral notice entry: the first part gives brief details of the interest protected and identifies that the entry is a unilateral notice; the second part gives the name and address of the person identified by the applicant as the beneficiary of the notice. When a Proprietor applies to cancel a unilateral notice, it is the beneficiary of the notice that is required to prove the validity of their interest. Certain interests may only be protected by an agreed notice. An HMRC charge in respect of a liability for Inheritance Tax is one such interest.

stem: D made an agreement with V to kill V so that V's children could benefit from V's life insurance policy. D arranged to run V over as V was crossing the road, but en route to the 'accident', D's car broke down and the plan was abandoned.
ask: Which option best states the criminal liability of the parties, if any?

options.en: D may be charged with conspiracy to murder
V may be charged with conspiracy to murder
D and V may be charged with conspiracy to murder
V may be charged with incitement to murder
Neither D nor V may be charged with conspiracy to murder

explanation.en: E is the best answer. Neither D nor V may be charged with conspiracy to murder. The necessary component of the crime of conspiracy is the agreement between two or more persons to carry out a criminal act. The actus reus is the agreement. However, a person cannot conspire with the intended victim of the offence if the only other party to the conspiracy is the victim of the offence. The Criminal Law Act 1977, s. 2(2)(c) states that a person is exempt from liability for statutory conspiracy if: 'the only other person or persons with whom he agrees are (both initially and at all times during the currency of the agreement)... an intended victim of that offence or each of those offences.' The incitement offence was abolished in 2008.
