The police officer is liable in negligence for failing to assist the drowning person, or for her failure to call the rescue services

explanation.en: E is correct. A negligent omission may give rise to a duty of care where a special relationship already exists between the claimant and defendant requiring the latter to act, e.g. as between a doctor and patient, or a parent and child. An off duty police officer would be under a duty to assist in these circumstances. Lead case: R v Dytham (1979) QB 722. go go aly of care

stem: Non-fatal offences against the person are where there has been an attack on an individual that has not resulted in their death. The crucial statutory provision for offences against the person is contained in The Offences against the Person Act 1861. in the way in which they use unlawful force against the physical body of another person
ask: Which of the following best describes what is an assault is?

options.en: An assault is an action where an individual intends or is reckless in the way in which they use unlawful force against the physical body of another person
An assault is an action where an individual intentionally or recklessly might • cause any hurt or injury calculated to interfere with the health or comfort of the victim
An assault is an action where an individual intentionally or recklessly causes any hurt or injury calculated to interfere with the health or comfort of the victim
An assault is a course of conduct by which an individual intentionally or recklessly causes another to fear, on at least two occasions, that violence will be used against him
An assault is an action where an individual intentionally or recklessly causes the

explanation.en: E is correct. An assault is an action which is either intentional or potentially reckless and causes the individual to be worried that they are likely to suffer an immediate and unlawful act of personal violence against them. Lead case: Fagan v MPC [1969].

stem: A mother and her daughter contribute equally to the purchase of a property which is registered in the sole name of the daughter.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The daughter is the sole legal and beneficial owner of the property
The daughter holds the property on a constructive trust for herself and her mother in equal shares
The daughter holds the property on a resulting trust for herself and the mother in equal shares
The daughter holds the property on a constructive trust for herself and her mother in equal shares
The mother holds the property on a resulting trust for herself and her daughter in equal shares

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. In circumstances where one party contributes to the purchase of a property but does not become a legal owner, equity presumes a resulting trust in favour of that party according to their contribution. However, that presumption can be rebutted, including by the presumption of advancement, which presumes that unless a contrary intention can be demonstrated, a father (or mother) always intends to make an outright gift to their child.

stem: A man and woman are the registered proprietors of 123 The Street, a freehold property which they hold on trust for themselves as tenants in common in equal shares. The man has a substantial business overdraft. When his business fails, his bank obtains a money judgment against him and a charging order charging his equitable interest in the property.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the?

options.en: The man's bank has the benefit of an equitable charge and would protect this by way of notice in the charges register of 123 The Street
The man's bank has the benefit of a legal charge and would protect this by way of notice in the charges register of 123 The Street
The man's bank has the benefit of an equitable charge and would protect this by way of a Restriction in the Proprietorship register of 123 The Street
The man's bank has the benefit of a legal charge and would protect this by way of Restriction in the charges register of 123 The Street
The man's bank has the benefit of an equitable charge and this would be registered as a Land Charge

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. As the bank only has a charge over the man's beneficial interest in the property, this can not be protected by notice. Only an equitable charge over the legal estate (where all debtors are the only people beneficially entitled to the property) can be protected by way of notice. In cases where the charge extends over the beneficial interest of one proprietor only, the charge can only be protected by way of a Restriction.

stem: A gay woman and the National Association for Gays (NAG), complained about the criminalisation of homosexual activity. Petra has, as yet, not been detrimentally affected by the legislation. NAG is a homosexual pressure group.
ask: Taking in to account European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) jurisprudence, which of the petitioners, if any, is likely to have standing to bring proceedings?

options.en: The woman's petition is likely to have standing, although NAG's petition is not
NAG's petition is likely to have standing, but the woman's petition is not
Neither NAG's nor the woman's petitions are likely to have standing
Both NAG's and the woman's petitions are likely to have standing
Standing is not a term of jurisprudence recognized by the ECtHR

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. According to established authority, the ECtHR would admit a complaint about the criminalisation of homosexual activity by an applicant who had not yet been detrimentally affected by that legislation. An application by a gay pressure group, however, would be rejected as inadmissible ratione personae, unless directly affected by the impugned legislation. Lead case: Norris v Ireland (1989) 13 EHRR 186 - 16 May 1985 Application number 10581/83. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 34. View Results

stem: Most government functions are guided by constitutional convention rather than by a formal written constitution. As part of this uncodified British constitution, constitutional conventions of British constitutional law play a key role. They are rules that are observed by the various constituted parts though they are not written in any document having legal authority.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the Salisbury Convention?

options.en: The Salisbury Convention ensures that treaties, although ratified using royal • prerogative, will not be ratified until the passing of a suitable statute law by Parliament
The Salisbury Convention ensures that all money bills must originate in the House of Commons

The Salisbury Convention ensures that all UK Government Ministers, including the Prime Minister, must be members of the House of Commons or the House of Lords, and are thereby accountable to the respective branches of the legislature
The Salisbury Convention ensures that the House of Lords shall not oppose • legislation from the House of Commons that was a part of the government's manifesto
The Salisbury Convention ensures that judicial all Cabinet members must be members of the Privy Council

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The Salisbury Doctrine, or "Convention" as it is sometimes called, emerged from the working arrangements reached during the Labour government of 1945-51, when the fifth Marquis of Salisbury was the leader of the Conservative opposition in the Lords. The Convention ensures that major government bills can get through the Lords when the government of the day has no majority in the Lords. In practice, it means that the Lords does not try to vote down at second or third reading, a government bill mentioned in an election manifesto.

stem: Without the doctrine of vicarious liability, it could be argued that there would be no incentive for employers to minimise the risks created in the course of business. The doctrine of vicarious liability holds that an employer is liable for the negligent acts of omissions of its employees in the course of their employment.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes how the courts discern whether a negligent employee was acting in the course of his or her employment?

options.en: An act is not considered to be in the course of employment if the employee's mode of doing a job is wrongful and unauthorised
An act is not considered to be in the course of employment if the employee's mode of doing a job is wrongful, even if it is authorised by the employer
An act is not considered to be in the course of employment if the employee was going about his work in a negligent or mistaken manner
An act is not considered to be in the course of employment if it is an act authorised by the employer
An act is considered to be in the course of employment if it is either an act authorised by the employer or an unauthorised method of doing an act authorised by the employer

explanation.en: E is correct. An act is considered to be in the course of employment if it is either an act authorised by the employer or an unauthorised method of doing an act authorised by the employer... wu.. act

stem: Your client has been offered the opportunity to buy some shares in a business. She is unsure if being a shareholder means she will have personal liability over the company's debts and obligations. Advise your client whether she
ask: Advise your client whether she would be liable as a shareholder.

options.en: Shareholders are not liable for the company's debts and obligations and so there is no risk whatsoever that they could lose some or all of their investment
A shareholder is only personally liable if they own over 50% of the company's shares
Shareholders are not personally liable for the debts and obligations of the business
Shareholders are only personally liable if they own 100% of the company's shares
Shareholders are only personally liable for the company's debts and obligations if it is a private limited company and if they own 100% of the company's shares

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Shareholders are not personally liable for the debts and obligations of the business, but if the business fails they could lose some or all of their investment.

stem: A man has granted a woman a twelve month tenancy of 123 The Street. The lease contains a clause by which the man purports to contract out of the statutory obligation to repair. One night, lightning strikes a nearby tree, which damages the property and makes it uninhabitable. The woman seeks to enforce the repairing covenant against the man and make him reinstate the property.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man cannot contract out of the statutory covenant to repair and must reinstate the property for the woman to occupy
The man cannot contract out of the statutory covenant to repair but need not reinstate the property for the woman to occupy
The man can contract out of the statutory covenant to repair but must in this case reinstate the property for the woman to occupy
The man can contract out of the statutory covenant to repair and need not reinstate the property for the woman to occupy
The statutory covenant to repair does not apply in this case as the man is not letting the property as part of a business

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. A landlord, regardless of whether they are letting the property as a business or not, cannot contract out of the statutory obligation to keep the property in good repair. However, where damage occurs to the property as a result of fire, flooding or inevitable accident, the landlord need not reinstate the premises under the repairing covenant.

stem: A medical student was excluded from lectures because she insisted on wearing an Islamic headscarf, contrary to the medical school's rules. She claims that her right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) has been infringed.
ask: Are the medical school's rules compatible with the medical student's rights under the?

options.en: The rules are compatible with her rights, because in deciding whether restrictions on freedom of religion are necessary for protecting public order and the rights and freedoms of others, national authorities have a margin of appreciation
The ban constitutes an unjustified interference with her right to freedom of • religion, and in particular, her right to manifest her religion under the Convention
The rules are compatible with her rights, because there has been no interference with her right to exercise her freedom of religion under the Convention

The rules are not compatible with her Convention rights to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, because the Convention protects every act motivated or inspired by a religion or belief and in all cases guarantees the right to behave in the public sphere in a way which is dictated by a belief

The rules are not compatible with her rights to freedom of thought, conscience and religion under the Convention, because there is a positive obligation on the state to guarantee the right to behave in the public sphere in a way which is dictated by a religious belief

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. National authorities have special importance where questions concerning the state-religion relationship arise, as this is a matter on which opinion in a democratic society may reasonably differ widely. Lead case: Sahin v Turkey Application no. 44774/98 (2005) 41 EHRR 8. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 9 ECHR.

stem: Your partner asks you to research the limitation period for an action for breach of trust brought by a beneficiary due to fraud by a trustee.
ask: Which of the following is the correct statutory limitation period for an action for breach of trust by a beneficiary due to fraud by a trustee?

options.en: Six years
Three years
12 years
No time limit whatsoever
No statutory time limit, but a claimant will not be permitted to sue if it is unconscionable for them to do so

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. No statutory time limit, but a claimant will not be permitted to sue if it is unconscionable for them to do so. This is known as the equitable doctrine of laches. The court will look at all the relevant factors, including any lengthy delays on the claimant's part, or if the claimant has told the defendant that he would not sue, before deciding whether to permit the action to commence. From this doctrine the equitable maxims "the law will not help those who sleep on their rights" and "equity aids the vigilant" are derived.

stem: On his last day of a trip-of-a-lifetime to London, a man orders a meal at an expensive restaurant.
ask: After eating, he decides not to pay and exits the restaurant, leaving no contact details and makes his way to the airport to catch his flight out of the UK, Which criminal offence has the man committed, if any?

options.en: The man has committed no criminal offence - it is a civil matter between the parties
The man has committed the offence of taking without consent
The man has committed the offence of fraud by false representation
The man has committed the offence of theft
The man has committed the offence of making off without payment

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is E. The man has committed the offence of making off without payment. The offence is defined under Section 3 of the Theft Act 1978 as where: "... a person who, knowing that payment on the spot for any goods supplied or service done is required or expected from him, dishonestly makes off without having paid as required or expected and with intent to avoid payment of the amount due...". The prosecution must prove that the man made off from the spot without having paid when payment was due (actus reus) and that the man knew that payment was due, and dishonestly intended to avoid payment (mens rea). The law was created to cover circumstances; in such a case, the offender was previously unable to be under the deception laws.

stem: A public authority has breached a statutory duty, and that breach has caused loss to the claimant. The public authority accepts that it breached its obligations. The claimant seeks to recover damages in respect of that loss.
ask: Which option best states the threshold of liability, if any, for a public body's breach of its statutory duty?

options.en: Breach of a statutory duty, by itself, is sufficient for the recovery of damages
Breach of a statutory duty is not actionable for the recovery of damages, unless the statutory duty was performed negligently by a public body
Breach of a statutory duty is sufficient for the recovery of damages if the statute uses the language of duty
Breach of a statutory duty is not actionable for the recovery of damages, unless the statutory duty was performed carelessly by a public body
Breach of a statutory duty, by itself, is not sufficient for the recovery of damages

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. E is the best option. It settled law that breach of a statutory duty, by itself, is not sufficient for the recovery of damages. Simply because a public body has breached a statutory duty, and that breach has caused loss to the claimant, does not necessarily mean that the claimant is entitled to recover damages in respect of that loss. The careless performance of a statutory duty will not be actionable, unless a right of action exists for breach of statutory duty simpliciter or a common law duty of care in negligence. Lead case: X (Minors) v Bedfordshire County Council [1995] 2 AC 633

stem: An auction company placed an advert in a local newspaper: "Auction of household furniture - without reserve - Sunday, April 11th, The Auction House, High Street, Donfield, 10am".
ask: A man made the highest bid of £200 for a kitchen suite, but the auctioneer refused to sell, saying a reserve price of £1,000 had been placed on the Which of the following statements best explains the parties' legal position?

options.en: The man has a realistic claim for breach of contract against the auction house, • because the notice gave rise to a contract that all the items mentioned would actually be put up for sale
The man has no realistic claim for breach of contract against the auction house, because the notice did not give rise to any contract that all the items mentioned would actually be put up for sale

The man has no realistic claim for breach of contract against the auction house, because the auctioneer had specified that the auction was 'without reserve"; therefore no legal commitment arose which bound the auctioneer

The man has a realistic claim for breach of contract against the auction house, because the auctioneer had specified that the auction was 'without reserve"; therefore a legal commitment arose which bound the auctioneer
The man has a realistic claim for breach of contract against the auction house, because a collateral contract arose upon him acting on the notice

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The auctioneer had specified that the auction was 'without reserve"; a legal commitment arose which bound the auctioneer. Lead case: Warlow v Harrison (1859)........... eserve;

stem: Your client did not use her annual gift exemption for Inheritance Tax (IHT) purposes in years 2011, 2012, 2013 or 2014. The current amount of annual gift exemption for IHT purposes is £3,000. Your client would like to know how much she can give as a gift during 2015 in order to fully use her gift exemption.
ask: Which of the following states the correct amount according to the current legal position?

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. £6,000. The annual gift exemption for IHT purposes can be carried over but only for a maximum of one year. Your client can carry over the exemption from the previous year and use the exemption for the current year. Thus, the maximum she can give in gifts will be £6,000 in 2015 if she wishes to stay within the annual gift exemption boundaries.

stem: A pedestrian fell down a man hole in the pavement that had been left exposed by a negligent council worker. The pedestrian injured his ankle in the fall. The financial value of the pedestrian's claim for damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity amounts to £850.
ask: Which option best advises your client in which court his claim will be allocated?

options.en: The claim will be allocated to the county court (small claims track)
The claim will be allocated to the county court (fast track)
The claim will be allocated to the county court (multi-track)
The claim will be allocated to the High Court (Chancery Division)
The claim will be allocated to the High Court (Queen's Bench Division)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is A. A personal injury claim will only be allocated to the small claims track, if the value of the claim for personal injury (i.e. the damages claimed for pain, suffering and loss of amenity) is not more than £1,000.

stem: A person entrusted with discretion in matters of public law must exclude from his consideration matters which are irrelevant to what he has to consider. If he does not obey those rules, he may truly be said, and often is said, to be acting "unreasonably".
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the "Wednesbury unreasonableness" standard in judicial review proceedings?

options.en: accepted moral standards that no sensible person who had applied his mind to the question could have arrived at it

The "Wednesbury unreasonableness" standard is engaged in judicial review proceedings when a person on whom public power is conferred has failed to exercise his inherent power at common law to determine whether the action is lawful or not

The "Wednesbury unreasonableness" standard is engaged in judicial review proceedings when a person on whom public power is conferred fetters the future exercise of his discretion by committing himself now as to the way he will exercise the power in the future

The "Wednesbury unreasonableness" standard is engaged in judicial review proceedings when a tribunal has passed a rule, or come to a determination, not to hear any application of a particular character by whomsoever made

The "Wednesbury unreasonableness" standard is engaged in judicial review proceedings where a decision fails to include sufficient reasons for particular proposals to allow those consulted to give intelligent consideration and an intelligent response when the ultimate decision is taken

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Under Lord Diplock's classification, a decision is irrational if it is "so outrageous in its defiance of logic or of accepted moral standards that no sensible person who had applied his mind to the question could have arrived at it." This standard is also known as "Wednesbury unreasonableness". Lead case: Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223.

stem: You have been instructed to act for a private company in relation to a share transaction. You are liaising with a junior employee and have commenced standard customer due diligence.
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed in respect of verification of identity?

options.en: You need only verify the identity of the junior employee
You need only verify the identity of the directors, whether they have day-to- day control over the company or not
You need only verify that the company is incorporated
You need to verify the identity of all the shareholders and directors
You need to verify any and all individuals who hold more than 25% of the • shares or voting rights in the company and you need to understand the ownership and control structure of the company

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Regulation 5(b) of the MLR requires you to verify the beneficial owner of the customer, where that beneficial owner is not the customer. You are also required to take measures to understand the ownership and control structure of the legal person. Regulation 6(1) defines a beneficial owner as any individual who holds more than 25% of the share or voting rights, or otherwise exercises control over the management of the company. The junior employee fits neither category, so Answer A is wrong. A director is not always someone who exercises control they necessarily shareholders (and not all shareholders are beneficial owners), so Answers B and D are wrong. Whilst you are required to understand the ownership and control structure of the company, verification of incorporation is not sufficient, nor does it identify the beneficial owner, so C is wrong.

stem: https @gits.litmos.com/course/6267/module/47354/Scorm?LPid =0 - MCT7 - Immediate Feedback An accountant is a volunteer director of a private company limited by shares which operates for charitable purposes. Three other people are also volunteer directors and none of the directors receive remuneration, although one of the directors acts as the de facto Financial Director. The company retains professional advisers, such as lawyers, accountants etc, to administer its affairs and protect its interests. It comes to light that the head of the company's accounts department has been defrauding the company and transferring money from the company accounts into his own.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: None of the directors could be held liable for a failure to prevent the fraud because the company had retained professional advisers
The accountant who is also a director would be expected to carry out her duties with a higher degree of care, skill and diligence due to her profession
The de facto Financial Director would be expected to carry out her duties with a higher degree of care, skill and diligence due to her position on the board

Both the accountant who is a director and the de factor Financial Director would be expected to carry out their duties with a higher degree of care, skill and diligence due to their profession and position on the board respectively
All of the directors have an equal statutory duty to carry out their functions with the same degree of care, skill and diligence

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. All directors must carry out their functions to a degree of care, skill and diligence which would reasonably be expected of someone (a) with the general knowledge, skill and experience that can reasonably be expected of someone carrying out the functions of a director, and (b) with the general knowledge, skill and experience that the particular director in question has. In this case, the accountant who is a director would be expected to carry out her functions with a greater degree of care, skill and diligence due to her profession and the de facto Financial Director due to her closer working knowledge of the company's finances.

stem: A woman, the registered proprietor of 123 The Street, grants a lease in writing to a man for 10 years.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The man does not need to protect the lease by way of a notice
The man must register the lease with its own title number
The man must protect the lease by way of a Restriction in the Proprietorship Register of the woman's title
The man should protect the lease by way of a notice in the Property Register of the woman's title
The man should protect the lease by way of notice in the Charges Register of the woman's title

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is B. The man must register the lease with its own title number. A legal lease granted for more than seven years must be registered with a separate title at the Land Registry. When an application is lodged for registration of a lease granted out of registered land that is required to be registered, no application is required to note the lease on the lessor's registered title. Notice will automatically be entered in the lessor's title on the Charges Register by the Land Registry. A lease not protected in this manner will not bind a subsequent purchaser as an overriding interest (unless the tenant is in actual and obvious occupation of the property, under Schedule 3.2 Land Registration Act with its own title number in order for the lease to operate at law. They will automatically be protected as an overriding interest against the registered freehold title. Note: while option E could also be correct under certain circumstances, B is still the best option.

stem: A house owner pinned up notices stating that his neighbour took a lawnmower from his garage, sold it the next day and pocketed all the money without his permission, and that, in the house owner's opinion, his neighbour stole the lawnmower. It transpired on the facts that the neighbour did not take the lawnmower from the garage but from the garden shed, and that he did not sell it the next day but a week afterwards.
ask: Which option best states the effect the house owner's mistakes would have on a defence of truth and honest opinion to the neighbour's claim, if at all?

options.en: The mistakes in the statement complained of and the matter justified are so • great they would defeat a defence of truth; the question of fact for the court would be whether the defendant has substantially justified the libel

The fact that the lawnmower was not taken from the garage but from the garden shed, and that the neighbour did not sell it the next day but a week afterwards does not prevent the defence of honest opinion from succeeding

The fact that the lawnmower was not taken from the garage but from the garden shed, and that the neighbour did not sell it the next day but a week afterwards does not prevent the defence of truth from succeeding

The fact that the lawnmower was not taken from the garage but from the garden shed, and that the neighbour did not sell it the next day but a week afterwards will prevent the defence of honest opinion from succeeding

The fact that the lawnmower was not taken from the garage but from the garden shed, and that the neighbour did not sell it the next day but a week afterwards will prevent the defence of truth from succeeding

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is the best option. The fact that the lawnmower was not taken from the garage but from the garden shed, and that the neighbour did not sell it the next day but a week afterwards does not prevent the defence of truth from succeeding. The defence of truth requires the defendant to prove that the words complained of were true or substantially true (section 2(1) of the Defamation Act 2013). The fact, therefore, that the neighbour did not take the lawnmower from the garage but from the garden shed, and that he did not sell it the next day but a week afterward would not prevent the defence of truth from succeeding.

stem: A husband and wife have been married for 3 years. The husband promises to pay his wife £400 per month to cover her expenses. They end up separating and the husband refuses to pay his wife any further.
ask: Which of the following statements best advises if the parties intended to make a legally binding contract?

options.en: Once married couples begin to haggle, it may safely be presumed that they intended to create legal relations
The presumption that domestic agreements are not intended to be legally binding does not apply when the parties are separated
The onus is on the defendant to rebut the presumption that in social and domestic arrangements there was no intention to contract
The law presumes that social agreements are intended to be legally binding
The law presumes that domestic arrangements involving married couples are intended to create legal relations

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The presumption against legal relations does not apply if the spouses are not living together in amity but separated or about to separate. Lead case: Balfour v Balfour [1919] 2 KB 571.

stem: A majority of the UK Supreme Court held that once a local authority had a contractual and proprietary right to possession of a property, there was nothing further to investigate. That decision was flatly contradicted by a subsequent decision of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR).
ask: In light of this statement, what approach must domestic lower courts adopt where domestic binding precedent conflicts with an ECtHR ruling?

options.en: Domestic lower courts must follow binding domestic precedent and not inconsistent authority from the ECtHR
Domestic lower courts must follow apparently inconsistent authority from the ECtHR

Domestic lower courts which would ordinarily be bound to follow the decision of another court higher in the domestic hierarchy are no longer bound to follow that decision if it appears to be inconsistent with a later ruling of the ECtHR
Domestic lower courts are bound to follow a later ECtHR ruling where the ECtHR ruling has been given since the domestic ruling on the point at issue

Domestic lower courts are bound to follow a later ECtHR ruling where the ECtHR has established a clear and authoritative interpretation of Convention rights based on an accurate understanding of UK law

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Lower courts must follow binding domestic precedent and not apparently inconsistent authority from the European Court of Human Rights. Lead case: Kay & Ors v. Lambeth London Borough Council & Ors [2006] UKHL 10. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 2(1) HRA 1998.

stem: A man and woman are shareholders of a small private limited company. They each hold 50% of the shareholding. The man is the sole director of the company. The woman has been out of the country for a number of months and appointed the man to act as her proxy for the purposes of voting in any shareholders' meetings. When the woman returns, she realises that the man has been using the company to run an illegal business and engage in criminal activity. She revokes the man's authority to vote on her behalf but the man continues to engage in criminal activity. The woman is unable to revoke the man's appointment as a director due to the fact that they each hold 50% of the shareholding and there is a deadlock. The woman wishes to wind up the company while it is still solvent, but the man will not agree to this.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman could apply to the court for relief under section 994 of the Companies Act on the basis that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner which is unfairly prejudicial to her
The woman could apply to the court for a winding up order under section 122 • Insolvency Act 1986 on the basis that the company is engaged in criminal activity and there is a shareholder deadlock
A winding up order under section 122 insolvency Act 1986 would not be available as the company is still solvent
The woman could bring a derivative claim under Part 11 Companies Act 2006
The woman could apply for a winding up order under section 122 insolvency Act 1985 or could bring a derivative claim under Part 11 Companies Act 2006

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. A winding up order from the court under section 122(1)(g) of the Insolvency Act 1986 would be available on the basis that there is a deadlock between the shareholders and that the company is being used for an illegal purpose. Such an order can be made whether the company is solvent or not. It would also be open to the woman to bring a derivative claim on behalf of the company on the basis that the man has breached his fiduciary duty to the company to act in its best interests. The woman has not necessarily been prejudiced by the man's actions in running the company for an illegal purpose and therefore it would be unlikely that an application under section 994 of the Companies Act would be

stem: A man transfers part of his freehold land to a woman. He includes in the transfer deed an obligation upon the woman "for the benefit of the retained land not to use the land transferred for any noisy, offensive or noxious trade or business". The man subsequently transfers the land that he has retained to a friend. The woman transfers her land to her sister.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The friend would enforce the covenant against the man at common law
The friend would enforce the covenant against the sister at common law
The friend would enforce the covenant against the man in equity
The friend would enforce the covenant against the sister in equity
The friend can not enforce the covenant against the man or sister

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The benefit of the covenant has passed to the friend in accordance with the common law rules, however the burden of the covenant can not pass to the sister at common law (the woman remains liable at law for the performance of the covenant). In order to enforce the covenant against the sister in equity, the friend must establish firstly that the burden has passed to the sister in equity and secondly that the benefit has passed to herself in equity. The burden has passed to the sister in accordance with the rule in Tulk v Moxhay because the covenant is negative, The man (the original covenantee) had at the time of the covenant retained land which was benefited by it, the covenant. The benefit of the covenant has passed to the friend because it touches and concerns the land, and is therefore deemed to be made with the man and his successors in title by virtue of s.78 Law of Property Act 1925. Words of annexation have also been used as the covenant is expressed to be "for the benefit of the retained land"

stem: A boyfriend and his girlfriend fell asleep watching a movie on TV. The girlfriend awoke when she felt an object hitting her head. The boyfriend, while still sleeping, was standing over his girlfriend, holding a laptop in the air, and striking her on the head with it. The boyfriend, who woke up immediately after the incident, testifies that he does not remember having hit his girlfriend. Expert witnesses agree that the boyfriend was sleepwalking at the time of the violent attack on his girlfriend.
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate defence available to the boyfriend under these circumstances?

options.en: The most appropriate defence available to the boyfriend under these circumstances is insanity
The most appropriate defence available to the boyfriend under these circumstances is non-insane automatism
The most appropriate defence available to the boyfriend under these circumstances is sane automatism
The most appropriate defence available to the boyfriend under these circumstances is diminished responsibility
The most appropriate defence available to the boyfriend under these circumstances is loss of control

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is the best answer. According to English case law, a defendant who pleads not guilty on the basis that he or she was asleep at the time of the alleged offence should be classified as putting forward the insanity defence. Sleepwalking was held to be a "disease of the mind" by the Court of Appeal in Rv Burgess [1991] and any such condition which results in violence is to be regarded as one of insanity. This is because such involuntary conduct is caused by the accused's sleepwalking, which is an internal factor that is liable to recur. The continuing danger theory therefore applies. Options B and C amount to the same thing since the terms are used interchangeably. Options D and E are not appropriate in the circumstances, because diminished responsibility and loss of control are partial defences to murder. Lead case: R v Burgess [1991] 2 All ER 769 Note: while sleepwalking per se is categorised as insane automatism, a one-off incident caused, for instance, by an external factor such as a blow to the head or drug taking, would probably be categorised as non-insane automatism. Sleepwalking in Bratty v Attorney General for Northern Ireland [1963] AC 386 was considered to be an archetype of non-insane automatism. Lord Denning observed obiter that: act is punishable if it is done involuntarily and an involuntary act... means an act which is done by the muscles without any control by the mind such as a spasm, a reflex action or a convulsion; or an act done by a person who is not conscious of what he is doing, such as an act done whilst suffering from concussion or done whilst sleep-walking...". Sleep-associated automatism, however, may be caused by functional disorders which affect the mind. In R v Burgess [1991] 2 All ER 769 the Court of Appeal sleepwalking was subsequently held to be a "disease of the mind", and any such condition which results in violence is to be regarded as one of insanity.

stem: Your client, along with a large group of people is arrested for rioting in a field on the outskirts of town. Your client claims that he owns the field and the offence of riot cannot be committed on private land. Advise your client whether this claim
ask: Advise your client whether this claim is correct under statute.

options.en: The offence of riot can be committed on private as well as public land
The offence of riot can only be committed on public land
The offence of riot can only be committed on private land
The offence of riot can be committed on private land but only if the land is owned by a business
The offence of riot can be committed on private land but only if the land is owned by an individual

explanation.en: • YUMMUNIs You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Under the Public Order Act 1986 the offence of rioting can be committed on public or private land.

stem: Your client owns a shop selling children's clothes. Although he has not reached the threshold for obligatory VAT registration, he is considering registering anyway, as he thinks it may benefit him financially. Advise your client whether he
ask: would benefit by registering for VAT under the current law?

options.en: If registered for VAT, your client could charge VAT at the standard rate and claim it back on any VAT the business paid
If registered for VAT, your client could charge VAT at the reduced rate and claim it back on any VAT the business paid
If registered for VAT, your client could charge VAT at the zero rate and claim it back on any VAT the business paid
Your client would be unable to register for VAT until he reaches the threshold
Your client cannot register for VAT due the type of goods he sells

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. If registered for VAT, your client could charge VAT at the zero rate and claim it back on any VAT the business paid. Children's clothes are subject to the zero rate of VAT. Although they are not exempt, the consumer doesn't actually pay any more because the VAT is 0%. If registered, your client's customers wouldn't pay any more but your client could claim back any VAT the business has paid on items coming back in to the business, thus benefiting the business.

stem: At the time of the ticket cases in the last century, it was notorious that people hardly ever troubled to read printed conditions on a ticket, delivery note or similar document. That remains the case now. In the intervening years the printed conditions have tended to become more complicated and one-sided in favour of the party who is imposing them.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes a condition?

options.en: A condition is a major term which is vital to the main purpose of the contract
A condition is where the effect of breach depends on the seriousness of the consequences of breach
A condition is anything the court considers that the parties intended to apply to a contract, but did not need express provision simply because it would have been taken for granted by the parties
A condition is something that does not go to the root of the contract and will probably only entitle the other party to claim damages
A condition is where the record of a transaction is embodied in a document and where extrinsic evidence is not generally admissible to vary or interpret the document or as a substitute for it

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. A condition is a major term which is vital to the main purpose of the contract.

stem: Over the past 11 months there have been a lot of disputes between the shareholders and directors of a company and accusations of wrongdoing. As a result, the shareholders would like the company to be wound up by the court, but as the company is still solvent they are not sure if this would be possible.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: A company can only be wound up if it becomes insolvent
If solvent, a company can only be wound up following agreement signed by all the shareholders
If solvent, a company can only be wound up following agreement by the majority shareholders
A solvent company can be wound up if the court considers it is just and equitable' to do so
A solvent company can be wound up by the court but only if there has been criminal activity taking place within, or in the name of, the company

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Under s122(l)(g) Insolvency Act a company can be wound up if the court considers it is 'just and equitable' to do so, even if the company is still solvent. In practice, it is a procedure which is rarely used but it could be applicable in instances where there is deadlock between the shareholders, where the conduct of the company has been oppressive, or where the company has been run for criminal activity, for example.

stem: The approach to the award of compensation in human rights cases has led to the conclusion - in a joint report produced in October 2000 by the Law Commission and the Scottish Law Commission - as a 'lack of clear principles [in the Strasbourg case-law] as to when damages should be awarded and how they should be measured'. All one can say with any certainty is that damages have been awarded for non-pecuniary loss.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the law relating to damages according to the principles established under the Human Rights Act (HRA) 1998?

options.en: Damages under the HRA may be claimed together with claims for prerogative • orders in judicial review proceedings; or alongside tortious damages in a public law claim
Damages under the HRA may be claimed together with claims for prerogative orders in judicial review proceedings; or alongside tortious damages in a private law claim
Damages under the HRA may be claimed together with claims for declarations in judicial review proceedings; or alongside exemplary damages in a private law claim
Damages under the HRA may be claimed together with claims for injunctions in judicial review proceedings; or alongside damages in a private law claim
Damages under the HRA may be claimed together with claims for prerogative orders in judicial review proceedings; or alongside special damages in a private law claim

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Damages under the HRA may be claimed together with claims for prerogative orders in judicial review proceedings; or alongside tortious damages in a private law claim. Section 8(3)(b) HRA 1998 provides that damages will be awarded only where, "the court is satisfied that the award is necessary to afford just satisfaction. " See Somerville v Scottish Ministers, where Lord Rodger stated at paragraph 127: "..In my view, that construction would pervert the purpose of section 8(3) and (4): the subsections do not exist to cap other remedies, but to give the court the power to grant further relief by way of damages, if, but only if, that is necessary to afford just satisfaction." In other rant turner renet vy way ur udmayes, ", but uny ", that is necessary to afford just satisfaction. " In other words, section 8(3) presupposes that all the other remedies provided by statute or the common law (including, if appropriate, the law of delict) are available and then allows the court to give an additional remedy by way of damages where that is necessary to afford just satisfaction. As Lord Bingham of Cornhill observed in R (Greenfield) v Home Secretary [2005] 1 WLR 673, 684, para 19, the HRA "is not a tort statute". So the damages that a court can award under section 8 have nothing to do with tort or delict: as section 8(6) says, they are ramanes for the unlawful art of the nuhlir authoritv tort or delict that the court would otherwise award. Equally, there is no warrant for interpreting section 100(3) of the Scotland Act as imposing a restriction on any common law remedy of damages for delict that section 8(3) and (4) of the HRA would not impose. --3 =- damages for the unlawful act of the public authority. There is therefore no conceivable reason why section 8 (3) or (4) should impinge on any damages for tort or delict that the court would otherwise award. Equally, there is no warrant for interpreting section 100(3) of the Scotland Act as imposing a restriction on any common law remedy of damages for delict that section 8(3) and (4) of the HRA would not impose. Lead case: Somerville v Scottish Ministers [2007] UKHL 44; [2007] 1 WLR 2734, para 127. Statute; rule; constitution: S. 8(3) and (4) HRA 1998.

stem: A man and woman act as trustees for a charitable trust founded to assist struggling law students in Oldcastle. The man dies, leaving the woman to administer the affairs of the trust. She is retired so is able to devote a lot of time to this, meaning that she never gets round to appointing a trustee to replace the man. The woman dies suddenly in a car accident. There is no appointer nominated in the trust instrument.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The trust fails as there are no trustees
The court must appoint a new trustee
The beneficiaries can appoint a new trustee
Either the man or woman's personal representatives can appoint a new trustee
The woman's personal representatives can appoint a new trustee

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The trust would not fail simply because there is no trustee. The equitable maxim that "equity will not allow a trust to fail for want of a trustee" would apply and the person with legal ownership of the trust property would become the trustee. As the woman was the last surviving trustee, this would be her personal representative. The woman's personal representative would also have the ability to use the statutory power of appointment at Section 36 Trustee Act 1925 to appoint one or more replacement trustees.

stem: Treaties make up one of the generally accepted trio of international law sources, the other two being customary international law and general principles of law. Every treaty in force is binding upon its parties (i.e. the states that have ratified/acceded to it), and must be performed by them in good faith.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes how treaties are ratified in the UK?

options.en: In the UK, treaties are ratified by the government, acting under international law
In the UK, treaties are ratified by the government, after a debate and vote in Parliament
In the UK, treaties are ratified by the government, acting under royal prerogative
In the UK, treaties are ratified by Parliament, acting under royal prerogative
In the UK, treaties are ratified by Parliament, after it debates and votes on the measure

explanation.en: No MER You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. In the UK, treaties are ratified by the government, acting under the royal prerogative. Please note; while the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 limits the prerogative, the Act allows governments to ignore Parliament if it wishes to do so. Note that the European Union Act 2011 requires a referendum, before the government could ratify a treaty which amends or replaces the current EU main treaties (TEU or TFEU). Statute; rule; constitution: Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010.

stem: A woman executes an express declaration of trust appointing two people as trustees of a large agricultural property, with the income being paid to the woman during her lifetime and the property vesting in her sister on the woman's death. The woman fails to execute the transfer of the legal title to the land to the trustees.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman holds the property on trust for herself during her lifetime and her personal representative holds it for her sister after the woman's death
The trustees hold the property on trust for the woman during her lifetime and for the woman's sister after the woman's death
The woman's sister holds the property on trust for the trustees during the woman's lifetime and thereafter the property vests in herself absolutely
The sister holds the property on trust for the woman during the woman's lifetime and for herself after the woman's death
The trust fails because the woman did not transfer legal title to the trust property to the intended trustees

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The equitable maxim that "equity will not allow a trust to fail for want of a trustee" would apply. The woman would hold the property on resulting trust for the original intended beneficiaries according to the terms of the trust. However the trustees would be under a duty to collect in the trust property and would have to sue the woman's personal representative for the trust property if necessary.

stem: A man and woman own 123 The Street together as joint tenants.

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Where one joint tenant dies, their share in the property automatically devolves to the surviving joint tenants in accordance with the Doctrine of Survivorship.

stem: A burglar was verbally challenged by the property owner. He sustained injury when jumping from a second story window to escape capture. One of the parties asserts ex turpi causa non oritur action.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the term ex turpi causa non oritur?

The term ex turpi causa non oritur action implies that from an immoral cause no action arises
The term ex turpi causa non oritur action implies that morality and immorality is of no significance in an action for tort

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Ex turpi causa non oritur action is Latin for 'no action can be based on a disreputable cause,' i.e. the courts may refuse to enforce a claim arising out of the claimant's own illegal or immoral conduct or transactions.

stem: An applicant successfully challenged a decision by a public health authority in judicial review proceedings. The remedy applied by the Administrative Court is a quashing order or order of certiorari
The remedy applied by the Administrative Court is a mandatory order or mandamus
The remedy applied by the Administrative Court is a declaration
The remedy applied by the Administrative Court is a prohibiting order

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. A quashing order nullifies a decision which has been made by a public body. The effect is to make the decision completely invalid.

stem: The claimants incurred expenditure in preparing for filming a television play. They subsequently entered into a contract with the defendant for him to play the leading role. The defendant repudiated the contract, and there being no substitute available, the claimants were forced to abandon the play. Which measure of damages

stem: On the advice of her solicitor, a woman executes an inter vivos deed of trust whereby she transfers her holiday home to a man as trustee, giving a friend a life interest with the woman's brother being given a vested remainder interest. However when the woman had initially met with her solicitor, she had actually intended to transfer the property to her friend absolutely by way of a gift. Her solicitor has misunderstood her instructions and drafted the deed incorrectly.
ask: Which of the following statements most accurately describes the position?

options.en: The woman has created a valid trust
The woman's trust has failed for lack of certainty of intention
The woman's trust has failed for lack of certainty of intention and objects
The woman's trust has failed for lack of certainty of objects and subject matter
The woman's trust has failed for lack of certainty of subject matter

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. Although the deed itself would tend to prima facie evidence an intention to create a trust, the woman in fact did not have the requisite intention to create a trust. She executed the deed as a result of a mistake. The trust would therefore fail for lack of certainty of intention. Certainty of objects (the woman's friend as life tenant and the woman's brother as remainderman) and subject matter (the holiday home) exist and therefore in all other respects, the trust would be valid.

stem: A man has been arrested and detained by the police on suspicion of a terrorist offence that resulted in the death of scores of Londoners. stem: A woman owns 80% of the issued share capital of a private limited company, while two other shareholders own 10% each. At the company's general meeting, a resolution is proposed and the matter is put to a show of hands. The woman votes against the resolution, with the other two shareholders voting in favour of it. ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The resolution would be passed

All resolutions on general meetings are, unless validly requested otherwise, decided upon by a show of hands. Subject to any rights or restrictions attached to any shares according to the articles of association, and in accordance with section 284 of the Companies Act 2006, when a show of hands is used, each member voting in the meeting has one vote, regardless of the number of shares that they hold. It is possible for a member to demand a poll, where each member has one vote per share held. In this case, however, the fact pattern does not state that any of the members has requested a poll neither that the company's articles place (hence, option C is incorrect). Therefore, since the matter is put to a show of hands, the woman has only one vote (regardless of her being the owner of 80% of the issued share capital), whilst the two other shareholders have one vote each (i.e., two votes in total). Since the two other shareholders vote in favour of the matter proposed, that resolution will pass, regardless of the voting rights of the shareholders (hence, option E is incorrect). stem: As with other criminal offences there are specific issues associated with attempted crimes. The actus reus and mens rea need to be shown for the offence to have been deemed to have been committed.
ask: Which of the following best states the actus reus that is required for an attempt?

options.en: The actus reus for an attempted offence is that at least two people do an act • which is more than merely preparatory to the commission of the offence with the intention of committing an offence
The actus reus for an attempted offence is that a person does an act which is more than merely preparatory to the commission of the offence

Under s. 1(1), Criminal Attempts Act 1981, the defendant has the actus reus of an attempt if he takes steps that are more than merely preparatory towards the commission of an offence. stem: An experienced electrician was killed while working on an electrified fence at a factory. The owners of the factory had actually warned the electrician of the danger.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the occupier's statutory duty, if any, in respect of risk?

stem: A woman and her daughter are beneficiaries of a will trust established by the woman's mother. If these conditions are not fulfilled then the capital must be paid to a local animal shelter. The woman's daughter is 21 and wants a new car. stem: A woman worked in a busy bar with two fellow employees for payment at the rate of £50 per shift. The woman phoned her boss and explained that the other two employees were off sick for the rest of the week and that the customers were becoming increasingly rowdy and aggressive towards her, because she wasn't able to cope alone.
ask: Although her boss told her that if she manages alone for the rest of the week, he would pay her double wages, he now refuses to pay her the extra money Which of the following statements best advises the woman whether she has a legal right to the extra pay which she was promised?

options.en: There is no consideration because the woman was only promising to do what she was already obliged to do under her existing contract

There is no consideration because by agreeing to the woman's demands there would be an increased risk in this type of situation whereby employees would blackmail employers into promising extra wages to avoid seeing their businesses close
There is consideration because the work had become so onerous that it was unreasonable to require the woman to continue alone

There is no consideration, because the two other employees being off sick was just part of the normal hazards of working in a bar

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The promise to pay the woman increased wages if she continued to work was supported by good consideration. The rowdy and aggressive environment discharged her from the original contract, as a result of which she was free to enter into the new contract. Lead case: Hartley v Ponsonby (1857).

stem: It is the year 2137 and it has been proclaimed that the (fictitious) only son (and second born child) of King William and the Queen Consort is to be married to a Roman Catholic. explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is the best option. The son would succeed to the throne. The Monarch is the Supreme Governor of the Church of England. The Monarch must join in communion with the Church of England, must declare him or herself to be a Protestant, and must swear to maintain the established churches in England and Scotland and take the coronation oath. Until the enactment of the Succession to the Crown Act 2013 (the "Act"), any Monarch marrying a marries a Catholic cannot retain his or her throne and must be removed from the line of succession. However, the Act has removed this restriction and allows the future Monarch to marry a Roman Catholic. Also, Methodists, Congregationalists, Church of Scotland, and Baptists can take Anglican Communion and are therefore not excluded. In addition, and until the Act came into force, the Crown passed to male heirs ahead of female heirs according to common law. However the Act also ends the principle of male primogeniture in deciding who ascends the throne. ••d -. or male primogeniture in deciding no ascenas ine throne. In this case then the eldest daughter would not success to the throne as she is a Roman Catholic and must be a Protestant to become the Queen. The succession would then follow through the blood line to the second born child, the son, who will become the King even if he marries a Roman Catholic. The youngest child is practising Buddhist (i.e., she is not a Roman Catholic) and will not be qualified in any event to succeed the throne).
