stem: According to the (fictional) Motor Vehicles (Construction and Use) Regulations, in order to park in a certain way, permission was required from a policeman in uniform. A police officer in uniform, who did so, was prosecuted and relied on the defence that he had given himself permission. The court rejected his defence and interpreted the grammatical and ordinary sense of the words so as to avoid the absurdity and held that "permission" meant that permission had to be given by one person in uniform to another.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario?

options.en: The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the Golden rule
The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the Literal rule
The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the Mischief rule
The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the Purposive approach
The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the Unified Common approach

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The Golden rule requires the court to take the whole statute and construe it all together, giving the words their ordinary significance unless, when so applied, they produce an inconsistency or an absurdity or inconvenience so great as to convince the court that the intention could not have been to use them in their ordinary signification, and to justify the court in putting on them some other significance which, though less proper, is one which the court thinks the words will bear.

stem: A workman was working on the roof of a house. A slate fell from the roof and landed on a person below causing her injury. Which of the following statements best describes what
ask: Which of the following statements best describes what is meant by the term res ipsa loquitur?

options.en: The term res ipsa loquitur means 'the thing speaks for itself'
The term res ipsa loquitur means 'to stand by things decided'
The term res ipsa loquitur means 'no wrong is done to one who consents'
The term res ipsa loquitur means 'as much as he deserves'
The term res ipsa loquitur means 'no action can be based on a disreputable cause'

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The term res ipsa loquitur means 'the thing speaks for itself'.

stem: As a criminal case is effectively the state taking an action against an individual, the parties to the case are the individuals who have been accused of the crime and the state. This explains why so many criminal cases are referenced as Rv an individual.
ask: Which of the following best states what the letter 'R' stands for in criminal cases in England and Wales?

options.en: The letter 'R' stands for 'Royal" in criminal cases in England and Wales
The letter 'R' stands for 'Regal' in criminal cases in England and Wales
The letter 'R' stands for 'Ruler' in criminal cases in England and Wales
The letter 'R' stands for 'Regina' in criminal cases in England and Wales
The letter 'R' stands for 'Regency' in criminal cases in England and Wales

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The letter 'R' stands for 'Regina' in criminal cases in England and Wales. As a criminal case is effectively the state taking an action against an individual, the parties to the case are the individuals who have been accused of the crime and the state. This explains why so many criminal cases are referenced as R v an individual. 'R' stands for 'Regina' and represents the state. In practice, however, the prosecution will be driven by the government body which is running the case, such as the Crown Prosecution Service or HM Revenue and Customs, depending on the nature of the case.

stem: Super-injunctions are a controversial recent development, owing to the extent to which they allegedly depart from open justice. They are controversial for another reason too, namely that they are the most obvious form of the recent development of the substantive law of privacy as a consequence of the enactment of the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA).
ask: What distinguishes super-injunctions from other forms of interim remedies?

options.en: The super element is that such injunctions are only used to protect confidential information which has passed between individuals in a commercial relationship
The super element is the automatic anonymisation of the parties
The super element is that such injunctions allow for routine derogations from open justice in claims for misuse of private information

The super element is that such injunctions are used to protect, and enforce, • substantive legal rights which are and of themselves determinative of the parties' rights in order to facilitate the administration of justice
The super element is a prohibition on the disclosure or communication of the existence of the order and the proceedings

explanation.en: E is correct. The super element is a prohibition on the disclosure or communication of the existence of the order and the proceedings. It is this which has authoritatively been identified as being the feature which transforms an injunction into a super-injunction. Lead case: Ntuli v Donald [2010] EWCA Civ 1276 at [43] ff. S. t

stem: A woman is the sole trustee of a medium-sized private family will trust, which does not permit self-dealing. The trust holds a controlling majority shareholding in a company, which was the former family business. The woman has recently lost her job and the remuneration that she is paid by the will trust is not enough to live off. She calls a general meeting of the company and uses the trust's shareholding to pass a resolution appointing herself as a director, with an attractive remuneration package. She has no idea about running a limited company.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman is a lawfully appointed director of the company and she is entitled to keep her remuneration
The woman is a lawfully appointed director of the company but must account to the trust for her remuneration
The woman is not a lawfully appointed director of the company but she is entitled to keep her remuneration
The woman is not a lawfully appointed director of the company and she must account to the trust for her remuneration
The woman is a lawfully appointed director of the company and is entitled to keep the remuneration with the consent of two thirds of the trustees

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. Within the meaning of the company's rules, the woman has been duly appointed as a director of the company, since the majority shareholder passed the resolution. Her appointment as a director would therefore be lawful. However, the remuneration arising out of that appointment is only available to her as a result of her position as a trustee. As she has a duty not to profit from the trust, she must account to the trust for any remuneration she receives as a result of her holding the directorship.

stem: A company has a share capital of £100 divided equally between two members. The company operates a coffee shop in the centre of Newtown from premises leased by the members from Newtown City Council for that purpose. Newtown City Council seeks to bring the tenancy to an end and the two members of the company claim the protection of Part Il of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954, which gives security of tenure to the tenants of leased land occupied for the purposes of a business carried on by the tenant.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The company would be able to claim the benefit of Part Il of the 1954 Act
The two members would be able to claim the benefit of Part Il of the 1954 Act
The two members would not be able to claim the benefit of Part Il of the 1954 Act because they are not the tenants
The company would not be able to claim the benefit of Part Il of the 1954 Act because it is not carrying on its business on the premises
The two members would not be able to claim the benefit of Part Il of the 1954 Act because they are not carrying on their business on the premises

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The two members are the tenants under the lease of the premises. Although they are the members of (and therefore regarded as the owners of) the company, the business itself is being carried on by the company and not by its members. This is due to the concept that the company has a separate legal personality to its members. The requirement that the business is being carried on by the tenant of the premises would therefore not be satisfied in this case.

stem: The significant rise in workload for the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) prompted changes in 1998. The new system of protection created a new, full-time ECtHR where all applications would go. Acceptance of ECtHR jurisdiction and the right of individual petition became compulsory features of membership.
ask: Which of the following best states how the ECtHR's final judgments are executed?

options.en: Execution of the ECtHR's final judgments is supervised by the Council of Ministers
Execution of the ECtHR's final judgments is supervised by the Commission of Ministers
Execution of the ECtHR's final judgments is supervised by the Committee of Ministers
Execution of the ECtHR's final judgments is supervised by the Convention of Ministers
Execution of the ECtHR's final judgments is unsupervised; it is the final court of appeal

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The Committee of Ministers was denied the decision- making role that had been thought essential in 1950. Its role is now to supervise the execution of judgments.

stem: A woman is the freehold owner of 123 The Street, an unregistered freehold property which is not within a compulsory first registration area. She grants a charge by way of legal mortgage to BankCo to secure repayment of a mortgage advance, and BankCo allows the woman to keep the title deeds. The woman grants a second charge by way of legal mortgage to MortgageCo. MortgageCo registers a Class C(i) Land Charge.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: MortgageCo takes its mortgage subject to the charge to BankCo because BankCo's legal mortgage binds the world
MortgageCo takes its mortgage free from the charge to BankCo because BankCo has not retained the title deeds
MortgageCo takes its mortgage free from the charge to BankCo because BankCo has not registered a Land Charge
MortgageCo takes its mortgage free from the charge to BankCo because BankCo has not retained the title deeds or registered a Land Charge
MortgageCo takes its mortgage free from the charge to BankCo because MortgageCo is a bona fide purchaser for value without notice of BankCo's interest

explanation.en: emind Charge. You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The Land Charges Act 1972 provides that all mortgages which are not protected by the deposit of title deeds (i.e. "puisne mortgages") will not bind subsequent interests in the land unless they are registered. As BankCo's mortgage is not protected by the deposit of title deeds, it will rank as a puisne mortgage within the meaning of the Act and therefore rank after the mortgage to MortgageCo.

stem: A woman was married to a man. The man abused the woman for a number of years.
ask: One evening, the woman poured petrol over the man whilst he was sleeping and set With regard to the Coroners and Justice Act 2009, which of the following statements best describes the situation of defendants charged with murder where the acts or omissions result in the death of the victim?

options.en: madone means a pod d party to the killing resulted from his loss of self-control; (2) the loss of self- control had a qualifying trigger, and (3) a person of the defendant's sex and age, with a normal degree of tolerance and self-restraint and in the circumstances of the defendant, might have reacted in the same or in a similar way to the defendant

Where a defendant kills or is a party to the killing of another, the defendant is not to be convicted of murder if: (1) his acts and omissions in doing or being a party to the killing resulted from his loss of self-control; (2) the loss of self- control had a qualifying trigger, and (3) a person of the defendant's sex and age, with a normal degree of tolerance and self-restraint and in the circumstances of the defendant, might suddenly have reacted in the same or in a similar way to the defendant

Where a defendant kills or is a party to the killing of another, the defendant is not to be convicted of murder if: (1) his acts and omissions in doing or being a party to the killing resulted from his sudden loss of self-control; (2) the loss of self-control had a qualifying trigger, and (3) a person of the defendant's sex and age, with a normal degree of tolerance and self-restraint and in the circumstances of the defendant, might have reacted in the same or in a similar way to the defendant

Where a defendant kills or is a party to the killing of another, the defendant is not to be convicted of murder if: (1) his acts and omissions in doing or being a party to the killing resulted from his loss of self-control; (2) the loss of self- control had a qualifying trigger, and (3) a reasonable person of the defendant's sex and age, with a normal degree of tolerance and self-restraint and in the circumstances of the defendant, would have reacted in the same or in a similar way to the defendant

Where a defendant kills or is a party to the killing of another, the defendant is not to be convicted of murder if: (1) his acts and omissions in doing or being a party to the killing resulted from his loss of self-control; (2) the loss of self- control had a sudden trigger, and (3) a person of the defendant's sex and age, with a normal degree of tolerance and self-restraint and in the circumstances of the defendant, might have reacted in the same or in a similar way to the defendant

explanation.en: aarone You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. Where a defendant kills or is a party to the killing of another, the defendant is not to be convicted of murder if: (1) his acts and omissions in doing or being a party to the killing resulted from his loss of self- control; (2) the loss of self-control had a qualifying trigger, and (3) a person of the defendant's sex and age, with a normal degree of tolerance and self- restraint and in the circumstances of the defendant, might have reacted in the same or in a similar way to the defendant. In relation to the reference "loss of self- control" within section 54(1)(b) Coroners and Justice Act 2009 it does not matter whether or not the loss of control was sudden.

stem: An airplane overflew a land owner's property and took aerial photographs from several hundred metres altitude. The land owner wishes to sue the pilot.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the most appropriate advice to give to the land owner?

options.en: Under these circumstances the actions of the pilot constitutes trespass to land
Under these circumstances the actions of the pilot does not constitute trespass to land
Under these circumstances the actions of the pilot constitutes a conversion
Under these circumstances the actions of the pilot constitutes trespass to land because the land owner's airspace was violated
Under these circumstances the actions of the pilot constitutes trespass to land but the doctrine of jus tertii affords a defence to the pilot

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The rights of landowners over airspace are not unlimited; in Bernstein of Leigh v Skyviews & General Ltd [1978], the action for trespass failed because the violation of airspace took place several hundred metres above the land. Lead case: Bernstein of Leigh v Skyviews & General Ltd [1978].

stem: You are the Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO) for your firm. You receive a disclosure from a partner who suspects that a high net worth client who he is representing in the middle of a property transaction is involved in money laundering, with clear evidence supporting this assertion. This client is a longstanding client of the firm and a significant source of the firm's income. You decide not to make a disclosure for those reasons.
ask: Which of the following best describes your position?

options.en: You have not committed any offence as you have discretion as to whether to make a disclosure to National Crime Agency (NCA)
You have committed a 'failure to disclose' offence, and have no defence
You have committed a 'failure to disclose' offence, but have a defence because the information came to you in privileged circumstances
You have committed an 'arranging' offence by not making a disclosure, as you • are allowing the transaction to proceed. However, you have not committed a 'failure to disclose' offence
You have committed both an 'arranging' offence, and a 'failure to disclose' offence

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. Under s331 POCA, a nominated officer commits an offence if, as a result of an internal disclosure under s330, he knows or suspects, or has reasonable grounds for knowing or suspecting, that another person is engaged in money laundering and he fails to disclose as soon as practicable to NCA. This information did not come to you in privileged circumstances, as it was disclosed by the partner actually acting for the client and in the middle of a transaction. You are failing to disclose on commercial grounds, which is not a defence to the s331 offence. You are not committing an 'arranging' offence because the act for which there is an arrangement has not yet

stem: A and B entered into contractual relations. During their negotiations, A made an oral promise to B, which B relied upon, but the contract contains a term which is inconsistent with the oral promise made to B.
ask: A seeks to adduce oral evidence of the Which legal doctrine may preclude B from giving evidence of the promise?

options.en: The legal doctrine that may preclude B from giving evidence of the promise is the rule of incorporation
The legal doctrine that may preclude B from giving evidence of the promise is the contra proferentem rule
The legal doctrine that may preclude B from giving evidence of the promise is the parol evidence rule
The legal doctrine that may preclude B from giving evidence of the promise is the rule that proper and reasonable notice
The legal doctrine that may preclude B from giving evidence of the promise is the rule of construction

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is the best option. The legal doctrine that may preclude B from giving evidence of the promise is the parol evidence rule. The parol evidence rule states that where the record of a transaction is embodied in a document, extrinsic evidence is not generally admissible to vary or interpret the document or as a substitute for it. In the case of Hutton v Watling it was held that the parol evidence rule does not apply re incompleteness.

stem: Your client wants to enter a building where an event of a corporate from which she was recently fired is taking place, in order to disrupt the activity.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes whether your client will commit the offence of aggravated trespass?

options.en: Aggravated trespass only applies to land in the open air
Aggravated trespass only applies to activities inside a building
Aggravated trespass applies to lands or buildings where an unlawful activity is taking place
Aggravated trespass applies to lands where a lawful activity is taking place
Aggravated trespass applies to lands or buildings where a lawful activity is taking place

explanation.en: UNMMUNIS You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is E. The Anti-Social Behaviour Act 2003 extended the provisions relating to the offence of aggravated trespass to cover trespass in buildings, as well as in the open air. The result is that the offence of aggravated trespass will be constituted where a person trespassing, whether in a building or in the open air, does anything which is intended to intimidate or deter persons from engaging in a lawful activity, or to obstruct or disrupt that activity.

stem: Once it is established that the defendant owes the claimant a duty of care, the second matter which must be established is that the defendant breached that duty of care, by failing, objectively speaking, to take reasonable care. Which of the following statements best describes
ask: what element a claimant must show to establish negligence, in addition to duty of care and breach of duty, from the?

options.en: In addition to duty of care and breach of duty, a claimant must establish fault arising from the breach
In addition to duty of care and breach of duty, a claimant will have to establish malice arising from the breach
In addition to duty of care and breach of duty, a claimant will have to establish loss or damage arising from the breach
In addition to duty of care and breach of duty, a claimant will have to establish negligence arising from the breach
In addition to duty of care and breach of duty, a claimant will have to establish liability arising from the breach

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. Damage is one of the three elements required to establish negligence.

stem: A man executes a trust deed in which he places certain property on trust for the benefit of a UK-based private boarding school which caters for the children of British expatriates living in India. The trustees want the trust to benefit from charitable status and therefore make an application to the Charity Commission to be recognised as such. You are asked to advise the Charity Commission as to whether the trust could be considered charitable.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the?

options.en: The trust is for a charitable purpose, has an identifiable benefit and benefits the public or a section of the public
The trust is not for a charitable purpose, has an identifiable benefit and benefits the public or a section of the public
The trust is not for a charitable purpose and has no identifiable benefit
The trust is not for a charitable purpose, has an identifiable benefit but does not benefit the public or a section of the public
The trust is a non-charitable purpose trust

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The trust is established for the benefit of the school and not for the advancement of education generally. It has certainty of objects and is therefore neither a charitable nor a non-charitable purpose trust. Although the school may itself fulfil the criteria for charitable status, the man has created a separate trust which, by virtue of the fact that it exists solely for the benefit of the school, does not directly benefit the public at large.

stem: Your client, who earns £12,000 a year on income support, applied for a hardship student loan, which is only available to students earning less than £15,000 a year. She ignored the part of the application form asking whether there was anyone else living in her house with her. In fact she lives in the same house as her fiancée who earns £25,000 per year.
ask: Which of the following best states your client's criminal liability, if any, under the?

options.en: Your client may be charged with fraud by false representation and fraud by obtaining services by deception under the Fraud Act 2006
Your client may be charged with fraud by obtaining services by deception under the Fraud Act 2006
Your client may be charged with fraud by abuse of position under the Fraud Act
Your client may be charged with fraud by false representation under the Fraud Act 2006
Your client may be charged with fraud by failing to disclose information under the Fraud Act 2006

explanation.en: E is correct. Your client's failure to declare that she lives with her fiancée in the same house could amount to fraud by a failure to disclose information which she has a legal duty to disclose.

stem: Gipsies, or travellers, had their licences to live on local authority-owned land summarily revoked. Mobile-home owners, who did not belong to the traveller population, did not have their licences revoked.
ask: Which right or rights, if any, are engaged under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention)?

options.en: The scenario engages the travellers' right to protection from discrimination
The scenario engages the travellers' right to protection from discrimination and the right to respect for the home
The scenario engages the travellers' right to right to respect for the home

The Convention is not engaged because the contractual and proprietary rights • to possession of a public authority landowner cannot be defeated by a defence based on an individual's right to respect for his home

The Convention is not engaged because it is not open to an individual to rely on an individual's right to respect for his home in answer to an unchallengeable claim to possession by a local authority landowner

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The scenario engages the travellers' right to protection from discrimination and the right to respect for the home. Any finding of a violation of Article 8, would likely not raise a separate issue under Article 14. A and C are both partially correct. Lead case: Connors v United Kingdom (2004) 40 EHRR 189. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 8 ECHR/Article 14 ECHR.

stem: A man and woman practise together in partnership as solicitors. The firm's debts to BankCo are secured by personal guarantees extended to BankCo by both the man and woman, as well as by second mortgages on their substantial homes. The man withdraws £5,000 from the firm's office bank account and uses it to buy a rare antique book, which he subsequently sells for £7,500. He repays the £5,000 to the firm and puts £2,500 into his own bank account.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man is under a fiduciary duty to the woman to repay the £2,500 to the partnership if asked to do so by the woman
The man is under a contractual duty to repay the £2,500 to the partnership only if the partnership agreement provides for this
The man is under no duty to repay the £2,500 to the partnership
The man is under a fiduciary duty to repay the £2,500 to the partnership only if the partnership agreement provides for this
The man is under a fiduciary duty to repay the £2,500 to the partnership and holds it on trust for the partnership in the meantime

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Section 29 of the 1890 Act provides that a partner is under a duty to account to the firm, whether asked to do so or not, for any profit that he makes from any use of the partnership's property. This is a positive duty imposed upon partners by the 1890 Act and it is not possible for the partners to contract out of it and it is not necessary to contract into it. The money in the office account belongs to the firm and therefore any profit derived from a transaction using that money also belongs to the firm.

stem: Your client is a company in the midst of restructuring its operations. It has decided to sell one of its buildings and is about to execute the deed of sale. The director responsible for signing on behalf of the company has never executed a deed before and wants to check whether he is permitted to sign on behalf of the company. The company has adopted the model articles of association; thus, the default statutory provisions for execution of documents by a company apply.
ask: Can a single director execute a deed on behalf of a company on his own?

options.en: Yes, but only by affixing the company seal
No, two authorised signatories are required
Yes, as long as it is in the presence of a witness
Yes, without the need for a witness
No, only a person specifically empowered with power of attorney to execute deeds on behalf of the company can do so

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Yes, as long as it is in the presence of a witness. This is provided for under Section 44(2)(b) of the Companies Act 2006. A company can execute a deed by affixing its seal, but this is not the only method of execution; signature by an authorised person is also permitted, which can include a director and the company secretary. The provisions governing the execution of deeds by a company are contained in the Companies Act 2006, but provision should also be made in the company's articles of association so as to allow for matters such as the appointment of an attorney to execute documents on behalf of the company.

stem: A court was confronted with a dispute over a term in a car insurance contract that purported to exclude liability for excess 'loads'. The car subject to the dispute, however, was carrying more passengers than the number which it was constructed to carry.
ask: This meant that the court had to engage in a process of interpretation regarding the meaning of the terms 'loads' and 'passengers' Which of the following statements best describes which rule the courts apply in the context of exemption clauses?

options.en: Where a term in an exemption clause is ambiguous, the courts will apply the 'rule of law' doctrine against the person putting it forward
Where a term in an exemption clause is ambiguous, the courts will apply the 'fundamental breach rule' against the person putting it forward
Where a term in an exemption clause is ambiguous, the courts will apply the 'de minimis rule' against the person putting it forward
Where a term in an exemption clause is ambiguous, the courts will apply the 'contra proferentem rule' against the person putting it forward
Where a term in an exemption clause is ambiguous, the courts will apply the 'rule of construction' against the person putting it forward

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. In the context of exclusion clauses, the language used by the parties may be ambiguous, in which case, the ambiguity is likely to be construed against the party who wishes to rely upon a particular term of the contract. Lead case: Houghton v Trafalgar Insurance [1954] 1 QB 247.

stem: A man has been a practising barrister for several years and recently saw an advert placed in legal journal for applications to become a Recorder.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes how Recorders are appointed?

options.en: Recorders are appointed by the Queen, on the recommendation of the Lord Chancellor
Recorders are appointed by the Prime Minister, on the recommendation of the Lord Chancellor
Recorders are appointed by the Lord Chancellor, on the recommendation of the Prime Minister
Recorders are appointed by the Lord Chancellor, on the recommendation of the Queen
Recorders are appointed by the Lord Chancellor, on the recommendation of the Judicial Appointments Commission

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Recorders are appointed by The Queen formally rather than by the Lord Chancellor.

stem: A man gives a woman a lift home from the office every evening after work. One evening they stopped at a pub for a drink and on the way back to the car the man made a pass at the woman in the dark and deserted car park. Frightened by the man's action, the woman ran away from him, on to the road where she was struck by an oncoming car and suffered severe, non-life threatening, bruising to her thigh.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the man's probable criminal liability,?

options.en: The man's probable criminal liability is for maliciously wounding or maliciously inflicting grievous bodily harm (GBH)
The man's probable criminal liability is for actual bodily harm (ABH)
The man would not be criminally liable because he did not directly inflict the harm
The man would not be criminally liable because he did not directly inflict actual bodily harm (ABH)
The man would not be criminally liable because he did not directly inflict grievous bodily harm (GBH)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. A defendant need not act intentionally or recklessly in causing the ABH as long as he acted intentionally or recklessly in causing the assault. Lead case: Rv Roberts (1971). Statute; rule; constitution: s47 of Offences Against the Person Act (OAPA) 1861.

stem: A man transfers part of his unregistered land to a woman, who intends to use the land as a dairy farm. The transfer triggers compulsory first registration. The transfer includes the grant of a right of way for the woman over the man's land for as long as the woman uses her land as a dairy farm.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the manner in which the woman would protect the right of way?

options.en: The woman would protect the right of way using a registered easement
The woman would protect the right of way using a Land Charge
The woman would protect the right of way using an agreed notice
The woman would protect the right of way by entering a unilateral notice on the title to the man's land
The right of way does not need to be protected as it is a legal interest

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The right of way is not granted for a fixed term of years or in perpetuity and it is therefore an equitable easement. As it is not a legal interest, it must be registered to bind a purchaser of the man's land. As the man's land would remain unregistered (compulsory first registration would only apply as to the part transferred to the woman) it must be registered as a Land Charge. Equitable easements are protected by way of a Class D(iii) Land Charge.

stem: A company agreed to ship to a buyer 100 barrels of engine oil.
ask: While it was customary in the oil trade to sell engine oil per gallon, the company had mistakenly offered to sell the oil by the barrel, which was significantly to its detriment and to the Which of the following statements best advises the parties of their respective rights under these circumstances?

options.en: Mutual mistake occurs where both parties contract, but contemplate different facts
There is a mistake where one party is mistaken as to the terms of the offer and the other party is aware, or ought to be, aware of it
Caveat emptor applies in situations whereby the courts will not save buyers from the consequences of their bad bargains
The doctrine of res extincta means a contract is not void where there is a mistake as to the existence of the subject matter of the contract
While an operative mistake will render a contract void, the mistake must occur during the formation of the contract

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Mistake as to the terms of the offer can occur where one party is mistaken as to the terms of the offer and the other party is aware, or ought to be, aware of it. Lead case: Hartog v Colin & Shields [1939)....... is a Y...

stem: A man walked in to a sports shop. The woman working in the shop overheard the man speaking in to his mobile phone saying, "I'm going to buy a baseball bat to beat up my next door neighbour".
ask: Although the woman believes that the man is likely use the baseball bat to assault his next door neighbour, she sells the baseball bat to him Assuming that the man committed the assault on his next door neighbour, which of the following best states the woman's criminal liability, if any?

options.en: that the man should attack his next door neighbour, even though she believed that the man was likely to use the bat to attack his next door neighbour

The woman is guilty of assault because she intended, desired or agreed that the man should attack his next door neighbour, and her belief that the man was likely to use the bat to attack his next door neighbour is sufficient to render the woman complicit in and liable for the man's offence

The woman is not guilty of assault despite the fact that she intended, desired or agreed that the man should attack his next door neighbour, because her belief that the man was likely to use the bat to attack his next door neighbour is insufficient to render Jessica complicit in and liable for the man's offence

The woman is guilty of assault despite the fact that she did not intend, desire or agree that the man should attack his next door neighbour, because her belief that the man was likely to use the bat to attack his next door neighbour is sufficient to render the woman complicit in and liable for the man's offence

The woman is not guilty of assault because she neither intended, desired nor • agreed that the man should attack his next door neighbour, nor did she believe that man was likely to use the bat to attack his next door neighbour

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The case law suggests that the woman is guilty of assault despite the fact that she did not intend, desire or agree that the man should attack his neighbour. The woman's belief that the man is likely to use the bat to attack his neighbour is sufficient to render the woman complicit in and liable for the man's offence. In sanctioning the conviction of the man for assault in the scenario, the current law arguably fails to afford proper weight to the principle that ought to underpin secondary liability, namely parity of culpability. Thus the man intended to attack his next door neighbour, whereas the woman did not intend that his next door neighbour should be attacked. HILAL MUVE BLIYINVUE

stem: A man executes a declaration of trust in which he places a large sum of money on trust to be used to establish a dance music club on the island of Ibiza.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The trust is valid
The trust has failed and the money reverts to the man's trustees
The trust has failed and the man's trustees hold it on a resulting trust for him
The trust has failed and the man's trustees hold it on a constructive trust for him
The trust has failed and the man's trustees hold it on an express trust for him

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The trust would be classified as a non- charitable purpose trust and would therefore fail. In those circumstances, the trustees would hold the trust property on a resulting trust for the donor.

stem: The position after the Human Rights Act (HRA) 1998 was stated by Laws LJ in Runa Begum v. Tower Hamlets LBC [2002]: "The extent to which the first instance process may be relied on to produce fair and reasonable decisions is plainly an important element. But it is not to be viewed in isolation.
ask: The matter can only be judged by an examination of the statutory scheme as a whole; that is the necessary setting for any intelligent view as to what is fair and reasonable." In light of the above declaration, which of the following statements best states the practical impact, if any, the HRA 1998 has had on judicial review proceedings?

options.en: Persons who are the victim of a violation of the HRA by a private body may apply for judicial review or rely on the breach when exercising any right of appeal which may be available to them
Persons who are the victim of a violation of the HRA by a public authority may • apply for judicial review or rely on the breach when exercising any right of appeal which may be available to them
Persons who are the victim of a violation of the HRA by a private authority may apply for judicial review
Persons who are the victim of a violation of the HRA by a public authority may • rely on the breach when exercising any right of appeal which may be available to them
Persons who are the victim of a violation of the HRA by a private authority may • rely on the breach when exercising any right of appeal which may be available to them

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. A person who is the "victim" of a violation of the HRA 1998 by a public authority may apply for, inter alia, judicial review or to rely on the breach when exercising any right of appeal which may be available to them (s7 HRA). The question relates to public authorities and applications against them. Statute; rule; constitution: S.7 HRA 1998.

stem: Two men and a woman are all partners in a firm. During the course of business, one of the men enters into a loan agreement on behalf of the firm. When they decide to dissolve the partnership the woman argues that she is not liable for the debt as she did not enter into it.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: Only the person who enters into the debt is liable for it
If the partnership if dissolved then none of the partners would be liable for the debt
All partners are liable for the debts of the partnership, unless it can be shown that the partner had no authority to carry out the transaction
All partners are liable for the debts of the partnership, unless the person he is dealing with knows this or knows or suspects that he is not a partner

All partners are liable for the debts of the partnership, unless it can be shown that the partner had no authority to carry out the transaction and that the person he is dealing with knows this or knows or suspects that he is not a partner

explanation.en: The best answer is E. Provided that the partner who entered into the loan agreement was doing so within the bounds of the law and subject to the partnership agreement (if any), every partner in the firm is liable jointly with the other partners for all debts and obligations of the firm incurred while he is a partner, per Section 9 of the Partnership Act 1890; it does not matter whether the female partner was a named party to the transaction on behalf of the firm. However, if it can be shown that the partner had no authority to carry out the transaction and that the person he is dealing with knows this or knows or suspects that he is not a partner, the firm will escape liability. Answers C and Dare both incomplete.

stem: In 1980 a woman and man purchase 123 The Street as their family home, and they hold it on trust for themselves as joint tenants. In 1995 they separate. The woman moves out and wants to sell the property. The man refuses to join in the sale.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman and man hold the property under a trust of land and the property must be sold
The woman and man hold the property on a trust for sale and the property must be sold
The woman and man hold the property on a trust of land and there is no obligation to sell the property
The woman and man hold the property on a trust for sale and there is no obligation to sell the property
As the woman and man hold the property as joint tenants, there is no obligation to sell the property

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is B. The land is held on a trust for sale. A trust for sale imposes an obligation to sell the property with a power to postpone the sale as long as all of the trustees unanimously consent. As soon as any trustee no longer consents to postponing the sale, the property must be sold. Note that trusts for sale were abolished in 1997, replaced by trusts for land. Since the events described in the fact pattern occurred prior to 1997, trust of land does not apply.

stem: The School Bus Act 2011 provides that each local council shall have the duty to subsidise school bus services within its area in the interests of school pupils. The mayor of Donfield Council, who is a 'born again Christian', decided to subsidise a weekly Sunday bus service to Donfield Evangelical Hall, a service used almost exclusively by fundamentalist Christians from within the electoral district which recently returned the mayor to office.
ask: Which is the best ground under judicial review, if any, that is raised by the mayor's decision to subsidise a weekly Sunday bus service to Donfield Evangelical Hall?

options.en: The best ground for judicial review raised by the mayor's decision to subsidise a weekly Sunday bus service to Donfield Evangelical Hall is a breach of natural justice
The best ground for judicial review raised by the mayor's decision to subsidise a O weekly Sunday bus service to Donfield Evangelical Hall is the duty to give reasons
The best ground for judicial review raised by the mayor's decision to subsidise a weekly Sunday bus service to Donfield Evangelical Hall is the failure to consult
The best ground for judicial review raised by the mayor's decision to subsidise a weekly Sunday bus service to Donfield Evangelical Hall is irrationality

The best ground for judicial review raised by the mayor's decision to subsidise a weekly Sunday bus service to Donfield Evangelical Hall is that the decision fails the Wednesbury unreasonableness test

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The decision to subsidise the weekly bus service to the Donfield Evangelical Hall - used almost exclusively by fundamentalist Christians who are also voters in the mayor's electoral ward - is that the decision is a breach of natural justice. •.. stem: A man has a machine component that needs repair, and engages a contractor to carry out the work. The man tells the contractor that the repair must be completed on 5 November, because the man has an order for which he needs the machine on 6 November, which he will lose if the machine is unavailable. Due to the contractor not repairing the component on time, the man lost the 6 November order and consequently lost another order from the Army, which suddenly had to deal with a conflict that had broken out in North Africa.
ask: Which of the following statements best describe which measure of damages the man will be entitled to?

options.en: The man will be able to claim for the lost profit on the order resulting from the North African conflict but not the 6 November contract
The man will be able to claim the lost profit on the 6 November contract, but not the order resulting from the North African conflict
The man will be able to claim the lost profit on the 6 November contract, and for the order resulting from the North African conflict
The man can claim neither the lost profit on the order resulting from the North African conflict nor for the 6 November contract
The man would not be entitled to recover lost profits, since the contractor could only be held liable for losses that were generally foreseeable

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. If the contractor, in breach of contract, fails to carry out the work, the man will probably be able to claim the lost profit on the 6 November contract. If the contractor had performed the contract properly, the man would have made the profit, and therefore it should be recoverable. Lead case: Hadley v Baxendale.

stem: A woman is the solicitor of a family trust, which holds 25% of the shares in a bakery company. She is concerned about what she believes to be underperformance of the company. On attending a general meeting of the company's members, the woman realises that the company's problems can be very easily resolved. The other trustees refuse to agree to purchase a larger holding in the company on behalf of the trust, so the solicitor, with the knowledge and consent of all of the other trustees, acquires a majority holding in the company. She is able to very quickly resolve the company's problems and pays a significant dividend to the shareholders, including the trust.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position relating to the solicitor's dividend?

options.en: The solicitor has not made an unauthorised profit from her position as trustee as she obtained the consent of the trustees
The solicitor has not made an unauthorised profit from her position as trustee because the trust did not want to invest in the company
The solicitor has made an unauthorised profit from her position as trustee but can keep it as she has generated a profit for the trust also
The solicitor has made an unauthorised profit from her position as trustee which will be held on resulting trust for the trust of which she is a trustee
The solicitor has made an unauthorised profit from her position as trustee which will be held on constructive trust for the trust of which she is a trustee

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The solicitor has made a profit from her position as trustee. She obtained the information as to the company's fortunes and how they could be rectified in her capacity as trustee; therefore, that information is itself trust property. In order to be authorised to generate such a profit, the consent of all beneficiaries who have legal capacity is required, not the consent of the other trustees. Whether the trust has suffered a loss or made a profit itself makes no difference, and the profits that the trustee makes will be held on constructive trust for the beneficiaries of the trust.

stem: The Human Rights Act (HRA) 1998 incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention). Specifically, the Convention accords respect for privacy and family life into domestic law. The courts have developed the common law in light of the Convention and its jurisprudence.
ask: What has been a common law consequence of this regarding the development of?

options.en: One consequence of this has been the development of the torts of breach of the peace and misuse of fiduciary data
One consequence of this has been the development of the torts of breach of trust and misuse of proprietary business information
One consequence of this has been the development of the torts of breach of • fiduciary duty and misappropriation of confidential and proprietary business information
One consequence of this has been the development of the torts of breach of confidence and misuse of private information
One consequence of this has been the development of the torts of breach of duty and misappropriation of confidential information

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Since the HRA incorporated the Convention, and specifically Article 8 into domestic law, the courts have developed the common law in light of the Convention and its jurisprudence. One consequence of this has been the development of the torts of breach of confidence and misuse of private information. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 8 ECHR.

stem: A woman has decided to leave her current employer and work for herself. However, her contract states that she is not able to compete with her former employer for one year following her resignation. In order to avoid this restriction, the woman sets up a limited company and argues that the company is a separate legal entity and she is not, therefore, breaching the contract.
ask: Advise the woman of the current legal position regarding this type of activity?

options.en: The action is valid as the new company is a separate legal entity and does not violate any contracts
The action is not valid as a contract cannot limit future action of an employee
The courts will ignore the fact that the company is a separate legal entity
The courts will look at the woman's role within the company to see if she is breaching the contract
The courts can never ignore the fact a company is a separate legal entity

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. If the purpose of a setting up a company is to evade legal responsibility then the court will ignore the fact that the company is a separate legal entity. In Gilford Motor Company Ltd (1933), Horne left the company and proceeded to set up a new company in order to avoid breaching his contract which stated he could not compete with the company. The judge went behind the 'veil of incorporation' and decided that Horne and his company were the same entity.

stem: ACo Limited owns an unregistered freehold plot of land. It constructs a block of flats known as King Edward's Court and grants long leases of the flats to residents. ACo transfers King Edward's Court to BCo Limited and this transfer triggers compulsory first registration. ACo retains the surrounding land. ACo omits to include part of the access road onto the public highway (which crosses the land that ACo has retained), meaning that the residents of the block must cross ACo's land with vehicles for access. Pedestrian access can be gained directly to King Edward's Court from the highway. ACo sells its retained land to CCo Limited and this triggers compulsory first registration.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position immediately after the transfer to CCo?

options.en: Any implied easements in existence at the time of the transfer to CCo will bind • CCo only as long as they are protected by way of a caution against the plot of land
Any implied easements in existence at the time of the transfer to CCo will bind CCo only as long as they are protected by way of a Land Charge
Any implied easements in existence at the time of the transfer to CCo will bind • CCo only as long as they are protected by a note on BCo's title to King Edward's Court
Any implied easements in existence at the time of the transfer to CCo will rank as interests which override an unregistered disposition
Any implied easements in existence at the time of the transfer to CCo will rank as interests which override a registered disposition

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Any implied easements over unregistered land are overriding interests under Schedule 1 Land Registration Act 2002. They therefore do not need to be protected in any other way to bind a purchaser.

stem: Three men set up a partnership two years ago. They all agreed to manage the company, but for the last six months two of the partners have made a lot of management decisions without allowing any input from the third partner. The third partner is unhappy and wishes to dissolve the partnership on this basis.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal situation?

options.en: The first two partners are acting within their rights as the majority of partners are making the management decisions
All partners must be involved in management decisions regardless of any clauses in the partnership agreement
Every partner must have a say in the management decisions unless the partnership agreement limits his right to do so
There must be one partner appointment to take management decisions
Dissolution can only follow death, criminal activity of a partner or the winding up of the company

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Unless the partnership agreement limits the right to do so, every partner must have a say in management decisions. If he or she is stopped from doing so, they will have the right to dissolve the firm.

stem: When a man bought, in good faith, a second-hand car from a car dealer, he was told by the car dealer that the odometer recorded 10,000 miles, but that the mileage was not warranted. Shortly thereafter, the man resold the car to the claimant, signing a document declaring that to the best of his knowledge and belief the odometer reading was correct. In fact the car's true mileage was over 80,000 and it was clear that the man had been misled when he bought the car.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes whether there had been a misrepresentation by the man?

options.en: There had been a misrepresentation, because it is irrelevant whether the man had been misled when the car was sold to him and was acting in good faith when he resold it
There had been no misrepresentation, because the man had been misled when the car was sold to him and was acting in good faith when he resold it
There had been a misrepresentation, because even if made innocently, the man's representation was false
There had been no misrepresentation by the man, because the concept of mere representation indicates that such a false statement of fact is not an actionable misrepresentation
There had been a misrepresentation by the man, because innocence does not mean that the belief was truly and reasonably held

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The traditional rule is that a representation must be a statement of fact, past or present, as distinct from a statement of opinion, or of intention, or law. A mere statement of opinion which proves to be unfounded will not be treated as a misrepresentation. Lead case: Humming Bird Motors Ltd v Hobbs' ([1986] RTR 276, CA.

stem: Police allege that your client climbed in to a house by a side window, having broken a pane of glass. He entered the living room where he picked up a laptop and exited through the same window. Your client is unsure of the elements of the mens rea for the offence of burglary, and asks for an explanation.
ask: Which of the following statements best defines the mens rea for the offence of?

options.en: The mens rea for burglary requires intention or recklessness regarding the • trespass and intention to commit theft or an ulterior offence at the time of entry
The mens rea for burglary requires knowledge or belief regarding the trespass and intention to commit theft or an ulterior offence at the time of entry
The mens rea for burglary requires dishonesty regarding the trespass and an intention to commit theft or an ulterior offence at the time of entry
The mens rea for burglary requires intention or recklessness regarding the trespass and an appropriation at the time of entry
The mens rea for burglary requires intention or recklessness to permanently deprive and an intention to commit theft or an ulterior offence at the time of entry

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Two elements must be proved to establish the mens rea for burglary: (1) Intention or recklessness in relation to the trespass; and (2) Intention to commit the ulterior offence (i.e. commit GHB, rape, unlawful damage) at the time of entry. According to Section 9 Theft Act 1968, the offence of burglary states that there must have been an intention or recklessness when it comes to entering the building as a trespasser and there must have been either the intention to commit stealing, inflicting GBH, rape, unlawful damage to the building or anything with it or entering the building and attempting to steal or inflict GBH.

stem: A person gifts £111,000 on the 1st of September 2012 and £260,000 on the 1st of June 2013. She dies on the 15th of August 2015, leaving an estate worth £300,000. Assumptions (if applicable): Nil rate threshold is £325,000 IHT rate = 40% of amount over nil rate band.
ask: What is the Inheritance Tax (IHT) liability?

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is the best answer. £134,800.00. Both gifts are potentially exempt transfers (PETs) and are now chargeable. Their values must be cumulated, having been made in the seven years before the deceased died, thus reducing the nil rate band applicable on death. Being lifetime transfers, the estate of the deceased is entitled to utilise the deceased's annual exemptions: two in respect of the 2012 transfer (the unused annual exemption that is rolled over into 2012 from 2011 and the annual exemption available in 2012) and one for the 2013 transfer (2013). A taxpayer can give away gifts worth up to £3,000 in total in each tax year and gifts will be exempt from Inheritance Tax. Any unused part of the £3,000 exemption can be carried forward to the following year, but if it is not used in that year, the carried-over exemption expires. £105,000 of the 2012 transfer will thus be taxed (£111,000 - £6,000), all of which falls within the deceased's nil-rate band, such that no IHT will be payable on the 2012 transfer. This leaves £220,000 of the deceased's nil rate band. £257,000 of the 2013 transfer will be taxed. £220,000 falls within the deceased's remaining nil rate band. £37,000 remains liable for IHT at 40% = £14,800.
