stem: Your client arranges a public assembly but is later held under the Public Order Act 1986 for not giving prior notice to police. She claims that no prior notice is required in relation to assemblies.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal?

options.en: The organiser of an assembly must give at least six days' notice (or as many as is reasonably practicable)
The organiser of an assembly must give at least 30 days' notice (or as many as is reasonably practicable)
Notice of an assembly must only be given if over 30 people will be attending
Notice of an assembly is not normally required
The organiser of an assembly must give at least 14 days' notice (or as many as is reasonably practicable)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Notice of an assembly is not normally required under the Public Order Act 1986. Organisers of public processions, on the other hand, are required by law to notify police at least six clear days before the event occurs, of the date, time, proposed route and the name and address of an organiser.

stem: A woman is a conveyancer deducing title to 123 The Street, an unregistered freehold property. The good root of title makes reference to a lease from 1920 for 50 years, a power of attorney under which the good root was executed, and a Deed of Grant dated 1950 granting certain easements over the land for a period of 50 years.
ask: Which of the pre-root documents should the conveyance send to her purchaser?

options.en: The conveyancer should send all of the pre root documents to the purchaser
The conveyancer should send the lease only
The conveyancer should send the Deed of Grant only
The conveyancer should send the power of attorney only
The conveyancer should not send any of the documents

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The conveyancer does not need to send the lease as this has determined by effluxion of time. She does not need to include the Deed of Grant as the easements granted by it have expired. However in order that the due execution of the good root of title can be confirmed, the conveyancer is required to include the power of attorney.

stem: A claimant intends to commence proceedings against a car driver after suffering both physical and psychiatric injury as a result of the driver's alleged negligence. The financial value of the claim is expected to be at least £12,000. The driver intends to defend the claimant's action in court. The claimant intends to call expert witnesses to give evidence on her behalf. One witness is an orthopaedic surgeon and the other witness is an expert on psychiatric injury.
ask: Which option best identifies the most appropriate venue for the claim to be heard?

options.en: The most appropriate venue for the allocation of the claim is the county court (small claims track)
The most appropriate venue for the allocation of the claim is the county court (fast track)
The most appropriate venue for the allocation of the claim is the county court (multi-track)
The most appropriate venue for the allocation of the claim is the High Court (Chancery Division)
The most appropriate venue for the allocation of the claim is the High Court (Queen's Bench Division)

explanation.en: You did not select the best answer. The best answer is B. A case will normally be allocated to the fast track where: it is not a case suitable for the swift and inexpensive small claims track; its financial value is over £10,000 but no more than £25,000 (or the value claimed for pain, suffering and loss of amenity relating to personal injury exceed £1,000); the trial is likely to last no longer than one day, and the case requires no more than expert evidence in two expert areas, with the parties having one expert each per area. An example would be a personal injury claim worth £12,000, with medical evidence from an orthopaedic surgeon regarding physical injuries and a psychiatrist regarding a depressive condition.

stem: A woman executes a will in which she leaves £100,000 on trust for the members for the time being of a bowls club an unincorporated association. She does not specify how the funds should be used or how any disputes as between the members regarding their application should be determined. After the woman's death, her children challenge the gift to the bowls club. They argue that as the club has no legal personality, it cannot enforce the terms of the trust against the beneficiaries and therefore the trust has failed.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the?

options.en: The trust has failed for lack of certainty of objects
The trust operates as a gift to the individual members of the club and therefore its objects are certain
The trust operates as a contract-holding gift and therefore its objects are certain
The trust operates as a gift to be held for the association as a quasi-corporate entity and therefore its objects are certain
Although the objects are certain, a trust in favour of an unincorporated association will always fail

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The wording of the trust would suggest that membership of the club is to be used as a means of identifying the objects of the trust, but the trust does not specify the manner in which the funds are to be applied as between the beneficiaries (i.e. if it has said "to be applied in accordance with the rules of the Club", which would indicate a contract-holding gift).

stem: All rights contained in the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) are regarded as equally important by the Convention. However, the tests that must be passed before a Convention right is deemed to be breached, and the remedies available, differ subtly.
ask: To ensure that courts do not overstep their boundaries and interfere with parliamentary sovereignty, the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA) restricts Which one of the following statements is a true statement as to the extent to which certain remedies are restricted under the HRA?

options.en: Damages under the HRA are restricted to a maximum of £250,000
When considering whether to grant an injunction likely to affect a party's freedom of expression, the court must balance Convention rights with the merits of the case
Domestic courts' jurisdiction to grant injunctive relief restraining publication by the press is severely limited due to the protection afforded to freedom of expression under the Convention

Domestic courts' jurisdiction to grant injunctive relief restraining publication by • the press is radically expanded due to the common law's introduction of the Convention's right of privacy into English law
If a remedy is unsatisfactory it is no longer open to an individual who has exhausted his domestic remedies to go to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. When considering whether to grant an injunction likely to affect a party's freedom of expression, the court must balance Convention rights with the merits of the case. In Douglas v Hello! Ltd [2001] the Court of Appeal held that s. 12(3) of the Human Rights Act required that, when considering whether to grant an injunction likely to affect freedom of expression, the court must consider Art 10(2) as well as Art 10(1), and all relevant Convention rights - such as Art 8 - and must look at the merits of the case. It affirmed that, although the claimants might establish at trial that publication of surreptitiously taken photographs of their wedding should not be allowed, the organised balance in favour of allowing publication. Damages would be an adequate remedy and accordingly the balance of convenience favoured the defendant and the injunction would be discharged. Lead case: Douglas v Hello! Ltd [2001] QB 967; [2001] 2 WLR 992; [2001] 2 All ER 289. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 8 HRA 1998/s.12 Human Rights Act.

stem: Your client is a minority shareholder in a private limited company. He believes that one of the directors has acted negligently and damaged the company and wants to take action. However, the majority shareholders have decided not to take further action and have told your client he is unable to do so as a minority shareholder.
ask: Advise your client regarding the current legal position?

options.en: Your client could make a derivative claim as a minority shareholder
Your client could make a derivative claim as a minority shareholder but will need the consent of the directors of the company
Your client cannot bring a claim as he is not a majority shareholder
Your client could make a derivate claim as a minority shareholder but will need the consent of at least half of the directors of the company
Your client can bring a claim as a minority shareholder but will be personally responsible for the costs, even if the claim is successful

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Previously, the case of Foss v Harbottle ruled that a minority shareholder would be unable to make a claim in a situation such as this. It was stated that a minority shareholder couldn't bring a claim against the majority shareholders in the company's name because the company itself was controlled by the majority shareholders. However, the Companies Act 2006 has set out a procedure under which minority shareholders can make a 'derivative claim'. The can make a claim on behalf of the company if a director has damaged the company due to negligence, default or a breach of duty or trust.

stem: You render an invoice for £2,000.00 plus VAT (£400.00) to your client. After a complaint from the client, you agree to reduce your fees by £750.00 plus VAT (£150.00). Your firm records abatements separately to the profit costs ledger.
ask: Which of the following represents the correct procedural position and the accounting entries you should make to remedy the situation?

options.en: You should record the abatements of profit costs and VAT in the abatement ledger account and the corresponding entries appear in the client ledger: Debit abatement ledger office account (£750.00) Credit client ledger (profit costs) office account (£750.00) Debit abatement ledger (VAT) office account (£150.00) Credit client ledger (VAT) office account (£150.00)

You should record the abatement of the combined profit costs and VAT in the abatement ledger account and the corresponding entry appears in the client ledger: Debit abatement ledger (profits costs and VAT) office account (£900.00) Credit client ledger (profit costs and VAT) office account (£900.00)

Reduce the profit costs and HMRC ledgers respectively: Debit profit costs ledger office account (£750.00) Credit client ledger office account (£750.00) Debit HMRC ledger office account (£150.00) Credit client ledger office account (£150.00)

You should record the abatement of the profit costs only in the abatement ledger account and the corresponding entry appears in the client ledger: Debit abatement ledger (profit costs and VAT) office account (£750.00) Credit client ledger (profit costs and VAT) office account (£750.00)

You should record the abatements of profit costs in the abatement ledger, the VAT in HMRC ledger and the corresponding entries appear in the client ledger: Debit abatement ledger (profit costs) office account (£750.00) Credit client ledger (abated profit costs) office account (750.00) Debit HMRC ledger (abated VAT) office account (£150.00) Credit client ledger (abated VAT) office account (£150.00)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. You should record the abatement of profit costs and VAT in the abatements ledger account and the corresponding entries appear in the client ledger. Where an abatements ledger is operated, the debit balance of the abatements ledger is transferred to the debit side of the profit costs ledger at the end of the accounting period. The VAT, however, is a separate matter, as the firm has to account to HMRC for VAT, so you cannot combine VAT with the profit costs on the abatements ledger. Another way to think of it is that the debit entries for abatement of profit costs are simply made in another ledger rather than the existing profit costs ledger.

stem: Your client returned home one evening after work to find the neighbour's dog was in his garden. He picked up a stone, threw it at the neighbour's dog, but it missed and smashed the neighbour's kitchen window.
ask: Which of the following statements best defines the meaning attributed to 'recklessness' concerning the law relating to criminal damage?

options.en: For the purposes of the law relating to criminal damage, a person acted recklessly with respect to: (1) a circumstance where he should realise a risk • existed or will exist if he thought about it; (2) a result when he is aware of a risk that it will occur; and (3) it is, in the circumstances known to him, unreasonable to take the risk

For the purposes of the law relating to criminal damage, a reasonable person acted recklessly with respect to: (1) a circumstance when he is aware of a risk that it exists or will exist; (2) a result when he is aware of a risk that it will occur; and (3) it is, in the circumstances known to him, unreasonable to take the risk

For the purposes of the law relating to criminal damage, a person acted recklessly with respect to: (1) a circumstance when he is aware of a risk that it exists or will exist; (2) a result when he is aware of a risk that it will occur; and (3) it is, in the circumstances known to him, unreasonable to take the risk

For the purposes of the law relating to criminal damage, a person acted recklessly with respect to: (1) a circumstance when he is aware of a risk that it exists or will exist; (2) a result when he should be aware of a risk that it will occur; and (3) it is, in the circumstances known to him, unreasonable to take the risk

For the purposes of the law relating to criminal damage, a person acted recklessly with respect to: (1) a circumstance when he is aware of a risk that it exists or will exist; (2) a result when he is aware of a risk that it will occur; and (3) it is, in the circumstances an obvious risk that is unreasonable to take

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. For the purposes of the law relating to criminal damage, a person acted recklessly with respect to: (1) a circumstance when he is aware of a risk that it exists or will exist; (2) a result when he is aware of a risk that it will occur; and (3) it is, in the circumstances known to him, unreasonable to take the risk. In R v G [2003], the House of Lords held that a defendant could not be properly convicted under s. 1 of the Criminal Damage Act 1971 on the basis that he was reckless as to whether property was destroyed or damaged when he gave no thought to the risk and, by reason of his age and/or personal characteristics, the risk would not have been obvious to him, even if he had thought about it. concentrate on whether or not the defendant was aware of the risk in question and if so, whether or not, in the circumstances known to the defendant, it was unreasonable for him to take the risk. Statute; rule; constitution: S. 1 Criminal Damage Act 1971.

stem: Your client was involved in a car accident caused due to the negligence of the third party driver. Thankfully, your client wasn't physically injured. However, he has suffered travel anxiety and clinical depression as a result of the accident.
ask: Can your client claim for psychiatric injury?

options.en: Yes, provided that the risk was foreseeable, because he was exposed to a risk of physical injury and may thus recover damages for psychiatric injury as a primary victim
Yes, because he was exposed to a risk of physical injury and may thus recover damages for psychiatric injury as a primary victim
No, because he was not physically injured and thus may not recover damages for psychiatric injury as a primary victim
Yes, but he must bring a separate action for the element of psychiatric injury
No, because he may only claim for damage to the vehicle and not for personal injury

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is A. Yes, provided that the risk was foreseeable, because he was exposed to a risk of physical injury and may thus recover damages for psychiatric injury as a primary victim. A primary victim personally experiences the risk of physical injury, whether such injury actually occurs or not. A primary victim subjected to the risk of physical injury but who is not, in fact, physically harmed, may also recover damages as a primary victim for psychiatric damage sustained, provided that the risk of physical injury was foreseeable, per Page v Smith [1996] AC 155. There is no requirement for a primary victim to prove foreseeability of the psychiatric injury as well.

stem: An offer is faxed to BCo Limited from ACo Limited's office. The acceptance is faxed by BCo Limited to ACo Limited's office during office hours but ACo Limited's fax is running out of ink so the words that are printed are illegible.
ask: Which of the following statements best advises when acceptance, if any, took effect?

options.en: A faxed acceptance is only complete, in these circumstances, if supplemented by a confirmatory phone call to show good faith
A person who sends an acceptance is entitled to believe that his message has • been received, and in these circumstances any communication failure is the responsibility of the recipient
A faxed acceptance takes effect, in these circumstances, at the place where it is sent, as any communication failure is the responsibility of the sender
A valid acceptance by fax, in these circumstances, can only take effect from when it has been read by the offeror
A valid acceptance by fax, in these circumstances, can only take effect from when it has been read and understood by the offeror

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Acceptance by fax is complete when it is received, rather than when it was sent; and any communication failure is the responsibility of the recipient if, for example, the ink on the teleprinter fails at the receiving end, and the recipient does not ask for the message to be repeated. Lead case: Entores v Miles Far East Corp.

stem: You are a constitutional adviser to the government. The reigning Monarch has just died.
ask: What happens now?

options.en: The heir apparent immediately succeeds to the throne and assumes corporation sole of the Crown
The Accession Council is convened to select a successor, who assumes corporation sole of the Crown on coronation
The heir apparent succeeds to the throne, but only on coronation
A successor must be elected by the public
The heir apparent succeeds to the throne, but must first deliver a religious oath to the Accession Council, which may take several days to convene

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is A. The heir apparent immediately succeeds to the throne and assumes corporation sole of the Crown. This gives rise to the maxim "the Crown never dies", as it avoids an interregnum or gap between the previous Monarch and the new Monarch. There is no coronation or procedure to follow. This process is governed by the Act of Settlement 1701. As a ceremonial formality, the Accession Council - comprised of dignitaries including Privy Counsellors, Members of the House of Lords, the Lord Mayor of the City of London and High Commissioners of some Commonwealth countries - will meet in London to make a formal proclamation of the accession of the new Monarch and to receive a

stem: A young man was badly injured in a car accident. Doctors have advised his parents that he is clinically dead and it would be in his best interests to turn off the life support machine. His parents refuse to give permission and the doctors must seek permission from the court to carry out their decision.
ask: Which of the following statements best identifies the relevant court the doctors must?

options.en: The relevant court the doctors must turn to is the High Court (Admiralty Court)
The relevant court the doctors must turn to is the High Court (Family Division)
The relevant court the doctors must turn to is the High Court (Chancery Division)
The relevant court the doctors must turn to is the High Court (Administrative Court)
The relevant court the doctors must turn to is the High Court (Queen's Bench Division)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The relevant court the doctors must turn to is the High Court (Family Division).

ask: Which of the following statements best describes a number of legal interests which can subsist in land?

options.en: An easement, the benefit of a restrictive covenant, the burden of a restrictive covenant, a mortgage
The benefit of a restrictive covenant, the burden of a restrictive covenant, a mortgage
An easement, the burden of a restrictive covenant, a mortgage
An easement, the benefit of a restrictive covenant, a mortgage
An easement, a mortgage

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is E. An easement and a mortgage are both capable of existing as legal interests in land. A restrictive covenant is only an equitable interest, as it does not appear on the list of legal interests set out in section 1(2) of the Law of Property Act 1925. Note: although the benefit of a restrictive covenant passes to a successor in common law (as long as certain conditions are fulfilled), this is an extension of contract law, and it is not considered a legal interest in land, but an equitable interest.

stem: The Chamber of seven judges in Strasbourg adjudicated the merits of an applicant's complaint against the UK. After hearing submissions on behalf of both the applicant and the UK, the Chamber found in favour of the UK.
ask: The applicant wishes to appeal Which of the following assertions best states the timeframe in which the applicant is allowed to lodge an appeal against the Chamber's verdict?

options.en: Appeals from the Chamber must be requested within one month of the Chamber's judgment
Appeals from the Chamber must be requested within two months of the Chamber's judgment
Appeals from the Chamber must be requested within three months of the Chamber's judgment
Appeals from the Chamber must be requested within six months of the Chamber's judgment
Appeals from the Chamber must be requested within nine months of the Chamber's judgment

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The merits of complaints are heard before the Chamber. Proceedings are adversarial. The judgment is passed by majority and is published, with reasons. In rare cases, proceedings may be in camera, if the ECtHR so decides, though typically they are public. Appeals from the Chamber are lodged to the Grand Chamber and must be requested within 3 months of the Chamber's judgment. The Chamber refers a judgment for review to the Grand Chamber.

stem: Three people are partners in a successful accountancy firm. One partner decides he would also like to work on a self-employed basis and see clients privately. The second partner has objected to this and claims the first partner would be competing with the firm.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: Partners have a duty not to compete with the firm and cannot do so unless other partners consent
Partners can compete with the firm providing they do not influence existing clients to move away from the firm
Partners are not limited in any way from working on a self-employed basis in addition to being a partner at the firm
Partners can only carry out additional work if they inform clients of their partnership status in another firm
Partners cannot compete with the firm regardless of what the other partners think

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Under s30 Partnership Act 1890, a partner may not carry out business of the same kind and compete with the firm, unless the other partners consent to him doing so. If a partner competes with the firm without the consent of the other partners, any profits made must be handed over to the partnership.

stem: The 1957 Occupiers Liability Act (OLA) does not define "occupier", so the courts use the common law definition. This is a question of fact. Thus it could be a tenant, a landlord manager or a combination of two or more of these because the concept of joint liability applies.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the current applicable test for the status of "occupier"?

options.en: The currently applicable test for the status of "occupier" is the degree of activity duty
The currently applicable test for the status of "occupier" is the degree of activity level
The currently applicable test for the status of "occupier" is the degree of visible control
The currently applicable test for the status of "occupier" is the degree of occupancy control
The currently applicable test for the status of "occupier" is the degree of visitant control

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The currently applicable test for the status of "occupier" is the degree of occupancy control. Statute; rule; constitution: Occupiers Liability Act 1957.

stem: A firm of solicitors are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) to carry out certain regulated activities. They persistently offer investment advice for which they do not have authority. This is very much to the advantage of the clients who consistently profit from the investments.
ask: Which of the following statements best represents the consequences for the firm?

options.en: No criminal offence has been committed but the FCA can take disciplinary action against the firm l
The firm has committed a criminal offence and any contracts made will be unenforceable
The firm has committed a criminal offence but any contract made will still be enforceable
No criminal offence has been committed but any contracts made will be unenforceable
The firm has committed a criminal offence, and so the FCA can take disciplinary action

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Under section 19 FSMA, nobody may carry on a regulated activity unless it is either authorised or exempt. The firm of solicitors are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, i.e. they have permission to carry on certain specific activities. Even if the firm does not have permission to investment advice, it will not be committing a crime, because the firm here has received "authorisation" under the Act. If the FCA considered that it was desirable to protect the interests of consumers, it could vary or cancel the firm's permission and if the firm were left with no permissions, it would lose its status as an authorised person altogether. A person who suffers loss may be per missons, it oula luse is status ds dri dutror seu person altogether. A person who suffers loss may be able to bring an action for breach of statutory duty, and under section 382 of the Act, the FCA can apply to the court for a restitution order. B is not correct as section 19 applies to firms that are not regulated. There is no offence if an authorised body provides advice outside of the permissions granted by the FCA. C is not correct as section 19 applies to firms that are not regulated. There is no offence if an authorised body provides advice outside of the permissions aranter hv the FCA if the firm is not authorised by the FCA. E is not correct. The FCA can apply sanctions such as revoking part or all of an authorisation and can apply to court for a restitution order, even though no criminal offence was committed under section 19, because the firm was authorised at the time.

stem: In England, the established church is the Church of England. In Scotland, there is no state church, the Church of Scotland having been formally recognised as not having that status with the Church of Scotland Act 1921; Wales and Northern Ireland have no established church.
ask: What role does the Sovereign play in the Church of England?

options.en: The Queen is the Supreme Leader of the Church of England
The Queen is Supreme Commander of the Church of England
The Queen is Supreme Governor of the Church of England
The Queen is Supreme Guide of the Church of England
The Queen is Supreme Counsellor of the Church of England

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The Sovereign is ex officio Supreme Governor of the Church of England, and is required by the Act of Settlement 1701 to "join in communion with the Church of England". Statute; rule; constitution: Act of Settlement 1701.

stem: In some jurisdictions, proportionality tests are applied in both vertical and horizontal effect cases. This could be problematic, at least in theory, though in practice it does not seem to cause difficulties for the courts.
ask: Which statement best describes the meaning of "vertical effect" within the Human Rights Act 1998 ("HRA")?

options.en: Where the HRA extends to disputes between individuals and potential competitors, it is called the "vertical effect"
Where HRA extends to disputes between individuals and the press, it is called the "vertical effect"
Where the HRA extends to disputes to private relationships between individuals, it is called the "Vertical Effect"
Where the HRA extends to disputes between individuals and public authorities, it is called the "vertical effect"
Where the HRA extends to disputes between individuals and private companies; it is called the "vertical effect"

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. "Vertical effect" in this context concerns individuals' rights as against state institutions.

stem: BankCo is the mortgagee of 123 The Street, a freehold property subject to a tenancy to which it has consented. The mortgagor has failed to pay the interest due on the mortgage loan and accordingly has defaulted. BankCo wishes to collect the rent from the property but does not wish to become liable as the landlord of the property.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: BankCo should collect the rent directly from the tenant. The mortgagor will remain liable to the tenant for performance of the landlord's obligations
BankCo should take possession of the property and grant a new tenancy
l BankCo should appoint a receiver
BankCo cannot recover rental income from the property without becoming liable as the tenant's landlord
BankCo should collect the rent directly from the tenant; there will be nobody to carry out the landlord's obligations under the lease

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Where a mortgagee collects rent in relation to a tenanted property, it assumes the responsibilities of the property's landlord. It would therefore be liable to the tenant for repair of the property etc. As a receiver is deemed to be the agent of the borrower, the appointment of a receiver allows the mortgagee to collect the rental income which is generated, whilst avoiding liability to the tenant.

stem: The case of General Pinochet showed that insanity could actually be used as a means of preventing a case from taking place in the first instance, as well as being used as a defence, once an individual has been found prima facie guilty.
ask: Which of the following best states the generally accepted definition of insanity in?

options.en: The prosecution must show, beyond reasonable doubt, that at the time at which the offence occurred, the defendant: (1) was not working under a defect of reason, which had arisen as a result of abnormality of mind; (2) had information as to the nature or the quality of the act that he was undertaking; or (3) he did, in fact, know what he was doing, and realised it was wrong

The prosecution must show, on the balance of probabilities, that at the time at which the offence occurred, the defendant: (1) was not working under a defect of reason, which had arisen as a result of abnormality of mind; (2) had information as to the nature or the quality of the act that he was undertaking; or (3) he did, in fact, know what he was doing, and realised it was wrong

The defence must show, on the balance of probabilities, that at the time at which the offence occurred, the defendant: (1) was working under a defect of reason, which had arisen as a result of abnormality of mind; (2) did not have any information as to the nature or the quality of the act that he was undertaking; or (3) if he did, in fact, know what he was doing, he did not realise it was wrong

The defence must show, beyond reasonable doubt, that at the time at which the offence occurred, the defendant: (1) was working under a defect of reason, which had arisen as a result of abnormality of mind; (2) did not have any information as to the nature or the quality of the act that he was undertaking; or (3) if he did, in fact, know what he was doing, he did not realise it was wrong

The defence must show that at the time at which the offence occurred, the defendant: (1) was working under a defect of reason, which had arisen as a result of abnormality of mind; (2) that he did not have any information as to the nature or the quality of the act that he was undertaking; or (3) if he did, in fact, know what he was doing, it was morally justifiable

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. On the balance of probabilities, the defendant needs to show that at the time at which the offence occurred, he was: (1) working under a defect of reason, which had arisen as a result of disease of mind; (2) that he did not have any information as to the nature of the act or the quality of the act that he was undertaking; or (3) if he did, in fact, know what he was doing, he did not realise it was wrong. Please note, S. 2 of the Homicide Act 1957 requires an "abnormality of mind" rather than the anachronistic description of a "disease of the mind" as applied by the M'Naghten Rules. Lead case: M'Naghten's Case (1843).

stem: ACo Limited is the parent company of BCo Limited. BCo Limited has recently entered into a lease agreement for some business premises and ACo Limited wrote to the landlord saying it was the general policy of ACo Limited to ensure that its subsidiaries were in a position to meet its liabilities. BCo Limited's business has been struggling and it now cannot pay the rent.
ask: Which of the following statements best advises whether the letter ACo Limited wrote means it is legally bound to pay the rent?

options.en: The letter ACo Limited wrote means it is legally bound to pay the rent, because • the consequences of its decision to repudiate its moral responsibility are matters a court cannot turn a blind eye to
The letter ACo Limited wrote means it is legally bound to pay the rent, because the landlord would obviously act in reliance on such a letter

The letter ACo Limited wrote means it is legally bound to pay the rent, because it will have been of paramount importance to the landlord that ACo Limited should ensure that its subsidiary was at all times in a position to meet its liabilities
The letter ACo Limited wrote means it is not legally bound to pay the rent, • because the letter was a statement of present fact, not a promise as to future conduct
The letter ACo Limited wrote means it is not legally bound to pay the rent, because so-called 'comfort' letters are of minimal commercial importance and entirely devoid of legal effect

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. There must be something in the letter to show that, as a matter of commercial probability or common sense, the parties must have intended the letter to be a contractual promise. If the promise is not expressly stated, it is a mere representation of fact. Lead case: Kleinwort Benson Ltd v Malaysian Mining Corp. Berhad [1988] 1 WLR 799.

stem: A proposed rule by a local authority was affirmed unlawful by the Administrative Court in judicial review proceedings. In order to resolve the legal position of the parties, the Administrative Court clarified the respective rights and obligations, without actually making any order.
ask: In light of the above, which of the following statements best describes the remedy applied by the Administrative Court in this instance?

options.en: The remedy applied by the Administrative Court in this instance is an ouster clause
The remedy applied by the Administrative Court in this instance is a quashing order or order of certiorari
The remedy applied by the Administrative Court in this instance is a mandatory order or mandamus
The remedy applied by the Administrative Court in this instance is a declaration
The remedy applied by the Administrative Court in this instance is a prohibiting order

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. A declaration is a judgment by the Administrative Court which clarifies the respective rights and obligations of the parties to the proceedings, without actually making any order.

stem: A man and woman are appointed as trustees of a trust which includes the freehold interest in 123 The Street among the trust property. The man has made and registered a lasting power of attorney appointing a friend as his attorney. The trustees are in the process of selling 123 The Street to a buyer when the man has an accident whilst riding his motorbike and is left lacking mental capacity.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman is able to sell the property herself and give a valid receipt for the sale proceeds
The man and woman are able to sell the property and give a valid receipt for the sale proceeds
A new trustee must be appointed to give a valid receipt for the sale proceeds
The friend must be appointed as a new trustee to give a valid receipt for the sale proceeds
The friend and the woman can give a valid receipt for the sale proceeds

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Two trustees are required in order to give a valid receipt for the sale proceeds of land (s.27 Law of Property Act 1925) and therefore the woman cannot do this on her own. The man can no longer give a valid receipt for the sale proceeds as he lacks mental capacity. However the friend, as the man's lasting attorney, is able to discharge the man's functions as a trustee on his behalf and the friend does not need to be appointed as a trustee in her own right to do this.

stem: A motorcyclist was killed after being hit by a ball kicked by a boy playing in a field with other boys adjoining the highway. The defendants had permitted the boys to play football on their land which was close to a road. The court decided to apply the 'magnitude of risk' test.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the magnitude of risk test?

options.en: The magnitude of risk test requires the degree of care to be proportionate to the degree of risk
The magnitude of risk test requires the degree of care to be precautionary to the degree of risk
The magnitude of risk test requires the degree of care to be preventative to the degree of risk
The magnitude of risk test requires the degree of care to be pre-emptive to the degree of risk
The magnitude of risk test requires the degree of care to be prudent to the degree of risk

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. When courts consider the magnitude of risk, the standard of care must be commensurate with the risk. If the risk is small then no precautions need be taken, since the defendant need only guard against reasonable probabilities, not fantastic possibilities. Lead case: Hilder v Associated Portland Cement Manufacturers Ltd [1961].

stem: A husband and wife are considering buying a shop. The wife is examining the accounts and believes that there is just one rate of VAT, but the husband argues that there are more.
ask: Which of the following best describe the current legal position?

options.en: There is one rate of VAT
There are two rates of VAT
There a five rates of VAT
There are three rates of VAT
There is one rate of VAT but it fluctuates depending on the size of the business

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. There are three rates of VAT- standard, reduced and zero.

stem: A brother and sister are at home when the brother displays an offensive sign to the sister and refuses to take it down. The sign makes the sister believe that immediate unlawful violence will be used against her. The sister wants the brother arrested under s4 Public Order Act 1986 (fear or provocation of violence).
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: A sign alone will not constitute an offence
The brother can be arrested for the offence
The brother will not be liable because they were both inside a dwelling when it took place
The brother can still be liable even though they were inside a dwelling when it took place
A sign alone could only constitute an offence if it was accompanied by actual violence

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Under the Public Order Act 1986 the offence of fear or provocation of violence will not be constituted if both persons were in a dwelling at the time of the alleged offence.

stem: A man is the long leaseholder of an apartment, which he has leased to a woman by way of a two year parol lease. The woman is moving away from the area and agrees orally with the man that she will surrender the lease back to him. The man is happy to agree this as he now thinks that he will get a higher rent for the property, and he accepts the keys back from her. After the woman has left, the man is unable to re-let the property and tells the woman that she owes him rent for the period that the property is unoccupied until he finds a new tenant.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: A surrender of the lease has taken place at law and the woman is not liable for rent due after the surrender
A surrender of the lease has taken place at law but the woman is still liable for rent due after the surrender
A surrender of the lease has not taken place at law but the woman is not liable for the rent
A surrender of the lease has not taken place at law and the woman is still liable for the rent
It is not possible to surrender a parol lease

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The lease would be surrendered by operation of law on the basis of the agreement reached between the landlord and the tenant. In accepting the return of the keys from the woman, the man would have accepted the surrender of the lease and the lease would have come to an end at that point.

stem: Your client sees a flat screen TV offered for sale on a website for £25. Due to a computer error it should have been priced at £250. He orders four screens but he has been informed that the pricing was a mistake and he cannot have the flat screens at
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the type of contract, if any, that has?

options.en: The type of contract that has been formed is a contract by deed
The type of contract that has been formed is a simple contract
The type of contract that has been formed is a bilateral contract
The type of contract that has been formed is a unilateral contract
No contract has been formed as the company's offer was merely an invitation to treat

explanation.en: E is correct. Posting an advertisement on a website (e- commerce) amounts to an invitation to treat.

stem: The number of members the House of Lords is not fixed. As of May 2011, the House of Lords had 789 members. The Lords Spiritual are 26 senior bishops of the Church of England. The Lords Temporal make up the rest of the membership of the House of Lords; of these, the majority are life peers. What is the procedure
ask: which allows life peers to take their seats in the House of?

options.en: The Prime Minister formally appoints life peers on the advice and recommendation of the Sovereign
The Sovereign formally appoints life peers on the advice and recommendation of the Prime Minister
Life peers are elected by constituents from a list of candidates standing for election every four to five years
Life peers are elected internally on the advice and recommendation of the House of Lords Appointments Commission
Life peers are elected by constituents from a list of candidates standing for election every four to five years using a system of proportional representation

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The Sovereign formally appoints life peers on the advice and recommendation of the Prime Minister.

stem: A woman saw her boyfriend dancing with another woman. She jealously threw a beer glass in her boyfriend's direction. Her boyfriend ducked and the glass hit a stranger, who was taken to hospital with a serious eye injury.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the girlfriend's liability, if any, under the tort of trespass?

options.en: The girlfriend is not liable in trespass for the tort of battery, because she had no intention of throwing the glass at the stranger
Although she had had not intended to harm the stranger, the girlfriend is liable in trespass for the tort of battery, because she intended to throw the glass
Although she had had not intended to harm the stranger, the girlfriend is liable • in trespass for the tort of negligent battery, because she recklessly threw the glass
The girlfriend is not liable in trespass for the tort of battery, because she did not intend to cause harm to the stranger
The girlfriend is not liable in trespass for the tort of battery; she did not possess the requisite hostility towards the stranger

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Although the defendant must intend to carry out the act which constitutes trespass for it to be valid, this does not require the defendant to intend harm. Lead case: Livingstone v MoD [1984].

stem: You are called to the police station to advise a person arrested for battery prior to police interview.
ask: He is unsure of the actus reus for the offence of battery, and asks for Which of the following best describes the actus reus required for battery?

options.en: The actus reus for battery requires the intentional or reckless causing the victim to apprehend immediate application of unlawful force
The actus reus for battery requires the unlawful force against the physical body of another person
The actus reus for battery requires the causing of the victim to apprehend the immediate application of unlawful force
The actus reus for battery requires the causing of any hurt or injury calculated to interfere with the health or comfort of the victim
The actus reus for battery requires the causing of another to fear, on at least two occasions, that violence will be used against him

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The actual action of battery is the infliction of any form of unlawful force by one person against another person, and it can be a very light touch; it merely has to be unlawful.

stem: A woman is looking to start a small business selling jewellery and asks her father if he will provide her with an initial investment of money to buy some stock. The father agrees to do this and, after transferring the money to the woman's bank, he sends her an email saying "I have transferred the money to your account, please make sure that you pay me back once the business has taken off and you have begun to make a profit. Good luck." The woman and her father subsequently fall out and she refuses to pay the money back to him, claiming that the presumption of advancement applies.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: As the presumption of advancement applies, a gift of the money is presumed and the woman does not hold the money on trust for the father
The woman holds the money on trust for the father on an automatic resulting trust as he did not make a declaration of trust when he transferred it to her
The woman holds the money on a presumed resulting trust for the father as it was a voluntary transfer and the presumption of advancement does not apply
The woman holds the money on a presumed resulting trust for the father. The presumption of advancement applies but it could be rebutted in the circumstances
The woman holds the money on an automatic resulting trust for the father due to the failure of a declaration of trust

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. As the woman's father provided the money, the presumption of advancement would apply. Therefore, unless the presumption could be rebutted, a gift would be presumed. However as the father made it clear to the woman that he expected the money to be repaid to him once the business had begun to make money, the presumption of advancement could be easily rebutted and a resulting trust would be presumed in favour of the father.

stem: A private company limited by shares has an issued share capital of £100,000 which is fully paid up. All of the shares in the company are owned by its holding company, also a private company limited by shares. The holding company has an issued share capital of £1 which is fully paid up and held by a member, who is also the sole director of the holding company, which does not have a secretary. The solder director and the holding company are the directors of the subsidiary company.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the situation in respect of re-listing the subsidiary company as a public company?

options.en: have to issue an additional £50,000 worth of shares, appoint an additional director and appoint a company secretary, and the holding company would have to issue an additional £49,999 worth of shares and appoint a company secretary

Before the subsidiary company could be re-listed as a public company, it would have to issue an additional £50,000 worth of shares and appoint a company secretary, and the holding company would have to issue an additional £49,999 worth of shares and appoint a company secretary
Before the subsidiary company could be re-listed as a public company, it would • have to appoint a company secretary and the holding company would need to take no action

Before the subsidiary company could be re-listed as a public company, it would have to appoint a company secretary and the holding company would need to issue a further £49,999 worth of shares and appoint a company secretary
Before the subsidiary company could be re-listed as a public company, it would have to issue a further £49,999 worth of shares and the holding company would have to appoint a company secretary

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Although the holding company is a member and director of the subsidiary company, the two companies have separate legal personality to each other and, therefore, provided that the holding company is properly constituted as a private company, the requirements for re-listing as a public company would only apply to the subsidiary company. The subsidiary company has sufficient paid up share capital and directors to enable it to re-list. It therefore only needs to appoint a company secretary.

stem: A man was browsing in a fashion store and saw a pairs of expensive sunglasses he really liked. He swapped price tags with a less expensive pair of sunglasses with a view to paying the lower price. He did not actually have the chance to pay for them, however, because the price-switching was detected at the sales counter before he had paid for the sunglasses. He was subsequently arrested.
ask: Which option best states the offence, if any, for which the man is criminally liable?

options.en: The offence for which the man is criminally liable for switching the price tags on the sunglasses is theft
The man is not criminally liable for any offence because the switching the price tags on the sunglasses does not amount to an appropriation
The offence for which the man is criminally liable for switching the price tags on the sunglasses is taking goods without the owner's consent
The offence for which the man is criminally liable for switching the price tags on the sunglasses is obtaining services dishonestly
The offence for which man is criminally liable for switching the price tags on the sunglasses is handling stolen goods

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. A is correct. The offence for which the man is criminally liable for switching the price tags on the sunglasses is theft. The offence is committed at the moment of appropriation. Therefore, it is irrelevant that the man had not left the store. It was immaterial that the man had not actually assumed all of the owner's rights. Switching of the price tags amounted to at least one assumption of the right of an owner and was therefore enough to amount to an appropriation of the property. Lead case: R v. Morris, Anderton v Burnside [1984] A.C. 320.

stem: The jurisdiction of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) is compulsory and individuals in the UK have a right to apply to the ECtHR. But the focus of the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention), is still on securing observance by member states of minimum standards in the protection of the human rights specified in the Convention.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the law relating to damages according to the principles established under human rights law?

options.en: In considering an award of damages on Convention grounds, judges should take into account the principles applied by domestic courts in awarding damages

In considering an award of damages on Convention grounds, English judges are to award damages so that claimants will be able to receive better compensation to what they would have received in domestic courts
In considering an award of damages on Convention grounds, English courts are to take into account the principles applied by the ECtHR in awarding damages

In considering an award of damages on Convention grounds, English courts are to take into account the principles applied by judicial precedent in awarding damages, so that claimants will be able to receive better compensation to what they would have received in Strasbourg

In considering an award of damages on Convention grounds, English courts are to take into account the principles applied by the ECtHR in awarding damages, so that claimants will be able to receive compensation from a domestic court equivalent to what they would have received in Strasbourg

explanation.en: E is correct. "...i)n considering an award of damages on Convention grounds, the courts are to take into account the principles applied by the European Court of Human Rights in awarding compensation, so that people will be able to receive compensation from a domestic court equivalent to what they would have received in Strasbourg. "The Human Rights Bill" (Cm 3782, 1 October 1997), paragraph 2.6. Please note that answer C is partially correct.

stem: You acted for a client on a commercial property transaction, as part of a chain. Your engagement letter contained information about your money laundering obligations. Your client presented three cheques from different banks for the deposit. Whilst you were not suspicious, nor objectively were there any reasonable grounds for suspicion, you made a disclosure to your Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO), who in turn disclosed to National Crime Agency (NCA), out of an abundance of caution. Due to waiting for consent from NCA to proceed, you missed completion and the chain collapsed. Your client is now threatening civil action.
ask: Which of the following best describes your position?

options.en: You are exposed to civil liability
You are exposed to civil liability, but can seek a contribution from NCA
You are not exposed to civil liability, because you made a disclosure to NCA and were complying with your obligations under anti-money laundering obligations
You are not exposed to civil liability, because the doctrine of ex turpi causa prevents civil action arising from criminal conduct, which applies here
You are not exposed to civil liability, because your engagement letter spelt out your money laundering obligations and so protects you from civil action

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The point of POCA is to deprive wrongdoers of proceeds of crime. It is not to compensate victims. Accordingly, where your compliance with anti-money laundering legislation renders you in breach of a retainer, you may face civil action from the client. It is for this reason that you must always notify your professional indemnity insurers whenever a disclosure is made. That said, you should also ensure that disclosures are only made when the criteria for making them is met - knowledge or suspicion of money laundering, or reasonable grounds to suspect the same. Defensive disclosures to NCA, as in this case, will not only expose you to civil liability, but

stem: The owner of a property granted a two year lease to a tenant, which does not require registration. The property is subsequently mortgaged and the owner failed to declare the tenancy to the mortgagee. The tenant, who is not party to the mortgage deed, is concerned that he may be exposed unless his lease is protected. You review the mortgage deed and note that it excludes the right for the mortgagor to grant leases that are binding on the mortgagee.
ask: What options are available to the tenant to protect his position, if any?

options.en: The tenant has no options, he must simply request that the mortgagee respect the lease
The tenant must enter a Notice on the Register of Title in respect of the lease
The tenant has statutory protection, as leases granted by a mortgagor are automatically binding on the mortgagee
The tenant should place a Restriction on the Register of Title for the property in respect of the lease
The leasehold estate is an overriding interest even though it is not registered; therefore, the tenant is protected

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The leasehold estate is an overriding interest even though it is not registered; therefore, the tenant is protected. A leasehold estate in land for a term of three years or less, except for any that have to be registered, cannot be protected by a Notice. A Restriction is not strictly necessary in this case, as the leasehold (which is for less than seven years) comes under the category of an unregistered interest which overrides registered dispositions, under the Land Registration Act 2002.The statutory protection of the mortgagor's right to grant binding leases has been excluded by the mortgage deed; therefore, the tenant cannot rely on the case of post-charge leases, although in the absence of an express or statutory power of leasing, a tenancy granted by the borrower can subsist by estoppel and be enforceable by and between the borrower and the tenant, it will be of no effect as against the lender, and the tenant will have no security of tenure. In this case, however, the lease was granted before the charge was taken over the property.

stem: A man and woman announced that they were going on a pre-nuptial round the world trip together. The woman's mother promised her daughter she would contribute £500 and the man's father promised the woman's mother that he would give the woman £1,000 on the safe return of the happy couple. A year later the couple returned but the man's father has reneged on his promise to pay the woman Which option best advises the woman as to whether she can enforce the promise under the common law doctrine of privity of contract?
ask: Which of the following statements best advises the woman as to whether she can enforce the promise?

options.en: The woman is entitled to enforce the promise, because the party to whom the • benefit accrues is entitled to rely on the terms of the contract between the man's father and the woman's mother
The woman is not entitled to enforce the promise because there were • insufficient ties of love and affection from the mother to the woman for consideration and privity to extend to both of them
The woman is entitled to enforce the promise, because a claimant in her position is considered to be a creditor beneficiary
The woman is not entitled to enforce the promise, because she was not party to the contract between the man and her mother
The woman is entitled to enforce the promise, because the mother in these • circumstances was agent for the woman in making the contract and the man's father ought to be bound

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The general rule is that someone not a party to a contract cannot be liable under it nor benefit from it. The contract was between woman's mother and the man's father. Please note, under section 1(1) of the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 a third party may enforce a term of the contract if: (1) the contract expressly provides that he/she may; or (2) the term purports to confer a benefit on the person. Section 1(1) provides a rebuttable presumption that third parties can enforce a term that confers a benefit upon them. Lead case: Tweddle v Atkinson (1861) 1 B & S 393; 121 ER 762.

stem: A police officer asked a Minister to leave Downing Street by another exit when the Minister departed Number 10 after a Cabinet meeting.
ask: The Minister became angry, swore at the police officer and allegedly calling him a "pleb" who "should know his • Despite subsequently denying using the word "pleb" and apologising for his bad behaviour, mounting public pressure subsequently forced the Minister's Which option best describes the constitutional convention the Minister deferred to?

options.en: The convention the Minister has deferred to is collective ministerial responsibility
The convention the Minister has deferred to is statutory ministerial propriety
The convention the Minister has deferred to is collective ministerial propriety
The convention the Minister has deferred to is individual ministerial responsibility
The convention the Minister has deferred to is individual ministerial propriety

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is the best option. This is a classic example of the constitutional convention individual ministerial responsibility. In October 2012, Prime Minister David Cameron accepted the resignation of Andrew Mitchell, the government's chief whip after weeks of pressure over an argument with police officers in Downing Street. While the Conservative MP admitted swearing at police officers in the incident, he denied calling police "plebs". He told David Cameron, who had publicly supported him during the ensuing furore, that "damaging publicity" meant he could no longer do his job. In his resignation letter, Mr Mitchell stated "it has become clear to me that whatever the rights and wrongs of the matter I is it fair to continue to put my family and colleagues through this upsetting and damaging publicity...". Mitchell added that the "...offending comment and the reason for my apology to the police was my parting remark "I thought you guys were supposed to f***ing help us'..". He conceded that it "...was obviously wrong of me to use such bad language and I am very sorry about it and grateful to the police officer for accepting my apology..."
