The Cabinet Secretary is the Minister responsible for government policy in the • Cabinet Office and for providing professional and corporate leadership to the Civil Service
The Cabinet Secretary is responsible for providing professional and corporate leadership to the Civil Service
The Cabinet Secretary is the Prime Minister's most senior policy advisor, responsible to all Ministers for the running of the Cabinet and its committees

explanation.en: E is the best option. The post of Cabinet Secretary and Head of the Home Civil Service was formerly held by one person. In 2012 it the was divided into three: the role of Cabinet Secretary was filled by Sir Jeremy Heywood; Sir Bob Kerslake became Head of the Home Civil Service, combined with his role as Permanent Secretary at the Department for Communities and Local Government; and lan Watmore became Permanent Secretary of the Cabinet Office. The official role of the Cabinet Secretary is now described as the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister's most senior policy advisor, acting as Secretary to the Cabinet, responsible to all Ministers for the running of the Cabinet and its committees. ny i ene cunmes una to committees

stem: A woman is considering establishing a charitable trust and has approached you for advice as to the advantages and disadvantages of charitable status.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Charitable trusts are not subject to the rule against perpetuities, but the trustees are required to act unanimously and are subject to control by the state
Charitable trusts have the benefit of tax exemptions and are exempt from the • rule against perpetuities, but the trustees are required to act unanimously and they are subject to control by the state
Charitable trusts have the benefit of tax exemptions, are exempt from the rule against perpetuities and are subject to control by the state
Charitable trusts subject to the rule against perpetuities and control by the • state, but the trustees are not required to act unanimously and have the benefit of tax exemptions
Charitable trusts are subject to the rule against perpetuities and are subject to control by the state

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is C. Charitable trusts attract many tax exemptions and are exempted from the rule against perpetuities, meaning that they can exist indefinitely without having to be wound up. The trustees have greater discretion and are only required to act with a majority, rather than unanimously. Their terms are enforced by the state as parens patriae via the Attorney General, but this in practice allows the trustees greater freedom to administer the trust than they would otherwise have had by having to account directly to the beneficiaries.

stem: Your client argued that the purchase of a Rolls Royce had been the culmination of a lifelong ambition. When the garage had not repaired it properly or quickly enough, this had caused him to suffer distress and inconvenience worthy of damages. Which measure of damages, if any,
ask: Which measure of damages, if any, do courts usually employ in contractual disputes?

options.en: There are no damages awarded for a claimant's disappointment and distress under these circumstances
Damages would be awarded for a claimant's disappointment and distress under these circumstances
The measure of damages which courts usually employ in contractual disputes of this nature is restitution
The measure of damages which courts usually employ in contractual disputes of this nature is reliance loss
Unliquidated damages would be awarded for a claimant's disappointment and distress under these circumstances

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. No damages would be awarded for the claimant's 'emotional anguish' while his car was being repaired: Lead case: Alexander v Rolls Royce Motor Cars Ltd. [1995]............. disputes of

stem: Your client is an employer that is being sued by an employee for personal injury caused by work equipment; namely, a hand-held drill. The employee had training and experience using power tools prior to his employment with your client, and your client relied on the claimant's prior expertise rather than training him directly in use of this particular tool. Your client feels that it is the employee's fault the injury was Under common law,
ask: what must an employer take reasonable care to provide to?

options.en: Health and safety training; a safe place of work; a safe system of work; and fit and competent staff
Proper and safe equipment; a safe system of work; fit and competent staff and full medical insurance
New equipment; a safe place of work; a safe system of work; and fit and competent staff
Proper and safe equipment; thorough and ongoing training in work equipment and practices; sufficient remuneration and fit and competent management
Proper and safe equipment; a safe place of work; a safe system of work; and fit and competent staff

explanation.en: The best answer is E. Proper and safe equipment; a safe place of work; a safe system of work; and fit and competent staff. These duties were laid down in Wilsons and Clyde Coal Co. Ltd v English [1938] AC 57. However, it should be noted that the statutory regime, incorporating European directives on workplace safety and management, often go into more detail and extend the duties further, often imposing strict liability on employers for breaches of the provisions of the statutes.

stem: The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) is a permanent court with its own official languages, judges and rules of procedure. The court is divided into five administrative sections, within which Chambers (the bodies which carry out the judicial functions) are formed. The court also maintains a Grand Chamber, which consists of: the President, Vice-Presidents and Section Presidents, in addition to a further selection of judges chosen by lot.
ask: Which option best states the number of Grand Chamber judges that review Chamber judgments in serious cases?

options.en: A Grand Chamber of 7 judges reviews Chamber judgments, in serious cases
A Grand Chamber of 11 judges reviews Chamber judgments, in serious cases
A Grand Chamber of 15 judges reviews Chamber judgments, in serious cases
A Grand Chamber of 17 judges reviews Chamber judgments, in serious cases
A Grand Chamber of 23 judges reviews Chamber judgments, in serious cases

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The 47 judges of the Court are elected by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe for renewable six- year terms. Cases are heard by Chambers of 7 judges; important or serious cases may be referred to a Grand Chamber of 17 judges. The execution of the Court's judgements is overseen by the Committee of Ministers, which has the authority to suspend or expel a State from the Council of Europe if the State does not comply with a Court judgment.

stem: A director wants to secure his continued employment with the company. He asks for your advice as to the rights of shareholders to remove a director from their office.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: Directors cannot be removed from office by shareholders unless they are held liable for misconduct
Directors who have been in the office for less than two years can be removed by shareholders if they are held liable for misconduct
Directors can be removed from office at any time by special resolution
Only directors who have been disqualified by court can be removed from office
Directors can be removed from office by the shareholders at any time by ordinary resolution

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Shareholders do retain the right to be able to remove directors at any time by ordinary resolution. A special notice is required of a resolution to remove directors before the end of their terms of office. Such notice must be given to the company at least 28 days before the meeting at which the resolution is moved. This can be passed by ordinary resolution.

stem: Your client is the borrower in a mortgage secured by a 20 year lease on commercial premises. Your client wishes to pay the debt early and redeem the mortgage. However, there is a clause in the mortgage deed that prevents redemption until 6 weeks before the end of the lease, which is still several years away.
ask: Can your client redeem the mortgage early?

options.en: Yes, because the restriction would amount to a 'clog on the equity' and thus be void and unenforceable
No; the restriction would not amount to a 'clog on the equity' and thus prevents your client from redeeming the mortgage only
Yes, only if your client gives 6 months' notice and pays 6 months' interest as a penalty
No; the restriction was validly entered into as part of a commercial transaction and is thus binding
Yes; the term is unconscionable and therefore automatically void

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is A. Yes, because the restriction would amount to a 'clog on the equity' and thus be void and unenforceable. Any provisions in a mortgage deed which purport to prevent redemption of the mortgage on payment of the debt (e.g. a condition preventing the mortgagor's redemption of the mortgage, until 6 weeks before the end of a 20- year lease, per Fairclough v Swan Brewery Co. Ltd [1912] AC 565), will be "clogs on the equity" rendering them void and unenforceable, but not necessarily unconscionable. Even if such a term were found to be unconscionable, it would require a declaration by the court of the same, rather than being automatically void. However, where the mortgaged estate is freehold and the mortgage is in relation to a business, the courts have

stem: A man and woman are not married. They contribute equally to the cash purchase of a house which they live in together, but the man alone holds the legal title and no express declaration of trust was made.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: An express trust has been created
An implied trust has been created
A charitable trust has been created
A testamentary trust has been created
An inter vivos express trust has been created

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. An express trust has not been created because the man and woman did not execute a declaration of trust in relation to the property. The trust exists solely to reflect the woman's contribution to the purchase price and has a fixed, identifiable beneficiary so it is not charitable. The trust is not testamentary because it did not arise on the death of the settlor.

stem: A man and woman own neighbouring areas of land. They agree that the woman will grant the man a right to draw water from a well on the woman's land via a pipeline which runs across the woman's land onto the man's in order to supply the man's garden centre with water. The garden centre is used for the man's business. The right is granted for a fixed period of ten years. The man sells his land to a friend, who wishes to continue to make use of the right.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The right is not an easement because there are no identifiable dominant and servient tenements
The right is not an easement because it does not accommodate the dominant tenement
The right is not an easement because the dominant and servient tenements were in common ownership at the time of the grant
The right is not an easement because it is not capable of forming the subject matter of a grant, and is limited for ten years
The woman has granted the man an easement which the friend can enforce against the woman

explanation.en: * the man's You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The right is not an easement because it does not accommodate the dominant tenement. The right to draw water from the well is granted for the purposes of supplying the garden centre (the man's business) with water. The supply is for the purposes of a business, not for the general use of the land. It cannot be said to accommodate the dominant tenement. As it does not accommodate the dominant tenement, the right cannot exist as an easement, as this is one of the requirements of an easement.

stem: A private company limited by shares has model articles of association. It has made a significant pre-tax profit and stands to pay a substantial amount of corporation tax. The Financial Director of the company has recommended to the board that the company must retain a certain amount of the profits and suggests reducing the tax liability by paying a bonus to the directors. The members of the company are unhappy with this course of action and table a resolution at the annual general meeting that the company will not pay the bonus, but will instead pay additional corporation tax and then pay a dividend to the members.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The members can table a resolution to declare a dividend without the involvement of the directors
The dividends can be paid by the directors without any involvement of the members
The dividends can be paid by the directors without any involvement of the members, but only if no less than two thirds of the directors agree
The members can table a resolution to declare a dividend, but only up to the amount recommended by the directors
The dividends can be paid by the directors without any involvement of the members, if authorised by the Financial Director

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Before members can declare a dividend, this must be recommended by a resolution of the board of directors. The members can not declare a dividend unless this course of action has been recommended by the directors and any dividend that the members declare cannot exceed any amount recommended by the directors. This is intended to ensure that the members cannot interfere with the day to day running of the company by taking more profits than the company can afford to have removed from its finances.

stem: The School Bus Act 2013 (fictitious) provides that each local council shall have the duty to subsidise school bus services within its area, in the interests of school pupils. A county council decided to subsidise a bus service for hikers, running from the city centre to a village in a neighbouring county.
ask: Which of the following statements best identifies the ground for judicial review, if any, raised by the county council's decision to subsidise a bus service running to the village in the neighbouring county?

options.en: The best ground for judicial review raised by the county council's decision to subsidise a bus service running from the city centre to the village in the neighbouring county is that the council has fettered its discretion

The best ground for judicial review raised by the county council's decision to • subsidise a bus service running from the city centre to the village in the neighbouring county is that the council is acting ultra vires

The best ground for judicial review raised by the county council's decision to • subsidise a bus service running from the city centre to the village in the neighbouring county is that the decision is disproportionate

The best ground for judicial review raised by the county council's decision to subsidise a bus service running from the city centre to the village in the neighbouring county is that the decision fails the Wednesbury unreasonableness test

The best ground for judicial review raised by the county council's decision to • subsidise a bus service running from the city centre to the village in the neighbouring county is that the decision shows a failure to consult

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The School Bus Act 2013 (fictitious) authorises the county council to subsidise bus services within the county. Therefore, in subsidising a service to outside the county, the council is exceeding its statutory powers and acting ultra vires.

stem: You act for a well-known local entrepreneur on a divorce matter. The entrepreneur has recently had his net worth wiped out after several businesses failed, which attracted significant press coverage. The entrepreneur presents a cheque for £500,000.00 to cover settlement to his wife. You suspect money laundering due to the sum involved and make a report to your Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO). You are contacted by a local journalist who requests information on the transaction.
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed?

options.en: You may provide the information to the journalist, as it is in the public interest to prevent further money laundering. You will not commit any offences
You may provide the information to the journalist as you have already made the report and your duty of client confidentiality has been superseded by the report to your MLRO
You may report suspicions to the journalist, but not that you have made a money laundering report
You must await permission from National Crime Agency (NCA) or your MLRO before providing the journalist with the information
You must not provide the information to the journalist as you will commit a tipping off offence and will be breaching your duty of confidentiality

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Giving this information to the journalist is tipping off, and the exemptions/defences in S333B-D of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 do not apply. Even though your duty of confidentiality to the client is overruled in certain circumstances by your money laundering obligations, it is not extinguished entirely, and disclosure to a journalist will be a clear breach of your professional obligations.

stem: The Home Secretary expelled an American preacher from the UK, asserting that the preacher's presence would damage community relations and risk public disorder breaking out. The preacher complained that his expulsion violated the right to freedom of expression, guaranteed under the European Convention on Human Rights (the "Convention"). The Home Secretary countered that Member States may restrict the political activities of foreigners.
ask: Which of the following statements is most relevant to the scenario?

options.en: The right to freedom of expression under the Convention does not apply when a foreign national is seeking permission to enter a country
While the right to freedom of expression is guaranteed under the Convention, Member States may restrict the political activities of foreigners

While Member States may restrict the political activities of foreigners, other • Member States' nationals that do not have citizenship of the Member State that restricts their activities are also considered foreigners for Convention purposes
The right to freedom of expression under the Convention implies an asylum or immigration right, which is designed to facilitate movement across borders
The right to freedom of expression under the Convention does not allow free speech to be restricted for the prevention of disorder

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. While the right to freedom of expression is guaranteed under Article 10 of the Convention, Article 16 allows member states to restrict the political activities of foreigners, even if this would be in conflict with Articles 10, 11 or 14. The European Court of Human Rights has ruled, however, that European Union Member States cannot consider the nationals of other member states to be foreigners. Lead case: Piermont v. France 314 Eur. Ct. H.R. (Ser. A) (1995). Statute; rule; constitution: Article 16 ECHR/Article 10

stem: A company would like to appoint a director. When discussing terms of the contract, the director requests that his contract guarantees employment for at least five years. The company are reluctant to guarantee employment and seek further advice.
ask: Which of the following best describe the regulations regarding guaranteed employment?

options.en: Directors' service contracts cannot guarantee employment for more than two • years, unless a resolution of the members of the company approves a longer period
Directors' service contracts cannot guarantee employment for more than twelve months, unless a resolution of the members of the company approves a longer period
Directors' service contracts cannot guarantee employment at all
Directors' service contracts can guarantee employment at the discretion of the contracting parties without any requirement for shareholder approval
Directors' service contracts can guarantee employment for up to five years, unless a resolution of the members of the company approves a longer period

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Section 188 of the Companies Act 2006 only allows service contracts to guarantee employment for a maximum of two years, unless a resolution of the members of the company approves a longer period.

stem: A woman is a property developer who owns a large unregistered plot of land. She plans to build a large block of leasehold apartments and advertises the apartments to be sold "off plan" so that she can fund the build using the deposit monies. A man wishes to buy one of the apartments but wants to make sure that his interest is protected until they are constructed and the woman can grant him the lease.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man should protect his interest using a caution against first registration
The man should protect his interest using a unilateral notice
The man should protect his interest as a Land Charge
The man should protect his interest using a Restriction
The man should protect his interest using an agreed notice

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Until the lease is granted, the man has the benefit of a contract to create the lease, which is an estate contract. This is protected by way of a Class C(iv) Land Charge registered against the woman.

stem: "No one should be in any doubt" said the Prime Minister (PM), "prisoners are not getting the vote under this government." The PM was speaking after a judgment by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) imposed obligations on the United Kingdom (UK) to expedite legislative proposals to amend the proscription of prisoners voting in general elections in a manner which is compliant with the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention), and further required the UK to enact the required legislation in order to implement the ECtHR's judgment. The Lord Chancellor seeks advice.
ask: Which option best advises the Lord Chancellor?

options.en: ECtHR's judgments are binding on national courts and are binding on the Member States affected
ECtHR's judgments are not binding on national courts, but are binding on the Member States affected
ECtHR's judgments are neither binding on national courts, nor are they binding on the Member States affected
ECtHR's judgments are binding on national courts, but are not binding on the Member States affected
An ECtHR judgment is binding in so far it forms part of the national law of a contracting Member State, and does not require implementing legislation

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is the best option. ECtHR's judgments are not binding on national courts, but are binding on the Member States affected. While the ECtHR's judgments are not binding on domestic or national courts, they are binding on national governments. By Article 13 of the Convention, the Member States agree to provide an effective remedy in their courts for violations of the Convention. By Article 46 of the Convention, contracting Member States agree to 'abide by the final judgment of the Court in any case to which they are parties. The obligation on contracting Member States to abide by judgments of the ECtHR has always been interpreted as an obligation to produce a specific result per se: "...the -g- ation an obligation to produce a specific result per se: "...the Court's judgment leaves to the State the choice of the means to be used in its domestic legal system to give effect to the obligation under Article 53..." (Belilos v. Switzerland judgment of 29 April 1988, Series A No. 132, para. 78). Further, the ECtHR's judgments have binding authority for the parties, namely, they are binding and definitive; the "sole object" of their definitive character "...is to make the Court's judgments not subject to any appeal to another authority..." (Ringeisen v. Austria judgments of 22 June 1972 (Article 50), para. 17, and of 23 June 1973, para. 13). The only other options for the UK government would be to prevaricate over the

stem: A trustee of a discretionary family trust has, for some time, received bribes from one of the beneficiaries in return for exercising discretionary powers of maintenance and advancement in that beneficiary's favour. She has finally saved up enough money to buy a beautiful seafront cottage in the countryside, where she retires. Five years later, the other beneficiaries discover what the trustee has been doing. The property has increased in value.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The full value of the property is held on resulting trust for the beneficiaries of the trust
The full value of the property is held on constructive trust for the beneficiaries of the trust
The increase in value of the property is held on resulting trust for the beneficiaries of the trust
The increase in value of the property is held on constructive trust for the beneficiaries of the trust
The trustee is the only one legally and beneficially entitled to the property

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The trustee has made a profit from an unlawful act, therefore all of the profits of that act will be held on constructive trust for the beneficiaries of the original trust. The unlawful act was that of accepting the bribes. As the property has been acquired wholly out of the profits of the unlawful act, the entire property, including the increase in value, is held on trust for the original beneficiaries.

stem: A husband and wife agreed to kill a man who had allegedly sexually abused the wife when she was a child. The husband persuaded his sister to help them lure the man to a wood, where the husband and wife would be waiting to attack and torture the man to death. However, the sister's car broke down on the day of the plot, so the plan was abandoned.
ask: Which of the following best states the criminal liability of the parties, if any?

options.en: Neither the husband nor wife may be charged with conspiracy to murder, but the sister may be
The sister and the wife may be charged with conspiracy to murder
The husband and wife may be charged with conspiracy to murder
The husband, wife and sister may be charged with conspiracy to murder
Neither the husband, wife nor sister may be charged with conspiracy to murder

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is the best answer. Although Section 2(2)(a) of the Criminal Law Act 1977 provides that a person is not guilty of a statutory conspiracy: "...if the only other person... with whom he agrees [is] (both initially and at all times during the currency of the agreement)... his spouse or, this does not apply if there is a third- civil partner..." party to the agreement. Since the husband's sister is a third-party, the married couple can in this case be held liable for the offence of conspiracy. Lead Case: Lovick [1993] Criminal Law Review 890. Statute; rule; constitution: 5. 2(2)(a) Criminal Law Act 1977.

stem: A purchaser in good faith bought a stolen car. The vendor (seller) had carried out improvements to the car before he sold it. The purchaser is being sued in conversion by the car's true owner.
ask: Which option best advises the parties?

options.en: sued in conversion by the true owner, allowance is made for improvements to the extent to which the value of the goods is attributable to it
If a person in good faith purchases a stolen car from the improver and is then sued in conversion by the true owner, damages are not available due to the principle of caveat emptor

If a person purchases a stolen car from the improver and is then sued in conversion by the true owner, the purchaser is entitled to compensation only if separate components and accessories which may have been added to the vehicle, are capable of being separately identified

If a person in good faith purchases a stolen car from the improver and is then sued in conversion by the true owner, no allowance will be made for improvements to the extent to which the value of the goods is attributable to it, if use has been made of the car in the intervening period

If a person in good faith purchases a stolen car from the improver and is then sued in conversion by the true owner, no allowance will be made for improvements to the extent to which the value of the goods is attributable to it, if the car has already passed to a third-party

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is the best option. Section 6(1) of the Torts (Interference with Goods) Act 1977 (the Act) provides that an allowance shall be made for improvements made to a vehicle owned by another to the extent to which the value of the goods is attributable to it. Where the true owner seeks an order for delivery up of the goods under Section 3(2) of the Act the court has discretion to require, as a condition for delivery up, that allowance is made to the innocent purchaser. The Act only applies where the improver acts in the honest belief that he had good title to the goods and it has no application where the true owner has reacquired the goods without the aid of the court.

stem: A buyer negotiated with a seller for the sale of a chain of hairdressers, in the course of which the seller made exaggerated statements about the business' earning capacity. However, the buyer commissioned their own audit, which in turn verified the seller's findings. In fact, the chain of hairdressers turned out to be worth significantly less than the seller had actually represented.
ask: Which of the following statements best describe the elements required for a false statement to induce a party to enter into a contract?

options.en: The requirements for a false statement to induce a party to enter into a contract • are that the misrepresentation was made intentionally and that it was relied upon
The requirements for a false statement to induce a party to enter into a contract are that the misrepresentation was made recklessly and that it was relied upon
The requirements for a false statement to induce a party to enter into a contract • are that the misrepresentation was either fraudulent or negligent and that it was relied upon
The requirements for a false statement to induce a party to enter into a contract are that the misrepresentation was material and that it was relied upon
The requirements for a false statement to induce a party to enter into a contract • are that the misrepresentation was made either recklessly or intentionally and that it was relied upon

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The false statement must have induced the representee to enter into the contract. The requirements here are that the misrepresentation must be material or that it must have been relied on. Lead case: Attwood v Small (1838),

stem: Your client and some friends decide to arrange a public procession. They notify the police accordingly and are angry when the police impose conditions on the procession. Your client feels their human rights are being infringed. Advise your client whether the police
ask: Advise your client whether the police can impose any conditions on the procession.

options.en: The police have no rights to impose conditions on public processions or assemblies
The police can only impose rights on assemblies but not on public processions
The police do have the right to impose some conditions on public processions for any reason they see fit

The police do have the right to impose some conditions on public processions but only if it is to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community
The police can either ban or allow a public procession but they cannot impose conditions on it

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. In order to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community, the police do have the right to impose some conditions on public processions.

stem: A judge observed in a case that it is not his function to make new law, only to decide cases in accordance with the law as it exists.
ask: In practice, he stated, this means that inferior courts are bound to apply the legal principles set down by the superior courts Which of the following statements best describes the doctrine that lies at the heart of all common law systems?

options.en: The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur lies at the heart of all common law systems
The doctrine of ratio decidendi lies at the heart of all common law systems
The doctrine of obiter dictum lies at the heart of all common law systems
The doctrine of stare decisis lies at the heart of all common law systems
The doctrine of ejusdem generis lies at the heart of all common law systems

explanation.en: D is correct. Stare decisis is the principle that similar cases should be decided according to consistent, principled rules, in order that similar results will be reached, and lies at the heart of all common law systems.

stem: A man owns a shop and is considering whether or not to register for VAT. He believes the choice is up to him but his friend advises him that he may be forced to register for VAT if his turnover is high enough.
ask: Which of the following best describe the current legal position?

options.en: There is no figure at which it becomes essential to register for VAT
Once a business has taxable supplies of at least £25,000 per year it must register for VAT
Once a business has taxable supplies of at least £53,000 per year it must register for VAT
Once a business has taxable supplies of at least £81,000 per year it must register for VAT
Once a business has taxable supplies of at least £100,000 per year it must register for VAT

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Although a business with smaller taxable supplies can opt to register for VAT, once a business has taxable supplies of at least £81,000 per year it becomes necessary to register for VAT. The threshold for necessary registration is subject to change and is normally announced in the Budget each year.

stem: You act for the executors of the estate of a deceased woman. The estate consists of various assets including a house; investment trusts; building society accounts; an endowment life policy and an ISA, where the money is invested in unit trusts. You are not authorised by the FCA.
ask: Which of the following best represents whether you should appoint an authorized third party (ATP)?

options.en: You always need to appoint an ATP when giving probate advice, as financial advice will not come under the necessary exception
You never need to appoint an ATP when giving probate advice.
When giving probate advice, investment advice always comes under the necessary exception
When giving probate advice, financial advice never comes under the necessary exception
When giving financial advice in the context of probate advice, it may come under the necessary exception, but otherwise the client should be referred to an ATP

explanation.en: E is the best answer. The house and building society accounts are not investments. The investment trusts, endowment policy and unit trusts in the ISA (as opposed to a mini-cash ISA) are investments. In the course of administering the estate, the executors will be likely to have to dispose of the assets, and you may well be arranging, and possibly advising, before such disposal. If the arranging and/or advising can be reasonably regarded as being a necessary part of the other services being provided (which is very likely where all the assets need to be sold), then no regulated activity will be carried out (Article 67 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 ("RAO") - 'Activities carried on in the course of a profession or non-investment business'). Otherwise, it seems that the firm would be carrying out a regulated activity - unless it used an ATP to advise and arrange the disposal (Article 29 RAO). A is not correct. Financial advice could come under the necessarv exception and so an ATP is not alwavs necessary exception and so an ATP is not always needed. In any event, the firm could also obtain authorisation. B is not correct. There is no precise definition of when financial advice is necessary for the purpose of the exception; it is safer to appoint an ATP. come under the necessary exception, such as when it does not concern one or more of the instruments listed to appoint an ATP.

stem: Two trustees are responsible for a will trust, which provides that the trust funds shall be held on trust until the youngest beneficiary attains the age of 21, with the trustees having a power to pay the income generated to the beneficiaries at their discretion. The trust does not make provision as to what is to happen to the capital after the youngest beneficiary attains the age of 21, but gives the trustees a general power of appointment.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The trustees hold the trust property on a resulting trust for the settlor's estate
The trustees hold the trust property on a constructive trust for the settlor's estate
The trustees could distribute the trust property to the beneficiaries
The trustees must pay the trust property into court
The trustees must form a protective trust

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. A power of appointment gives the trustees the ability to pay capital assets from the trust to a person or persons of their choosing. Depending upon the terms of the power, this could either be a general power (giving them a general discretion to pay as they see fit) or else a special power (which allows the discretion to pay within a class of beneficiaries).

stem: BankCo has the benefit of a first-ranking charge by way of legal mortgage to secure a loan facility it has offered to the mortgagor. The facility allows the mortgagor to draw down funds from BankCo up to a maximum of £500,000. BankCo has entered a notice on the register in accordance with section 49 Land Registration Act 2002 ('tacking"). The mortgagor applies for a second mortgage with MortgageCo and, at the time of this advance, BankCo has advanced £300,000 on its facility.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position if BankCo were to make further?

options.en: Any further advances by BankCo will rank in priority after the loan from MortgageCo no matter what
Any further advances by BankCo will automatically rank in priority ahead of the loan from MortgageCo no matter what
Any further advances by BankCo up to a total of £300,000 will automatically rank in priority ahead of the loan from MortgageCo
Any further advances by BankCo will rank in priority after the loan from MortgageCo unless BankCo obtains a deed of postponement
Any further advances by BankCo over £200,000 will rank in priority after the loan from MortgageCo unless BankCo obtains a deed of postponement

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The notice on the register automatically protects priority for the first £500,000 that BankCo advances in accordance with section 49 Land Registration Act 2002. The fact pattern states that BankCo has already advanced £300,000 on its facility, therefore it could further advance up to £200,000, i.e., a total limit of £500,000. If BankCo wises to make further advances over this limit, these will rank after the loan from MortgageCo unless BankCo can obtain a deed of postponement from MortgageCo.

stem: Two directors are also majority shareholders in a private limited company. The company also has two minority shareholders. Rather than pay dividends, the two directors have decided to award themselves bonuses instead. The minority shareholders are unhappy with this and claim that this decision is unfair. They want to know if there is any action they can take against the decision.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: The directors are within their rights in choosing to pay themselves a bonus and not pay dividends
Although it is unfair, there is no legal action available to the minority shareholders
The minority shareholders can petition the court that the decision is unfairly prejudicial to their interests
The minority shareholders will only be able to make a claim once the company is sold or wound up
Whether the minority shareholders can make a claim depends on the amount of shares they hold and the contents of the shareholders' agreement

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Under s994 of the Companies Act 2006, shareholders of a company can make petition the court if they feel that the affairs of the company have been conducted in a way that is 'unfairly prejudicial' to their interests. If the court is satisfied by the petition, it can make an order regarding the future conduct of the company, or an alternative order which will remove the unfair prejudice.

stem: A witness was murdered by a defendant prior to giving evidence at trial. In a subsequent compensation claim, the judge established that the police were under a duty to take preventive measures in relation to a witness and that the police had breached that duty when they failed to react to signs of danger to the witness. The judge went on to establish a causal connection between that breach and the loss claimed.
ask: The judge also found that the police had acted incompatibly with the victim's right to life under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Which of the following statements best states the test that the judge was entitled to rely on when awarding damages for breach of the victim's Convention rights?

options.en: The judge was entitled to rely on the 'subjective intention test' when awarding damages for breach of the victim's Convention rights
The judge was entitled to rely on the 'incremental test' when awarding damages for breach of the victim's Convention r
The judge was entitled to rely on the 'reasonable foreseeability test' when awarding damages for breach of the victim's Convention rights
The judge was entitled to rely on the 'but-for test' when awarding damages for breach of the victim's Convention rights
The judge was entitled to rely on the 'close connection test ' when awarding damages for breach of the victim's Convention rights

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Section 8 Human Rights Act 1998 obliges domestic courts to look to the approach of the ECtHR to the application of Article 41, which is the approach of a test that requires the court to consider what would have happened 'but for' the violation. Lead case: Van Colle v Chief Constable of the Hertfordshire Police [2007]. Statute; rule; constitution: S. 8 HRA 1998.

stem: A consumer bought faulty fireworks from a supplier. The consumer wants to return them to the producer. When he approached the supplier, however, he was told that the producer is somewhere in China and cannot be traced.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the liability, if any, of suppliers for the purposes of the Consumer Protection Act 1987 (CPA)?

options.en: The supplier of goods is jointly liable with the producer for any damage under the CPA
If the producer cannot be identified, then there is no claim against a mere supplier of goods under the CPA
The supplier of goods is exclusively liable for any damage under the CPA
If the producer cannot be identified, then, under the CPA any person who supplied the goods may be liable for any damage the goods cause
Joint and several liability arises automatically for any damage under the CPA, which includes the producer and the supplier of the goods

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. If the producer cannot be identified, then any person who supplied the goods may be liable for any damage the goods cause. Statute; rule; constitution: s. 2(3) Consumer Protection Act 1987.

stem: Not all terms within a contract are of equal importance. In a contract for the provision of a service, for example, terms specifying the dates on which the service is to be provided and the date for payment will be likely to be more important than, for example, a term requiring the supplier of the service to submit an annual account of the work done.
ask: In light of the previous statement, which of the following statements best describes an innominate term?

options.en: An innominate term is where the parties have communicated to one another that a particular form of words is to be a part of the contract between them
An innominate term is where the effect of any breach depends on the seriousness of the consequences of the breach
An innominate term is where the court considers that the parties intended it to apply and did not mention a particular term simply because its existence would have been taken for granted
An innominate term is where the term does not go to the root of the contract and will probably only entitle the other party to claim damages
An innominate term is where a term is so obvious that it 'goes without saying'

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. An innominate term is one whereby the consequences of a breach of that term may determine whether the party not in breach has a right to bring the contract to an end. Lead case: Hong Kong Fir Shipping Co v Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha Ltd [1962] 2 QB 26. - i ser ve dugo so be rever me Contract

stem: There were proposals to reform the prerogative powers of the Sovereign. One of these was set out in detailed proposals in a White Paper and draft bill in March 2008 titled "The Governance of Britain - Constitutional Renewal".
ask: The draft bill addressed some areas of the prerogative, including managing the civil service on a statutory Which of the following statements best describes the role of a White Paper?

options.en: The primary function of a White Paper is to serve as a consultative government report of a proposal without any commitment to action
The primary function of a White Paper is to set out the government's official statement of guidance and good practice
The primary function of a White Paper is to set out the government's proposals for legislation on a particular subject
The primary function of a White Paper is to enforce amendments to clauses in parliamentary bills on a particular issue
The primary function of a White Paper is to set out the timetable for completion of different stages of a bill's progress through the House of Commons

explanation.en: . The draft bill addressed You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. White papers are documents produced by the government setting out details of future policy on a particular subject. A White Paper will often be the basis for a bill to be put before Parliament. The White Paper allows the government an opportunity to gather feedback before it formally presents the policies as a Bill.

stem: Your trainee is new to England and is not sure of the powers of the devolved legislatures in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
ask: What is the extent of the powers of the Scottish Parliament, the National Assembly for Wales and the Northern Ireland Assembly?

options.en: Northern Ireland Assembly can make legislation within its areas of legislative competence and amend Westminster Acts of Parliament so far as they relate to Northern Ireland
The Scottish Parliament, National Assembly for Wales and Northern Ireland Assembly all have unfettered legislative competence
None of the Scottish Parliament, National Assembly for Wales or Northern Ireland Assembly has any legislative competence

The Scottish Parliament has legislative competence over all matters that are not explicitly reserved to the Westminster Parliament and amend Westminster Acts of Parliament so far as they relate to Scotland; the National Assembly for Wales • has can pass primary legislation in 20 legislated subject areas; and the Northern Ireland Assembly can make legislation within its areas of legislative competence but no power to amend Westminster Acts of Parliament so far as they relate to Northern Ireland

All three legislatures may pass legislation subject to restrictions, but royal assent must be given to any and all laws passed by the National Assembly for Wales and the Northern Ireland assembly, but not the Scottish Parliament

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is A. The Scottish Parliament has legislative competence over all matters that are not explicitly reserved to the Westminster Parliament; the National Assembly for Wales has can pass primary legislation in 20 legislated subject areas; and the Northern Ireland Assembly can make legislation within its areas of legislative competence and amend Westminster Acts of Parliament so far as they relate to Northern Ireland.

stem: A woman has been arrested for allegedly stealing a dress from a ladies' fashion store. You are called to the police station to advise her prior to police interview. She is unsure of the basic elements of theft and asks for an explanation.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains the offence of theft?

options.en: A person is guilty of theft if she dishonestly, with a view to gain, appropriates property, belonging to another with the intention of depriving the other of it
A person is guilty of theft if she appropriates property, for her own benefit, • belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it
A person is guilty of theft if she dishonestly appropriates property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it
A person is guilty of theft if she dishonestly makes a false representation and intends to make a gain for herself or another, with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it
A person is guilty of theft if she dishonestly handles property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The Theft Act 1968 has established that a person will be guilty of theft if they 'dishonestly appropriate property with the intention of permanently depriving the owner of it'. The important issue here is that the intention to deprive permanently is present, not that the owner is actually permanently deprived. For example, if one goes to a restaurant and, by mistake, takes another's scarf instead of one's own, one has physically deprived the other of the use of the property, but the mistake prevents one from forming the mens rea (i.e., because the belief is that one is the owner; there is no dishonesty nor intention to deprive the "owner" of it), so no crime has been committed at this point.

stem: A woman executes a will in which she leaves £100,000 (which is part of her estate) to be distributed as her trustees see fit amongst members of the book club of which she is a member, who are living within London at the time of her death. By the time the woman dies, there are no members of her book club living in London.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The £100,000 will fall into the woman's residuary estate and be distributed according to her will
The £100,000 will be applied cy-près by the court
The £100,000 will be distributed in accordance with the Intestacy Rules
The £100,000 will be held on constructive trust by the trustees of the woman's
The £100,000 will be held on a resulting trust by the trustees

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Where a testamentary trust is void for uncertainty, a partial intestacy will occur. The intended trust property will be dealt with in accordance with the Intestacy Rules (as though it had not been the subject of a will) but the remainder of the deceased's estate subject to a valid will trust will pass according to the will. Option B is incorrect as the funds will be distributed to the members of the club, not to the club itself. Therefore the cy-près will not be applied by the court in this case.

stem: A partner at a firm with twenty four partners doesn't think they are required to display the names of all partners on their partnership documentation.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: Irrespective of the number of partners at a firm, the names of all partners must be on partnership documentation, displayed at each place of business and given to anyone who asks
Irrespective of the number of partners at a firm, the names of all partners must be on partnership documentation
If the firm has over twenty partners, names need not be on partnership • documentation, but the documentation must state that this information is available on request
If the firm has over twenty five partners, names need not be on partnership documentation, but the documentation must state that this information is available on request
Irrespective of the number of partners at a firm, the names of at least five partners must be on partnership documentation

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. If the firm has over twenty partners the firm does not have to list them on all partnership documentation (letterheads etc.), but it must be made clear that this information is available. Source: Business Names Act 1985 s4.

stem: A woman is the freehold owner of 123 The Street. She grants a lease by parol to a man for twelve months at a market rent. The arrangement is recorded in writing, but does not contain any landlord's covenants. The woman later converts adjacent land, which she also owns, into a chemical processing plant, which produces noxious fumes which severely affect the man's enjoyment of the land.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman is in breach of an implied covenant for quiet enjoyment
The woman is in breach of an express covenant for quiet enjoyment
The woman is in breach of an implied covenant not to derogate from grant
The woman is in breach of an express covenant not to derogate from grant
As no written agreement was entered into in respect of landlord's covenants, the woman has not given the man any covenants that can be breached

explanation.en: womanis You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Even though a written agreement has been entered into which is silent on the issue of landlord's covenants, the law still implies a covenant not to derogate from grant, which means that the landlord will not do any act on their own land which renders the property unfit for the use as whatever purposes the lease was granted for.

stem: A decision at the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) is in direct contradiction to existing Dutch government policy. The Dutch government is expecting a clash of international law and domestic law in the domestic courts as a result of the ECtHR decision.
ask: Dutch law is based on the so-called monist approach to international Which of the following best states how international law is implemented pursuant to the monist theory?

options.en: Pursuant to the monist theory, international law forms part of the law of the land, without any need for internal implementation
Pursuant to the monist theory, international conventions require that treaty norms be implemented through legislation in order to have legal effect on domestic law
Pursuant to the monist theory, international law is only applicable domestically if there has been some kind of incorporation into the domestic legal system
Pursuant to the monist theory, international law and domestic law are considered separate
Pursuant to the monist theory, domestic courts could not adjudicate on rights conferred by international treaties

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Pursuant to the monist theory, international law forms part of the law of the land, without any need of internal implementation. The monist theory treats international law and domestic law as forming a unity. The rules of international law automatically form part of domestic law. Much of Europe shares a firmly entrenched monist tradition. The situation is different in the UK.

stem: You represent a client who is seeking to minimise their Inheritance Tax Liability and to minimise taxation during his retirement. You provide generic advice about pension policies and life insurance.
ask: Which introduction, if any, can you make if you are not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority?

options.en: You can introduce the client to either an independent financial adviser or a tied agent
You can only introduce the client to a tied agent
You may introduce the client to any provider for any product, regardless of the client's interests
You can only introduce the client to an independent financial adviser
You cannot make any introductions and the client must take financial advice themselves

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is A. You can introduce the client to either an independent financial adviser or a tied agent. B, D and E are incorrect. C is not the best answer. Whenever you recommend that a client uses a particular person or business, your recommendation must be is in the best interests of the client and does not compromise your independence; the client must be fully informed of any financial or other interest which you have in referring the client to another person or business; and the client must be in a position to make informed decisions about how to pursue their matter.

stem: A man applied for a job as a solicitor. When filling out the application form, he omitted to mention that he had a County Court Judgement against him for a dishonoured telephone bill.
ask: Which of the following best states the man's criminal liability, if any, under the Fraud?

options.en: The man cannot be charged with fraud by false representation under the Fraud Act 2006, because he made no gain
The man may be charged with fraud by false representation and by failing to disclose information under the Fraud Act 2006
The man may be charged with fraud by abuse of position under the Fraud Act
The man may only be charged with fraud by false representation under the Fraud Act 2006
The man may only be charged with fraud by failing to disclose information under the Fraud Act 2006

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. A false representation for the purposes of the Fraud Act 2006 can be by omission. In this scenario, the man has represented himself as financially scrupulous when the opposite is true. Further he has also failed to disclose this information. The offence of fraud by failure to disclose is complete when a person "dishonestly fails to disclose to another person information which he is under a legal duty to disclose and he intends thereby to make a gain for himself or cause a loss, or risk of loss, to another." This offence requires the Crown to, first of all, establish that the Defendant was under a duty to make some kind of disclosure. The Crown will try to establish this by evidence of a relationship the defendant and the alleged victim, e.g. a legal duty to disclose can arise as a result of a contract between two parties or because of the existence of a particular type of professional relationship between them, such as a solicitor/client or solicitor/regulator relationship. The intention behind the non-disclosure must be to make a gain or cause loss, or risk of loss, to another. Thus this offence is complete as soon as the defendant fails to disclose information that he was under a legal duty to disclose, together with the requisite dishonest intent. It does not matter whether or not any one is deceived, or whether any property is actually gained or lost.

stem: Land subsidence caused a large mound on the defendant's land to collapse slowly onto the claimant's property. The claimant had warned the defendant, but the defendant refused to act.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes what a claimant must show to succeed in a nuisance action?

options.en: To succeed in a nuisance action, a claimant must show that the defendant's use of the land was unreasonable
To succeed in a nuisance action, a claimant must show that the defendant was at fault
To succeed in a nuisance action, a claimant must show that the defendant was at fault by failing to exercise reasonable care and skill
To succeed in a nuisance action, a claimant must show that there was a sufficient relationship of proximity between the parties
To succeed in a nuisance action, a claimant must show that there was a sufficient relationship of proximity such that the nuisance caused was in the reasonable contemplation of the defendant

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. To succeed in a nuisance action, a claimant must show that the defendant's use of the land was unreasonable.

stem: A person dies in July 2015. They gave their spouse £50,000, in 2012, and their child £70,000, in 2013. The estate, which is bequeathed to the child, is valued at £326,000. Assumptions (if applicable): Nil rate threshold is £325,000 IHT rate = 40% of amount over nil rate band.
ask: What is the Inheritance Tax (IHT) liability?

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is C. £26,000. The 2012 transfer is exempt as a transfer to a spouse, and does not, therefore, affect the cumulative total. The 2013 transfer, however, was a potentially exempt transfer (PET), which has now become chargeable. Assuming the deceased has not utilised the annual exemptions for the last and current tax year, the value transferred, in 2013, was: £70,000 - £6,000 = £64,000. IHT is not charged on the nil rate band, i.e. the first £325,000. The £64,000 transfer, which is now chargeable as a PET, must be deducted from this sum. £261,000 of the nil rate band remains (£325,000 - £64,000).

stem: A vintner in London ordered several hundred casks of wine from Chile. The ship carrying the wine sank in shallow water as it entered the river Thames after it had crossed the Atlantic Ocean. The vessel was raised and the cargo salvaged, but on arrival at the port of discharge, the wine, while appearing good, was found to be contaminated with salt water.
ask: Which of the following statements best advises whether the contract is frustrated?

options.en: The contract was frustrated, because total destruction of the goods is not necessary; mere destruction of the merchantable quality of the goods is sufficient
The contract was not frustrated, since it is enough that on arrival the wine existed in species as wine, even if it was not merchantable
The wine might have deteriorated, but it was still merchantable as wine, so the contract was not frustrated
Obligations are not discharged by a frustrating event, and a party who fails to perform as a result of such an event would still be in breach of contract
The contract was not frustrated, because total destruction of the goods is necessary; mere destruction of the merchantable quality of the goods is insufficient

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The contract was frustrated, because total destruction of the goods is not necessary; mere destruction of the merchantable quality of the goods is sufficient. Lead case: Asfar v Blundell [1896] 1 QB 123..o.... act VI CUST

stem: A husband returns home from after drinking a few pints in the pub to find his wife in bed with a younger man, who escapes by jumping through the bedroom window. His wife goes to take a shower, but the husband goes to the kitchen, returns with a bread knife and stabs her to death. Realising what he has done, he swallows sleeping pills, in a suicide attempt, but is arrested for murder when he later awakes in hospital.
ask: With regard to the Coroners and Justice Act 2009, which of the following statements best describes the most appropriate defence, if any, available to the husband under these circumstances?

options.en: The most appropriate defence available to the husband under these circumstances is intoxication
The most appropriate defence available to the husband under these circumstances is provocation
The most appropriate defence available to the husband under these circumstances is diminished responsibility
The most appropriate defence available to the husband under these circumstances is 'a thing or things done or said'
There is no defence available to the husband under these circumstances for murder

explanation.en: E is correct. A is wrong because intoxication, which in this case is voluntary, is not a complete defence in law, only a denial of mens rea. B is wrong because the common law defence of provocation was abolished by the Coroners and Justice Act 2009. C is the wrong answer because it is unlikely that the husband would fit the criteria for diminished responsibility. amount to a qualifying trigger. Therefore "a thing or things done or said" does not include sexual infidelity. Statute; rule; constitution: 5.55 (6) (c) Coroners and Justice Act 2009.

stem: The traditional "sufficient interest" test has been eroded in recent years. Whether a claimant has established a "sufficient interest" will depend on whether the court views him as a 'public spirited person', rather than a 'meddlesome busybody'.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the "sufficient interest" test in judicial review proceedings?

options.en: The traditional "sufficient interest" test asserts that claimants have to be personally affected by a private decision in order to challenge it
The traditional "sufficient interest" test asserts that claimants have to be personally affected by a public decision in order to challenge it
The traditional "sufficient interest" test asserts that claimants have to be publicly affected by a private decision in order to challenge it
The traditional "sufficient interest" test asserts that claimants have to be publicly affected by a public decision in order to challenge it
The traditional "sufficient interest" test asserts that claimants must not be personally affected by a public decision in order to challenge it

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The traditional "sufficient interest" test asserts that claimants have to be personally affected by a public decision in order to challenge it. Under the Civil Procedure Rules, an application for judicial review will only be admissible if permission for judicial review is obtained from the High Court, which has supervisory jurisdiction over public authorities and tribunals. Permission may be refused if the applicant does not have sufficient interest in a matter to which the application relates. This requirement is known as the requirement of locus standi, or standing. The High Court will not necessarily refuse permission if the above condition is in doubt. It may, at its discretion, -3 - -••5 of sufficient interest can also lead to the court refusing to grant a remedy after it had considered the case on its merits. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 31(3) Supreme court Act 1981. -3

ask: In registered land, where would the burden of a legal easement be recorded?

options.en: The Property Register of the registered title
The Proprietorship Register of the registered title
The Charges Register of the registered title
The title deeds
The Land Charges Register

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. A legal easement affecting a registered title is recorded in the Charges Register of that title.

stem: The defendant negligently ran over a pedestrian. The pedestrian filed a claim in trespass to the person, because the claim in negligence was time-barred.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the general principle behind trespass to the person?

options.en: The general principle is that a trespass to the person must be a direct and • careless act, whereas if it was indirect or unintentional, the tort of negligence is more appropriate
The general principle is that a trespass to the person must be a direct and • negligent act, whereas if it was indirect or unintentional, the tort of negligence is more appropriate
The general principle is that a trespass to the person must be a direct and • reckless act, whereas if it was indirect or unintentional, the tort of negligence is more appropriate
The general principle is that a trespass to the person must be a direct act or an omission, whereas if it was indirect or unintentional, the tort of negligence is more appropriate
The general principle is that a trespass to the person must be a direct and intentional act, whereas if it was indirect or unintentional, the tort of negligence is more appropriate

explanation.en: E is correct. The general principle is that a trespass to the person must be a direct and intentional act, with indirect or unintentional acts falling under the tort of negligence. Lead case: Letang v Cooper [1964].

stem: A brother and sister hold 50% each of the issued shares of a private limited company. The brother has appointed a woman to act as a director of the company and the sister has appointed a man as to act as a director. The directors consider a proposal to begin investing in a controversial cosmetic product which is widely known to be tested on animals. Despite the controversy, the directors are advised by their consultants that this would present a very good investment, with the potential to provide a very high return for the company. The sister objects to animal testing on a moral level and instructs the man she appointed as a director to reject the proposal when it is to be considered by the board of directors.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man is under a duty to act as directed by his appointing shareholder and there is no scope for him to act otherwise
The man is under a duty to act as directed by his appointing shareholder except • where he is authorised to act otherwise by a unanimous resolution of the board of directors
The man has a discretion to ether follow the directions of his appointing shareholder or follow the decision of the other directors
The man is under a duty to exercise independent judgment when making all • decisions except where this directly conflicts with the interests of his appointing shareholder
The man is always under a duty to exercise independent judgment when making all decisions regardless of the interests of his appointing shareholder

explanation.en: : "-wing The correct answer is E. A director is under a duty to exercise independent judgment when performing their functions and must always base their decisions on their overriding duty to act in the best interests of the company. Whilst a director will naturally seek to protect the interests of those shareholders who support their appointment, they are only permitted to do this insofar as this does not conflict with their duty to the company. Source: Companies Act 2006 s173.

stem: Two women and a man are trustees of a private family trust. They take the professional advice of an investment manager, and without considering the advice properly, advise him to proceed with their own investment proposal. The trust loses a significant amount of money and the trust manager tells the beneficiaries that he advised the trustees against investing in the way that they did, but they failed to follow his advice. The two women have no personal assets, but the man is very wealthy and has sufficient assets to meet the liabilities of the trust.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The three trustees are each only liable to the beneficiaries of the trust for one third of its losses
The beneficiaries can recover all of the trust's losses from the man, who has no recourse against the two women
The beneficiaries can recover all of the trust's losses from the man, but he will have a right of contribution from the two women
The beneficiaries can only recover the total amount of the trust's losses from all three trustees jointly
The beneficiaries have no right to recover all of the trust's losses from the man alone

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Trustees are jointly and severally liable to the beneficiaries for losses arising from breach of trust. This means that the beneficiaries can pursue any of the trustees individually for the whole of the loss according to each of the trustees' means. The trustees would then have a right of contribution from each other under the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978.

stem: An employee takes a laptop home with her, which belongs to her employer. The employee's intention is to permanently deprive her employer of the laptop. The day after, she subsequently changes her mind and returns the laptop to her employer.
ask: Which option best states the employee's criminal liability, if any?

options.en: The employee has committed the offence of theft since a subsequent change of mind will not prevent the commission of the offence
The employee has committed the offence of theft since the moment she formed the intention to take the laptop home with her she became criminally liable

The employee has not committed the offence of theft since she appropriated the laptop believing that she would have her employer's consent if the employer knew of the appropriation and the circumstances of it
The employee has not committed the offence of theft since it appears that in the context of this case - she merely borrowed the laptop
The employee has not committed the offence of theft since she took reasonable steps in returning the laptop to her employer

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is the best option. A subsequent change of mind will not prevent the commission of the offence, even though the employee may not have the necessary mens rea at the outset. A defendant's mind need not remain unchanged throughout the incident. Option B is not correct because the employee's mens rea did not coincide with the actus reus of the offence.

stem: It is not always clear why vicarious liability is imposed on a party. It may be argued that a far more effective way to analyse and apply the concept of vicarious liability would be to identify and evaluate the purposes served by its implementation, then turn to the case law to see how far those purposes and implementation are adequately reflected in the current law.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the rationale behind the doctrine of?

options.en: The only rationale behind the doctrine of vicarious liability is that it is only right that the employer, who derives benefit from the service of his employee, should shoulder the burden as well
The only rationale behind the doctrine of vicarious liability is that the employer will have deeper pockets than the employee, and is therefore the most practical person to sue
The only rationale behind the doctrine of vicarious liability is that the employer owes a duty of common humanity

The rationale behind the doctrine of vicarious liability is that it is only right that the employer, who derives benefit from the service of his employee, should shoulder the burden as well, and that the employer will have deeper pockets than the employee and is therefore the most practical person to sue

The rationale behind the doctrine of vicarious liability is that it is only right that the employer, who derives benefit from the service of his employee, should shoulder the burdens as well; the employer will have deeper pockets than the employee and is therefore the most practical person to sue; and that the employer owes a duty of common humanity

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The advantages in suing the employer over his employee is that the employee will not generally have the funds available to meet the damages claim, nor will he have an insurance policy to meet the claim, whereas the employer will normally have the latter, if not the former (solvency). It is also argued that it is only right that the employer, who derives benefit from the service of his employee, should shoulder the burdens as well. Lead case: Morris v C W Martin & Sons Ltd [1966].

stem: You have been instructed to act for a client. He urgently needs to lease a house, as his current property was gutted by fire. Thereafter, you will be advising him on separate probate and income tax matters. Unfortunately, all the client's documentation was destroyed in the fire so he cannot yet verify his identity. Whilst he appreciates you will not be able to transfer funds or property before the completion of client due diligence, he asks you to commence work on the matter whilst he sources a replacement passport to verify his identity.
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed?

options.en: You must not act for the client until you have completed customer due diligence
You may act for the client and need not complete the customer due diligence immediately, as long as it is completed before the entire transaction concludes
You may act for the client but must complete the customer due diligence before any final agreements are signed or funds or property are transferred (i.e. as soon as possible)
You may forego customer due diligence entirely on the client due to the circumstances
You must conduct enhanced due diligence on the client due to his convenient position of having no documents to confirm his identity at this stage

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Normally, you must verify you client's identity (and that of any beneficial owner) before you establish a business relationship or carry out an occasional transaction. If you cannot complete the customer due diligence, you cannot act for a client (Regulation 11 MLR). However, Regulation 9(3) provides that verification may be completed during the establishment of a business relationship where it is necessary not to interrupt the normal course of business, and there is little risk of money laundering or terrorist financing. Here, not acting until customer due diligence is complete would clearly interrupt the normal course of business due to the urgency of the - *3 long as you complete verification as soon as possible after the initial contact, which will presumably be complete on sight of his replacement passport. **S-
